questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: praised
designed
resisted
funded
questions.rationale: The second sentence tells what the parents did about the decision: they kept their children home and sued the school board, and they won. Refusing to go along with a decision and fighting it in court is to have “resisted” it.
reasons: Parents who praised the decision would not have kept their children home and taken the board to court.
The text says the school board ordered the separate schoolhouse; nothing suggests the parents designed the arrangement they opposed.
Nothing indicates that the parents paid for the separate schoolhouse; they fought the decision in court.
questions.text: In 1931, when the school board in Lemon Grove, California, ordered Mexican American children to attend a separate two-room schoolhouse, their parents ______ the decision. They kept their children at home and took the board to court, winning what historians consider the first successful school desegregation lawsuit in the United States.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “industry” most nearly mean?
choices: Manufacturing
Erudition
Productivity
Diligence
questions.rationale: As used in the text, “industry” means diligence, or steady hard work. Nikoläiev’s table is buried in books, drawings, and maps, and he has been preparing “for many months” without a break for an examination he has already failed twice; “unremitting industry” describes that persistent effort.
reasons: Industry can mean the making of goods, as in a nation’s industry, but Nikoläiev is studying for an examination, not producing anything.

Erudition means deep learning, which the piles of books might suggest, but the text describes how hard Nikoläiev is working, not how much he knows; having failed the examination twice, he is still trying to master it.

Productivity is the amount a worker produces, a meaning tied to industry in its economic sense. The text says nothing about what Nikoläiev’s study has yielded; “unremitting” describes the constancy of his effort.
questions.text:
The following text is from a 1916 translation of Aleksandr Kuprin’s 1905 novel The Duel. Romashov, a young officer, has come to visit Nikoläiev, a fellow officer, and his wife.

Nikoläiev sat with his back to them at the table that was almost hidden by piles of books, drawings, and maps. Before the year was out he had to make another attempt to get admitted to the Staff College, and for many months he had been preparing with unremitting <u>industry</u> for this stiff examination in which he had already twice failed.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: recurrent
calamitous
acrimonious
quotidian
questions.rationale: “Calamitous” means disastrous. Burgess and Donaldson found that once railroads reached a district, local prices and mortality rates responded less to a shortfall of rain. A drought that no longer drove up prices and deaths as much was less of a disaster for the people there.
reasons: “Recurrent” means happening again and again. Railroads could not change how often rain fell short; the text says only that prices and mortality rates responded less to a shortfall, which concerns how harmful it was, not how often it happened.
“Acrimonious” means bitter and angry, as a quarrel can be. The text says nothing about disputes over rainfall shortfalls.
“Quotidian” means ordinary or everyday. The text says nothing about shortfalls becoming more or less ordinary; it describes how much they affected prices and mortality rates.
questions.text: In colonial India, agriculture depended on rainfall, and regional famines were commonplace. But as railroads reached more and more districts between 1861 and 1930, economists Robin Burgess and Dave Donaldson found, a rainfall shortfall in a district became less ______: local prices and mortality rates grew less responsive to it.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains the cause of the shrub’s inability to produce seeds, which is described in the previous sentence.
It presents a finding that, according to the following sentence, researchers have since called into question.
It describes the method that researchers used to date the fossil leaves mentioned in the following sentence.
It reports a finding that supports the view of the shrub’s population presented in the following sentence.
questions.rationale: The underlined sentence reports that all of the roughly 500 plants in the population are genetically identical. The following sentence says that researchers therefore treat the population as a single plant, possibly a very old one. The genetic finding is what supports that view, as choice D says.
reasons: The first sentence, not the underlined one, explains why the shrub cannot make seeds (it has three sets of chromosomes), and the previous sentence describes how it spreads.
The following sentence builds on the finding rather than questioning it.
The underlined sentence describes genetic tests of living plants; it says nothing about how the fossil leaves were dated.
questions.text: King’s holly (Lomatia tasmanica), a shrub native to the rainforests of southwestern Tasmania, possesses three sets of chromosomes instead of the usual two, which renders it incapable of producing seeds. It reproduces exclusively when a fallen branch takes root and develops into a new plant. <u>Genetic analyses of the approximately 500 plants in its best-known population have found them all to be identical.</u> Researchers consider that population a single organism, one that, judging from fossil leaves of the species dated to about 43,600 years ago, may be among the oldest living things on Earth.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the difficulty discussed in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that seasonal changes in a bear’s weight make photographs a less dependable basis for identification than genetic tagging
By noting that BearID distinguishes individual brown bears more accurately than genetic tagging does
By indicating that facial features recorded in photographs may offer a less costly way to tell individual brown bears apart
By recommending that researchers concentrate on bear populations in regions where photographs of known individuals already exist
questions.rationale: Text 1 says that brown bears are hard to tell apart in photographs, because they lack markings and their weight changes, so researchers rely on expensive genetic tagging. Clapham’s team built BearID, which identifies individual bears from their faces in photographs, and they suggest it could offer a cost-effective way to monitor populations. The author of Text 2 would therefore respond that facial features in photographs may offer a cheaper way to tell bears apart.
reasons: BearID identified bears from photographs taken across seasons with about 84 percent accuracy; Text 2 presents photographs as a workable alternative to genetic tagging, not a weaker one.
Text 2 gives BearID’s accuracy but never compares it with the accuracy of genetic tagging; its advantage is cost.
Text 2 mentions where the training images came from but recommends no geographic focus for future research.
questions.text:
Text 1

Many methods for monitoring wildlife populations depend on distinguishing one individual from another. Species with distinctive coat patterns can be told apart in photographs from camera traps, but brown bears lack consistent markings, and a bear’s appearance changes considerably as it gains and loses weight between seasons. Studies of brown bears have therefore relied heavily on genetic tagging, which identifies individuals from samples of their DNA but is expensive.

Text 2

Melanie Clapham and her collaborators have developed BearID, a deep-learning application that locates a bear’s face in a photograph, extracts its features, and compares them with those of known individuals. Tested on images of 132 brown bears from British Columbia and Alaska, it identified individuals with about 84 percent accuracy. Paired with camera traps, the researchers suggest, it could offer a cost-effective way to monitor populations.

questions.stem: According to the text, what was one difficulty faced by supporters of the free produce movement?
choices: Quakers in Philadelphia were unwilling to shop in stores that sold only goods made with free labor.
Goods made with free labor usually cost more than goods produced by enslaved people did.
Stores that sold goods made with free labor could not obtain cotton, so they sold only sugar and rice.
Supporters disagreed about whether the movement should avoid sugar as well as cotton.
questions.rationale: The text says that free-labor goods were usually more expensive than other goods, sometimes hard to find, and occasionally of poor quality. Choice B restates the first of these difficulties.
reasons: Philadelphia Quakers founded the Free Produce Society; the text gives no sign that they refused to shop at free-labor stores.
The text says free-labor goods were sometimes hard to find and that some sugar and rice was poor, not that stores could sell nothing but sugar and rice.
The text names cotton and sugar together among the goods the movement avoided and mentions no disagreement among supporters.
questions.text: In 1827, a group of Quakers in Philadelphia founded the Free Produce Society, part of a broader effort by abolitionists to boycott cotton, sugar, and other goods produced by enslaved people. Supporters of this free produce movement opened stores that sold only goods made with free labor, hoping to undermine slavery economically. Yet the movement achieved little success. Free-labor goods were generally more expensive than other goods and were sometimes difficult to obtain, and one shopkeeper often received sugar and rice of noticeably poor quality.

questions.skill: Hypothetical finding supports a hypothesis (treatment vs control outcome)
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Conroy and his team’s hypothesis?
choices: Young children who drank water from bottles left on roofs had episodes of severe diarrhea less often than young children who drank water from bottles kept indoors.
Water in bottles left on roofs became noticeably warmer during the day than water in bottles that were kept indoors.
Many families in the trial continued leaving their water bottles in the sun after the researchers’ visits had ended.
Children in the trial preferred the taste of water from bottles kept indoors to the taste of water from bottles left in the sun.
questions.rationale: The hypothesis is that sunlight-treated water protects young children from severe diarrheal illness. If children drinking water from the sunlit bottles had severe diarrhea less often than children drinking water kept indoors, the sunlight treatment would appear to protect them. Choice A gives that finding.
reasons: Warmer water says nothing about whether the children became ill less often.
Families keeping up the practice shows that they found it worth doing, not that it protected children’s health.
Which water the children preferred to drink does not show whether the treated water reduced illness.
questions.text: Sunlight can destroy many of the bacteria that make drinking water unsafe. In a trial involving Maasai families, researchers led by Ronán Conroy distributed clear plastic bottles to households. In some households, children’s drinking water was left in bottles on the roof of the house, exposed to full sunlight; in others, it was kept in bottles indoors. Conroy and his team hypothesized that drinking sunlight-treated water would protect young children from severe diarrheal illness.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Looney and Lusin’s claim?
choices: Korean enrollments rose in every census year shown, from 7,146 in 2006 to 13,936 in 2016.
Enrollments in Ancient Greek fell in every census year shown, whereas enrollments in Portuguese rose until 2013 and then fell.
Korean enrollments were lower than those in Ancient Greek, Biblical Hebrew, and Portuguese in 2013 but higher than those in all three languages in 2016.
Korean enrollments had surpassed those in Biblical Hebrew and Portuguese by 2013 and then surpassed those in Ancient Greek by 2016.
questions.rationale: To show that Korean overtook three languages, Korean must have been behind them in an earlier census and ahead of them in a later one. In 2013 Korean (12,256) trailed Ancient Greek (16,961), Biblical Hebrew (12,596) and Portuguese (12,407); in 2016 Korean (13,936) led all three (13,264, 9,587 and 9,827). Choice C describes this reversal.
reasons: Korean enrollments did rise in every census shown, but growth alone does not show that Korean moved past any other language, which is what Looney and Lusin claim.
Both trends are accurate, but the option says nothing about Korean, so it cannot show Korean overtaking these languages.
In 2013 Korean (12,256) was still slightly behind both Biblical Hebrew (12,596) and Portuguese (12,407); it passed all three only in 2016.
questions.text: Since 1958, the Modern Language Association (MLA) has periodically surveyed American colleges and universities about enrollments in languages other than English. Between the 2013 and 2016 censuses, total enrollments declined by more than 9 percent, and of the fifteen most commonly taught languages, only Japanese and Korean registered gains. Analyzing the 2016 census, Dennis Looney and Natalia Lusin observed that Korean’s growth had carried it past three of those languages, advancing it to eleventh place in the rankings.
questions.table_title: Fall Enrollments in Four Languages at US Colleges and Universities, 2006–2016

questions.skill: Literary quotation illustrates a claim (translated drama, two-part contrast)
questions.stem: Which quotation from The Cherry Orchard most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “I’ve always scattered money about without holding myself in, like a madwoman, and I married a man who made nothing but debts.”
“Grandmother sent fifteen thousand roubles from Yaroslav to buy the property in her name—she won’t trust us—and that wasn’t even enough to pay the interest.”
“What is to be done with such a fool as I am! At home I’ll give you everything I’ve got. Ermolai Alexeyevitch, lend me some more!”
“My poor Varya feeds everybody on milk soup to save money, in the kitchen the old people only get peas, and I spend recklessly.”
questions.rationale: The claim needs Ranevsky to admit her own extravagance and to set it against other people’s thrift. In choice D she notes that Varya serves milk soup “to save money” and the old servants “only get peas,” then admits “I spend recklessly,” so both parts are there. Choices A and C admit her extravagance or foolishness but never mention anyone else saving money.
reasons: She admits she has always wasted money, but the contrast is with her husband's debts, not with anyone in her household being careful.
It is about the family's money troubles and the grandmother's distrust, not Ranevsky admitting her own spending.
She calls herself a fool and keeps borrowing, but nothing shows others in the household economizing.
questions.text: The Cherry Orchard is a 1904 play by Anton Chekhov, translated in 1916 by Julius West. In the play, Madame Ranevsky, whose indebted estate faces auction, acknowledges that her own extravagance contrasts with the thrift of others in her household: ______

questions.skill: T3 consequence: principle (social benefits grow with audience) applied to a site block
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: prompted editors outside mainland China to edit more often, since each of their contributions would now count for more on a smaller site.
reduced the number of edits made from mainland China while leaving the activity of editors elsewhere largely unchanged.
led many editors who could still reach the site to contribute less, since the audience for their work had shrunk.
encouraged editors outside mainland China to shift their efforts toward other websites that could still be read across China.
questions.rationale: Zhang and Zhu argue that editors’ social benefits grow with the number of people who read and respond to their work. Blocking the site in mainland China removed many of those readers, so even editors who could still reach the site would gain less from contributing and would likely contribute less, as C says.
reasons: This is what the long-held view in the first sentence would predict. The question asks what follows if Zhang and Zhu are correct, and on their view a smaller audience lowers editors’ benefits, so contributions would fall.
Editors in mainland China would indeed edit less, but on Zhang and Zhu’s view editors elsewhere would also be affected, because the readers who gave them recognition were cut off.
The text says nothing about other websites; the question is how the block affected contributions to this site.
questions.text: Economists have traditionally predicted that the incentive to contribute to a public good diminishes as the number of contributors increases, since any individual’s effort then matters less. Analyzing the Chinese-language edition of Wikipedia, economists Xiaoquan Zhang and Feng Zhu argue that for the site’s volunteer editors the relationship can be reversed: contributors receive social benefits, such as recognition, that increase with the number of people who read and respond to their work. In 2005 the site was blocked in mainland China but remained accessible elsewhere. If Zhang and Zhu are correct, the block most likely ______

questions.skill: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: in
in,
in:
in—
questions.rationale: “In the weak electric field” is a prepositional phrase that tells where the distortions occur. No punctuation belongs between the preposition “in” and its object, “the weak electric field.”
reasons: A comma cannot separate a preposition from its object.
A colon must follow a complete clause; here it would split the preposition “in” from its object.
A dash has no role between a preposition and its object, and nothing in the sentence pairs with it.
questions.text: The elephantnose fish, found in murky rivers of West and Central Africa, hunts mostly at night. Its trunklike chin is covered with sensors that detect tiny distortions ______ the weak electric field the fish generates, allowing it to locate insect larvae buried in mud.

questions.skill: Semicolons between list items that contain commas
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Persia,
Persia
Persia;
Persia:
questions.rationale: The sentence lists three frescoes, and an item contains a comma of its own (“a group portrait of six monarchs, among them ...”), so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after “donkeys” shows. A semicolon after “Persia” correctly separates the second item from the third.
reasons: A comma here doesn’t match the semicolon that separates the first and second items; the items must be separated by semicolons throughout.
With no punctuation, the second and third items run together.
A colon can’t separate two items in a list.
questions.text: The interior of Qusayr Amra, an eighth-century bathhouse in the Jordanian desert, is decorated with elaborate frescoes, including a hunting scene in which horsemen pursue wild donkeys; a group portrait of six monarchs, among them the rulers of Byzantium and ______ and a domed ceiling depicting the constellations of the zodiac.

questions.skill: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that specifies it
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: transport; the
transport. The
transport: the
transport, it was the
questions.rationale: The clause “In 2011, ecologist ... proposed an improbable means of transport” is complete, and what follows is a noun phrase that identifies that means of transport. A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation after a complete clause.
reasons: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “the digestive tracts of birds ...” is a noun phrase; its verb “passed” belongs to a relative clause.
The period makes “The digestive tracts of birds ... passed alive” a sentence fragment: the only verb sits inside the relative clause “through which ...”.
“It was” turns the phrase into an independent clause, which is then joined to the first clause with only a comma.
questions.text: Land snails crawl so slowly that their dispersal across islands has long puzzled biologists. In 2011, ecologist Shinichiro Wada and colleagues proposed an improbable means of ______ digestive tracts of birds such as the Japanese white-eye, through which roughly 15 percent of the minuscule snails they fed to captive birds passed alive.

questions.skill: Subject-verb agreement: singular head behind an appositive holding a plural noun and its own plural verb
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: dictate
are dictating
have dictated
dictates
questions.rationale: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “the bhagavata”; the phrase between the commas describes this singer. The singular verb “dictates” agrees with “bhagavata.”
reasons: “Dictate” is plural; it agrees with “drummers,” not with the subject, “the bhagavata.”
“Are dictating” is plural and doesn’t agree with “the bhagavata.”
“Have dictated” is plural and doesn’t agree with “the bhagavata.”
questions.text: Yakshagana, a form of theater from coastal Karnataka, India, combines dance, music, and improvised dialogue in costumed performances that often last all night. The bhagavata, a singer who narrates the story while two drummers keep the rhythm, ______ the pace of each scene.

questions.skill: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner before its plural antecedent, singular attractors in the previous sentence
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: its
it’s
they’re
their
questions.rationale: The claws belong to the ones doing the raising, “dozens of males,” the subject of the main clause that follows the blank. The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees in number with “males,” indicating that the claws belong to the males.
reasons: The singular determiner “its” doesn’t agree with the plural noun “males,” the ones raising the claws.
“It’s” is the contraction for “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.
“They’re” is the contraction for “they are,” not a possessive determiner.
questions.text: A male fiddler crab’s enlarged claw can account for nearly half of the animal’s weight, a burden it carries to attract prospective mates. Raising ______ outsized claws and waving them in approximate synchrony, dozens of males assembled along a tidal mudflat can resemble a single undulating organism, a spectacle that may help draw the attention of passing females.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: As a result,
Previously,
For instance,
Similarly,
questions.rationale: The first sentence describes a 1934 law requiring family names. The blank sentence, in the past perfect, describes how people were identified before that law. “Previously” signals that the second sentence refers to an earlier time.
reasons: The 1934 law could not have caused people to be known by given names alone; that practice came before the law.
Being known by a given name and a title is not an instance of adopting a family name; it describes the practice the law replaced.
Using given names and titles is not similar to adopting family names; the second sentence describes the earlier, different system.
questions.text: In 1934, the Turkish parliament passed the Surname Law, requiring every citizen to adopt a hereditary family name and register it officially. ______ most people in Turkey had been identified by a given name alone, frequently supplemented by a nickname, a patronymic, or an honorific title such as “Bey” or “Pasha.”

questions.skill: Purpose: a belief or goal, then the deliberate act that serves it
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Regardless,
In comparison,
Meanwhile,
To that end,
questions.rationale: The first sentence states Heringer’s goal: the money for building the school should stay with the villagers rather than go to outside industries such as cement makers. The second sentence describes what she did to meet that goal: local people built the school from local earth, straw, and bamboo. Because the second sentence is the action taken to serve the goal, “To that end” is the logical transition.
reasons: “Regardless” would mean Heringer’s goal did not matter to how the school was built, but the building method carries out that goal.
Nothing is being compared: the second sentence describes the same school, not a different one.
The construction is not a separate event happening alongside Heringer’s goal; it is the way she pursued it.
questions.text: German architect Anna Heringer meant the school she designed for the Bangladeshi village of Rudrapur to serve the local economy as well as its pupils: the construction budget, she argued, should stay with villagers rather than flow to outside industries such as cement manufacturing. ______ the METI school, completed in 2005, was built largely by local craftspeople and villagers from earth, straw, and bamboo.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how much rain falls in Mawsynram. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: With an average of approximately 11,870 millimeters of rainfall annually, Mawsynram is among the wettest places on Earth.
Most of the rain in Mawsynram falls during the monsoon season, from June through September.
Mawsynram is a village in the state of Meghalaya in northeastern India.
Residents of Mawsynram often protect themselves with knups, full-body umbrellas woven from bamboo and leaves.
questions.rationale: Choice A gives the yearly total, approximately 11,870 millimeters, and stresses that it places Mawsynram among the wettest places on Earth.
reasons: It tells when the rain falls, not how much.
It tells where Mawsynram is.
It describes what residents wear in the rain, not the amount of rain.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mawsynram is a village in the state of Meghalaya in northeastern India.
• It receives an average of approximately 11,870 millimeters of rainfall annually.
• That total ranks among the highest recorded anywhere on Earth.
• Most of the rain falls during the monsoon season, from June through September.
• Residents often wear knups, full-body umbrellas woven from bamboo and leaves.

questions.skill: Difference on a named attribute (Unlike opener)
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the tusks of the two species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Savanna elephants roam grasslands and open woodlands, whereas forest elephants inhabit dense rainforests.
Forest elephants’ straighter, downward-pointing tusks may help them move through the thick vegetation of central and western Africa.
Though scientists long treated them as one species, savanna elephants and forest elephants have tusks that differ in shape.
Unlike savanna elephants, whose tusks curve outward and forward, forest elephants have straighter tusks that point downward.
questions.rationale: Choice D sets the two kinds of tusk side by side: savanna elephants’ tusks curve outward and forward, while forest elephants’ tusks are straighter and point downward.
reasons: It contrasts the species’ habitats, not their tusks.
It describes forest elephants’ tusks but says nothing about savanna elephants’ tusks.
It states that the tusks differ in shape but never says what the difference is.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Africa’s elephants belong to two species that scientists long treated as one.
• Savanna elephants, the larger species, roam grasslands and open woodlands across much of the continent.
• Their tusks curve outward and forward.
• Forest elephants inhabit the dense rainforests of central and western Africa.
• Their tusks are straighter and point downward, which may help the animals move through thick vegetation.

questions.skill: Explanation plus example (which plant is the nurse)
questions.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of a nurse plant. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Nurse plants enhance the survival of seedlings belonging to other species, as the saguaro does when it shelters young palo verde trees from extreme heat and frost.
A nurse plant protects other species’ young; the palo verde, for instance, shields growing saguaros from summer heat and nighttime cold.
Young saguaros, which are vulnerable to extreme heat and frost, frequently germinate beneath palo verde trees in the Sonoran Desert.
A nurse plant shelters seedlings that will eventually replace it, as when a mature saguaro outcompetes the palo verde it germinated beneath.
questions.rationale: Choice B explains what a nurse plant does (it protects the young of other species) and gives an example: the palo verde, whose canopy keeps young saguaros from overheating in summer and from freezing on cold nights.
reasons: It reverses the roles. The notes say young saguaros germinate beneath palo verde trees, so the palo verde is the nurse plant, not the saguaro.
It describes young saguaros growing under palo verde trees but never explains what a nurse plant is.
It defines a nurse plant as one whose seedlings replace it. The notes define it by the shelter it gives and say only that a mature saguaro may compete with its palo verde.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A nurse plant is one whose shelter enhances the survival of seedlings belonging to other species.
• Young saguaro cacti grow slowly and are vulnerable to extreme heat and frost.
• In the Sonoran Desert, saguaros frequently germinate beneath palo verde trees.
• The trees’ canopies shade the seedlings during summer and keep them warm on cold nights.
• A mature saguaro may later compete with its palo verde for groundwater, sometimes contributing to the tree’s death.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: surprising
predictable
profitable
fashionable
questions.rationale: The drawings are now shown as art, but Kunz did not make them to be seen as art; she treated them as part of her healing work. Seeing them in art exhibitions would therefore probably have surprised her.
reasons: Kunz did not intend the drawings to be seen as art, so their appearance in art exhibitions is the opposite of what she would have expected.
Nothing in the text concerns money; the contrast is between how the drawings are shown now and how Kunz regarded them.
The text does not say whether showing the drawings is fashionable; it says Kunz did not see them as art at all.
questions.text: Swiss healer Emma Kunz’s large geometric drawings, created on graph paper beginning in 1938, now appear in art exhibitions alongside abstract paintings. Kunz herself might have found this ______: she never intended the drawings to be considered art, and instead of assigning them titles or dates, she recorded what she understood to be their medical significance.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: glacial
frenetic
staccato
erratic
questions.rationale: “Glacial” here means extremely slow. The text says that Radigue’s music moves through tonal shifts so small they are almost imperceptible and that each Adnos piece takes roughly 70 minutes to transform, so the music changes very slowly.
reasons: “Frenetic” means wildly fast and excited. Shifts that are almost imperceptible and pieces that transform over 70 minutes describe music that changes slowly, not frantically.

“Staccato” is a musical term for short, sharply separated notes. The text describes the music as unfolding through tiny shifts, which suggests smooth, gradual change rather than abrupt, detached sounds.
“Erratic” means irregular and unpredictable. The text says nothing about sudden or irregular changes; it stresses how small and gradual the shifts are.
questions.text: Much of composer Éliane Radigue’s electronic music evolves at a ______ pace, unfolding through a series of almost imperceptible tonal shifts: each of the three compositions in her Adnos cycle, which she created on an ARP 2500 synthesizer over eight years in the 1970s and 1980s, transforms over approximately 70 minutes.

questions.skill: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: mercurial
salutary
insular
tenacious
questions.rationale: Tenacious means holding firmly and lasting a long time. Because the mistrust is carried in “norms and beliefs internal to individuals,” it travels with people and is passed down, and the text says it is still present, “outlasting the trades themselves by generations.”
reasons: Mercurial means changeable and quick to shift. The text says the mistrust has lasted “by generations” beyond the slave trades, so it has been stable, not changeable.
Salutary means beneficial. The text reports that the slave trades left people less trusting of others; nothing presents this mistrust as good for them.
Insular means narrow or cut off from outside influence, a word sometimes used of attitudes. The sentence explains why the mistrust has lasted so long, and insular says nothing about lasting.
questions.text: Nathan Nunn and Leonard Wantchekon found that Africans whose ancestors were most heavily raided during the slave trades tend to be less trusting of others today. Since this effect operates mainly through norms and beliefs internal to individuals, the mistrust has proved ______, outlasting the trades themselves by generations.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe the household tasks the narrator performs in the attic each day
To convey the narrator’s fear that a joyful experience will never be repeated
To explain why the narrator prefers the company of animals to that of people
To convey how a place helps the narrator recall a rare and treasured experience
questions.rationale: The “visitation” is the moment of joy described in the context line. Though it came “but seldom,” its “taste” stayed in the attic: whenever the narrator creeps in and hears the bees, smells the stored apples, and watches the twigs against the sky, she remembers it “and forget[s] all else.” So the text conveys how the attic lets her call back a rare and treasured experience, as choice D says.
reasons: The narrator goes to the attic to listen, smell, and watch, not to do chores; no tasks are mentioned.
The text says the experience came seldom, but it expresses no fear that it will never return; the attic keeps its “taste” with her.
The bees are one of the sounds that help her remember; the text compares no animals with people.
questions.text:
The following text is from Mary Webb’s 1924 novel Precious Bane. Prue Sarn, the narrator, lives on her family’s farm in rural England in the early 1800s. She has just described a moment of intense, unexplained joy that once came to her while she sat alone in the farmhouse attic.

Though the visitation came but seldom, the taste of it was in the attic all the while. I had but to creep in there, and hear the bees making their murmur, and smell the woody, o’er-sweet scent of kept apples, and hear the leaves rasping softly on the window-frame, and watch the twisted grey twigs on the sky, and I’d remember it and forget all else.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Dundas and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the hypothesis presented in Text 1?
choices: By conceding that liquid water formed the new deposits but arguing that the water came from melting frost rather than from underground
By suggesting that the deposits reported in 2006 were too small for the earlier spacecraft’s camera to have detected reliably
By pointing out that gullies are less widespread on Mars than the hypothesis requires them to be
By noting that the timing of recent gully activity points to a cause that does not depend on liquid water
questions.rationale: Malin, Edgett, and colleagues proposed that “liquid water may still occasionally seep from underground” to form new gully deposits. Dundas and colleagues found new flows “almost always during the season when frozen carbon dioxide frosts the slopes and temperatures are far too low for liquid water,” and they propose that the frost itself moves the sediment. They would respond that the timing of the activity points to a cause that does not depend on liquid water.
reasons: Text 2 says the frost “converts directly to gas” when temperatures are “far too low for liquid water,” so it does not concede that liquid water formed the deposits.
Text 2 mentions a higher-resolution camera, but it does not question whether the earlier camera could detect the deposits reported in 2006.
Text 2 describes “hundreds of gully locations” and never suggests gullies are rarer than Text 1 says; Text 1 calls them “widespread.”
questions.text:
Text 1

Gullies—narrow channels descending the walls of craters and other slopes—are widespread on Mars. In 2006, Michael Malin, Kenneth Edgett, and colleagues reported that bright new deposits had appeared in two gullies between photographs an orbiting spacecraft captured several years apart. Because the deposits appeared to have been transported by a fluid rather than by dry dust, the team proposed that liquid water may still occasionally seep from underground and flow down Martian slopes.

Text 2

Since 2006, a higher-resolution camera aboard another orbiter has repeatedly photographed hundreds of gully locations. Colin Dundas and colleagues documented new flows and channels at dozens of them, almost always during the season when frozen carbon dioxide frosts the slopes and temperatures are far too low for liquid water. As the frost converts directly to gas, they propose, it may dislodge sediment and lubricate its descent.

questions.stem: Based on the text, why do some namazu-e most likely show construction workers celebrating the catfish?
choices: The workers believed that the deity had finally pinned the catfish beneath its stone.
The prints were meant to reassure the public that another earthquake was unlikely to strike Edo soon.
The rebuilding that followed the earthquake gave them work paid for with money from wealthy households.
The workers had predicted the earthquake by watching catfish in nearby rivers.
questions.rationale: The text says that rebuilding Edo required vast expenditures, much of them paid out by wealthy households, and that in some prints construction workers celebrate the catfish while gold coins rain down. Putting these together, the prints most likely show the workers celebrating because the earthquake led to rebuilding work that paid them with money from the wealthy.
reasons: Prints showing the deity pinning the catfish are a different group of prints; the celebrating workers appear in prints that treat the catfish generously.
The text never says the prints were meant to reassure anyone about future earthquakes.
The text says only that people believed a giant catfish caused earthquakes; it says nothing about predicting earthquakes from the behavior of real catfish.
questions.text: In the weeks after a devastating earthquake shook Edo (present-day Tokyo) in 1855, great numbers of woodblock prints called namazu-e, or catfish pictures, circulated through the city. According to popular belief, earthquakes were caused by a gigantic catfish thrashing beneath the earth, and many prints depict a protective deity pinning the creature down with a stone. Others portray the catfish more generously. Reconstruction required enormous expenditures, a large share of them disbursed by wealthy households, and in some prints construction workers celebrate the catfish as gold coins shower down around them.

questions.stem: Which quotation from “Lobo, the King of Currumpaw” most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Old Lobo, or the king, as the Mexicans called him, was the gigantic leader of a remarkable pack of gray wolves, that had ravaged the Currumpaw Valley for a number of years.”
“His voice at night was well-known and easily distinguished from that of any of his fellows.”
“A great price was set on Lobo’s head, and in consequence poison in a score of subtle forms was put out for him, but he never failed to detect and avoid it.”
“Lobo, generally, came into this part of the range in the early part of each week, and passed the latter part, it was supposed, around the base of Sierra Grande.”
questions.rationale: The claim is that Lobo could not be tricked by poisoned bait. In choice C, poison “in a score of subtle forms” is set out for Lobo, but he “never failed to detect and avoid it,” which illustrates the claim directly.
reasons: This describes Lobo as the huge leader of a destructive pack but says nothing about poison.
This notes that Lobo’s howl was easy to recognize, not that he avoided poison.
This describes where Lobo spent different parts of the week, not how he dealt with poisoned bait.
questions.text: Wild Animals I Have Known is an 1898 collection of stories by Ernest Thompson Seton. In the story “Lobo, the King of Currumpaw,” the narrator emphasizes that the wolf Lobo cannot be fooled by poisoned bait: ______

questions.skill: Data description: a pattern followed only inconsistently, supported by a two-part exception
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student’s conclusion?
choices: The emperor penguin, which breeds farther south than any other species in the table, has an average body mass more than five times that of any other species shown.
The Magellanic penguin breeds farther south than the African penguin does and has a greater average body mass than the African penguin has.
The little penguin breeds farther from the equator than the Galápagos penguin does, yet its average body mass is lower than that of the Galápagos penguin.
The African penguin breeds farther south than the little penguin does and has a lower average body mass than the little penguin has.
questions.rationale: The student concludes that penguins follow only inconsistently the pattern in which species of colder places are larger. A species that breeds farther from the equator but is smaller than one breeding nearer to it is an exception to that pattern. The little penguin breeds between 30°S and 47°S, much farther from the equator than the Galápagos penguin, yet averages 1.2 kilograms against the Galápagos penguin’s 2.0. Choice C describes that exception.
reasons: This is accurate, but the heaviest penguin breeding farthest south fits the pattern; it does not show that penguins follow it only inconsistently.
This is accurate, but a more southern species being heavier is what the pattern predicts, so it does not support the student’s conclusion.
The African penguin breeds farther north than the little penguin (25°S–33°S against 30°S–47°S) and is heavier (3.1 against 1.2 kilograms).
questions.text: Biologists have long noted that among closely related species of warm-blooded animals, those living in colder environments tend to be considerably larger, perhaps because a big body loses heat more gradually for its mass than a small one does. Penguins, which breed from the equator to Antarctica, offer an opportunity to test this generalization. Using body mass and distribution data that biologist Barbara Ramos and her colleagues compiled for penguin species, a student concluded that penguins follow the pattern only inconsistently.
questions.table_title: Breeding Range and Average Body Mass of Five Penguin Species

questions.skill: Hypothetical finding supports a conclusion (a separate emotion, not a variety of a related one; dissociation)
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
choices: Participants who listened to recordings of scraping sounds and recordings of retching reported similar levels of discomfort and showed the same changes in heart rate in response to both.
Participants who rehearsed a plan for suppressing grima reacted less strongly to scraping sounds than other participants did but just as strongly to disgusting sounds.
Spanish speakers of all ages reported knowing the word “grima,” though younger speakers said they used it in conversation less often than older speakers did.
English and German speakers who heard the same scraping sounds reported feeling uncomfortable but used several different words to describe the feeling.
questions.rationale: The researchers conclude that grima is its own emotion rather than a mild version of disgust. If a strategy aimed at grima weakened people’s reactions to grima-inducing sounds while leaving their reactions to disgusting sounds untouched, the two reactions would be working separately, which is what a distinct emotion would predict. Choice B therefore supports the conclusion.
reasons: Matching discomfort and the same heart-rate changes for scraping sounds and disgusting sounds would make grima look like a form of disgust, the view the researchers reject.
How often different age groups use the word says nothing about whether the feeling it names is separate from disgust.
Speakers of other languages describing the feeling with several words fits grima being a distinct emotion or a variety of disgust equally well; it concerns vocabulary, not the emotion.
questions.text: Spanish speakers use the term “grima” to describe the intensely unpleasant sensation provoked by certain sounds, such as fingernails scraping across a chalkboard, an experience for which neither English nor German has a single equivalent term. When psychologists Inge Schweiger Gallo, José-Miguel Fernández-Dols, and colleagues asked Spanish speakers to evaluate the meanings of various emotion words, grima was judged more similar to disgust than to any other emotion, which might suggest that it is merely a mild variety of disgust. On the basis of subsequent experiments, however, the researchers concluded that grima constitutes a distinct emotion in its own right.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: urban workers acquire their heat tolerance by acclimating to the warmer temperatures they experience during development.
the greater heat tolerance of urban colonies most likely reflects evolved genetic differences between urban and rural populations.
the conditions that field-collected queens experienced were primarily responsible for the urban workers’ greater heat tolerance.
acorn ant populations in other cities have probably evolved greater heat tolerance more rapidly than those in Cleveland have.
questions.rationale: Three explanations are in play: workers acclimate during development, mothers' field conditions shape their offspring, or the populations differ genetically. Rearing under identical conditions ruled out the first, and the difference survived even when the mothers too were laboratory-born, which rules out the second. What remains is an evolved genetic difference, as B says.
reasons: The passage says rearing under identical conditions excludes acclimation during development, yet the difference persisted.
Workers whose mothers were born in the laboratory, and so never experienced field conditions, still showed the difference.
Only Cleveland's populations are described; nothing is said about ants in other cities or rates of evolution.
questions.text: Acorn ants from urban colonies in Cleveland, Ohio, whose acorn nests are warmed by the city’s heat island, tolerate higher temperatures than do acorn ants from surrounding rural colonies. Biologist Sarah Diamond and colleagues found that the difference persists among laboratory-born offspring of field-collected queens reared under identical conditions, which rules out the possibility that workers simply adjust to the temperatures they experience as they develop. Because those queens had matured in the field, however, maternal environmental effects remained possible. In a subsequent experiment, Diamond’s team reared workers whose mothers had themselves been born in the laboratory, and these workers exhibited the same urban–rural difference, suggesting that ______

questions.skill: Commas between items of a simple series
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: magnesium
magnesium,
magnesium;
magnesium:
questions.rationale: The sentence lists three items: “magnesium,” “calcium,” and “sodium sulfates.” Items in a simple list are separated by commas, so a comma belongs after “magnesium.”
reasons: Without a comma, the first two items of the list run together.
Semicolons separate list items only when the items contain commas of their own; these items don’t.
A colon can’t separate two items in a list.
questions.text: Each summer, most of the water in Spotted Lake, a site in British Columbia considered sacred by the Syilx people, evaporates, leaving behind hundreds of separate mineral pools. Compounds dissolved in the water, including ______ calcium, and sodium sulfates, tint the pools shades of green, blue, and yellow.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: science,
science;
science
science:
questions.rationale: The subject of the second sentence runs from “female students” to “computer science,” and its verb is “reported.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.
reasons: A single comma would separate the subject (“female students ... computer science”) from its verb “reported.”
A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the words before the blank are only a subject with no verb.
A colon must follow a complete clause; here it would split the subject from its verb.
questions.text: Psychologist Sapna Cheryan studies how physical settings signal who belongs in them. In one experiment, female students surveyed in a classroom containing a Star Trek poster, video game boxes, and other objects stereotypically linked to computer ______ reported less interest in the field than male students did, a gap that disappeared in a room with neutral objects.

questions.skill: Supplementary adverb closing clause 1 (L, though; R)
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: record; though
record, though;
record, though
record, though,
questions.rationale: The sentence contains two main clauses: “These samples do not constitute an unbroken climate record, though” and “the ice ... atmosphere.” A semicolon joins them, and a comma sets off “though,” which belongs to the first clause: it signals that this limitation contrasts with the impressive age reported in the previous sentence. The second clause then explains the limitation.
reasons: With “though” opening the second clause, that clause becomes dependent and cannot follow a semicolon; it would also illogically present the discontinuous ice as a contrast, when it is the reason the samples do not form an unbroken record.

Here “though” introduces the second clause, illogically presenting the discontinuous ice as a contrast to the samples’ not forming an unbroken record, when it is the reason for it; “though” has to close the first clause, which qualifies the impressive age reported in the previous sentence.
Setting off “though” with commas leaves the two main clauses joined by only a comma.
questions.text: Ice recovered from Antarctica’s Allan Hills Blue Ice Area exceeds two million years in age, more than double the age of the oldest ice in any continuous core available in 2019. These samples do not constitute an unbroken climate ______ the ice, as geoscientist Yuzhen Yan and colleagues reported that year, is stratigraphically discontinuous, so it preserves only isolated snapshots of Earth’s ancient atmosphere.

questions.skill: Possessive determiner after its singular antecedent, plural nouns between
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: they’re
their
it’s
its
questions.rationale: The builders are those of “a single nest,” the subject of the second sentence. The singular possessive determiner “its” agrees with “nest” and shows that the nest outlasts the birds that built it.
reasons: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner.
The plural “their” matches nearby plural nouns such as “birds” and “generations,” but the builders belong to the singular “nest.”
“It’s” is the contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.
questions.text: Sociable weavers, sparrow-sized birds native to the Kalahari Desert, build the largest communal nests of any bird species, usually in the branches of camel thorn trees. A single nest, which may house several hundred birds, can stay in use for generations, frequently outlasting ______ original builders by decades.

questions.skill: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Produced by ...), passage-final blank; the patterns (Chladni figures) are the right subject
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Chladni showed that the sand gathers along the lines where the plate is not vibrating.
the sand gathers into these patterns, now known as Chladni figures, along lines where the plate is not vibrating.
it is along the lines where the plate is not vibrating that the sand gathers into these patterns.
Chladni figures, as these patterns are now known, trace the lines where the plate is not vibrating.
questions.rationale: What is produced by bowing a sand-covered plate is the pattern, so the patterns must be the subject that follows the comma. Choice D puts “Chladni figures, as these patterns are now known,” there, so the sentence says the figures are produced this way and trace the plate’s still lines.
reasons: The subject is “Chladni,” so the sentence illogically says that the physicist himself was produced by drawing a bow along a plate.
The subject is “the sand,” but the sand is not produced by the bowing; the patterns it forms are.
The opening phrase is followed by “it,” which cannot be what the bowing produces, so the phrase is left dangling.
questions.text: In 1787, German physicist and musician Ernst Chladni published a treatise demonstrating that the vibrations of a resonating object can be rendered visible as intricate geometric patterns. Produced by drawing a violin bow along the edge of a thin metal plate sprinkled with sand, ______

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: in other words,
consequently,
however,
in particular,
questions.rationale: The first sentence says that every frog examined had lungs. The second reports a frog with no lungs at all, which breaks that pattern. “However” marks this contrast between the earlier record and the new finding.
reasons: The second sentence does not reword the claim that every frog examined had lungs; it reports a frog that breaks that pattern.
The earlier record of frogs with lungs did not cause Bickford’s finding of a lungless frog.
The lungless frog is not a particular case of frogs having lungs; it is an exception to that pattern.
questions.text: Among amphibians, lunglessness was known only in a large family of salamanders and in one caecilian; every frog examined had possessed lungs. On a 2007 expedition to Indonesian Borneo, ______ biologist David Bickford confirmed that Barbourula kalimantanensis, a flattened stream-dwelling frog, has no lungs, absorbing oxygen entirely through its skin.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: In other words,
Furthermore,
Specifically,
Admittedly,
questions.rationale: The first two sentences claim that a gyotaku print is an exact record because it comes straight from the fish. The blank sentence admits a limit to that claim: one part, the eye, is not printed at all but painted in by hand. “Admittedly” introduces a fact that qualifies the claim without overturning it.
reasons: The blank sentence does not reword the claim that the print is an exact record; it points out a part of the print that is added by hand.
“Furthermore” would add another point in support of the print’s accuracy, but an eye painted in by hand is a limit on that accuracy.
The eye is not one of the details the print preserves exactly; it is the one detail the print fails to capture, so the sentence does not specify the earlier claim.
questions.text: Gyotaku, a printmaking technique that originated in nineteenth-century Japan, gave anglers an exact record of their catches. Because each print is pulled directly from an inked fish, it preserves the animal’s true size and the precise arrangement of its scales and fins. ______ the eye, which rarely prints clearly, is typically painted in by hand afterward.

questions.skill: Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the Okavango Delta floods during Botswana’s dry season. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The Okavango Delta is an inland wetland in northern Botswana that does not drain into any sea or ocean.
The Okavango Delta’s inundated area is largest from July to September, late in Botswana’s dry season.
Rainfall from Angola’s central highlands is transported slowly southward by the Okavango River.
Because its floodwater falls as rain in Angola months earlier, the Okavango Delta floods during Botswana’s dry season.
questions.rationale: An explanation must link the flood to its cause. The notes say the floodwater falls as rain in the Angolan highlands and travels slowly south, reaching the delta months later, so the flood peaks late in Botswana’s dry season. Choice D makes that link with “because.”
reasons: It describes what kind of place the delta is and notes that it does not drain into a sea, which says nothing about when or why it floods.
It states when the delta’s inundated area is largest but gives no reason, so nothing is explained.
It describes where the floodwater comes from and how it travels but never says that the delta floods in the dry season, so the cause is not tied to the flooding.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Okavango Delta, an inland wetland in northern Botswana, does not drain into any sea or ocean.
• Its floodwater originates as rainfall in Angola’s central highlands, where the rainy season lasts from about September to April.
• The Okavango River transports this water slowly southward, so it reaches the delta months later.
• The delta’s inundated area is largest from July to September, late in Botswana’s dry season.

questions.stem: The student wants to contrast how the yarn is wrapped in the two kinds of knots. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: While a symmetrical knot is wrapped around two neighboring warps, an asymmetrical knot is wrapped fully around only one, merely passing behind the next.
Asymmetrical knots can be packed more densely than symmetrical knots can, which allows weavers to create finer detail.
Both symmetrical and asymmetrical knots are made by tying short pieces of yarn around the vertical threads of a carpet.
Turkish and Persian knots are the two main kinds of knots in hand-knotted carpets, and they are tied in different ways.
questions.rationale: The goal is a contrast in how the yarn is wrapped. Choice A gives both: a symmetrical knot wraps two warps, while an asymmetrical knot wraps fully around only one.
reasons: It contrasts how densely the knots can be packed, not how the yarn is wrapped.
It states what the two knots have in common.
It says the knots are tied differently without saying how the yarn is wrapped in either.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hand-knotted carpets are made by tying short pieces of yarn around vertical threads called warps.
• Weavers traditionally use two principal kinds of knots.
• A symmetrical, or Turkish, knot is wrapped around two neighboring warps, with both ends emerging between them.
• An asymmetrical, or Persian, knot is wrapped fully around one warp but merely passes behind the next.
• Asymmetrical knots can be packed more densely, allowing finer detail.

questions.skill: Make and support a generalization (one level above the cases)
questions.stem: The student wants to make and support a generalization about how island mammals’ body sizes can compare with those of related mainland species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
choices: Island mammals can become either much smaller or much larger than related mainland species, as the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus and Menorca’s Nuralagus rex show.
Like the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus, which weighed a fraction of what its mainland relative does, mammals that colonize islands such as Menorca tend to shrink over time.
At about 200 kilograms, the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus weighed far more than Nuralagus rex, an extinct rabbit from Menorca that weighed about 12 kilograms.
According to paleontologists who study island mammals, both the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus and Menorca’s Nuralagus rex disappeared about 10,000 years ago.
questions.rationale: The goal is a generalization, with support, about how island mammals’ sizes compare with related mainland species. The dwarf hippopotamus weighed “about 200 kilograms” against the common hippopotamus’s “over 1,500 kilograms,” while Nuralagus rex weighed “about 12 kilograms” against the European rabbit’s “less than 2 kilograms.” Choice A generalizes that island mammals can become either much smaller or much larger and cites both animals as support.
reasons: It makes and supports a generalization, but the generalization is wrong: Nuralagus rex, from Menorca, weighed far more than the European rabbit, so island mammals do not simply tend to shrink.
It compares the two island animals with each other rather than with related mainland species, and it makes no generalization.
The notes give the date of disappearance only for the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus, and the sentence says nothing about body size.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Paleontologists compare extinct island mammals with related mainland species to determine how body size changes on islands.
• The Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus, which disappeared about 10,000 years ago, weighed about 200 kilograms.
• The common hippopotamus, a close relative from mainland Africa, can weigh over 1,500 kilograms.
• Nuralagus rex, an extinct rabbit from the Mediterranean island of Menorca, weighed about 12 kilograms.
• The European rabbit, a relative from the nearby mainland, typically weighs less than 2 kilograms.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: predicted
praised
revisited
avoided
questions.rationale: To “revisit” a subject is to return to it again. The text lists three of Ghatak’s films, all made years after 1947, that each portray the upheaval the partition caused. Since he came back to the partition in film after film, he repeatedly revisited it.
reasons: The films listed came out in 1960 and 1961 and later, long after the 1947 partition, so they could not have predicted it.
The films portray the “lasting upheaval” the partition caused, which suggests it is treated as a painful event; nothing in the text suggests Ghatak praised it.
The text gives several films that all deal with the partition, so Ghatak did not avoid the subject; he returned to it again and again.
questions.text: Indian filmmaker Ritwik Ghatak repeatedly ______ the 1947 partition of Bengal in his work. His films Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960), Komal Gandhar (1961), and Subarnarekha, for example, all portray the lasting upheaval caused when the region was divided between India and what became East Pakistan.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: corroborated
unfounded
belated
exaggerated
questions.rationale: “Exaggerated” means made to seem larger than it really is. The ethnographers described dramatic differences between cultures, while Stivers’s team found that every language avoided overlap and long silences and that the languages differed only slightly in timing. The accounts described a real difference as much bigger than it is, so they were exaggerated.
reasons: If the accounts had been “corroborated,” or confirmed, the study would have found large differences in timing. Instead it found that every language avoided overlap and long silences, which goes against the accounts.

“Unfounded” would mean the accounts had no basis at all. The text says the languages did differ in their average gaps, just not by much, so the accounts overstated a real difference rather than inventing one.
“Belated” means coming too late. The text says nothing about when the ethnographic accounts appeared; it compares what they claimed with what the study found.
questions.text: Ethnographers have characterized some cultures as comfortable with lengthy silences between speakers and others as prone to continual overlapping talk, but the findings of linguist Tanya Stivers and colleagues suggest that such accounts are ______. Analyzing conversations in ten languages, the team discovered that speakers of every language avoided both overlap and prolonged silence; the languages did differ, but each one’s average gap between turns fell within a quarter second of the cross-language average.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: inconsequential
salutary
deleterious
precarious
questions.rationale: “Salutary” means beneficial. “Yet” sets the finding against the officials’ expectation, and the finding is that domestic farmworkers’ wages and employment did not increase faster where braceros had been excluded. For that to contradict the expectation, officials must have expected wages and employment to rise, that is, expected the exclusion to benefit American-born farmworkers.
reasons: “Inconsequential” describes what the economists found, an exclusion with no measurable effect. Officials who had expected no effect would not be contradicted by that finding, but “Yet” marks the finding as a contrast with their expectation.

“Deleterious” means harmful. If officials had expected the exclusion to hurt domestic farmworkers, finding that their wages increased no faster where braceros left would not contrast with that expectation.

“Precarious” means insecure or risky. The text gives no sign that officials expected the exclusion to make farmworkers’ situation uncertain; the contrast concerns whether wages and employment would rise.
questions.text: When the United States terminated the bracero program in 1964, barring the Mexican seasonal workers who had done much of its agricultural labor, officials expected the exclusion to prove ______ for American-born farmworkers. Yet economists Michael Clemens and colleagues found that domestic farmworkers’ wages and employment increased no faster in states that had depended heavily on braceros than elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show Mrs. Wiggs deciding that her other children must give up some of their blankets for their sick brother
To portray a mother concealing her distress over her family’s poverty in order to reassure her ill son
To illustrate how Jim’s illness has spread to his younger sisters and brother
To convey Mrs. Wiggs’s relief that her other children are sleeping peacefully despite the cold
questions.rationale: Looking for something more to cover Jim, Mrs. Wiggs sees that the little girls share one old quilt and that Billy’s blankets are not enough even for him. She covers her face and sobs for a moment, yet when she returns to the stove she has “a smile ready for the sick boy.” The text portrays her hiding her distress at the family’s poverty so that she can reassure her son, as choice B says.
reasons: She does look at the other children’s bedding, but it is too thin to spare; she turns away abruptly, and the text never shows her taking their blankets.
The girls’ faces are “pale and sunken” from hunger and cold, and only Jim is called “the sick boy”; nothing says his illness has spread.
The sight of the children under thin covers brings her to tears; she feels grief, not relief.
questions.text:
The following text is from Alice Hegan Rice’s 1901 novel Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch. Mrs. Wiggs’s son Jim, who is ill, has asked her for another covering.

Mrs. Wiggs got up and went toward the bed. The three little girls lay huddled under one old quilt, their faces pale and sunken. She turned away abruptly, and looked toward the corner where Billy slept on a pallet. The blankets on his bed were insufficient even for him. She put her hands over her face, and for a moment dry sobs convulsed her. The hardest grief is often that which leaves no trace. When she went back to the stove she had a smile ready for the sick boy.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Giné and Karlan (Text 2) most likely respond to the underlined assumption in Text 1?
choices: By suggesting that borrowers in the Philippines tend to be more reliable than borrowers in Bangladesh or Bolivia
By arguing that the weekly meetings, rather than the repayment schedule, were what kept repayment rates high
By agreeing that lenders must hold borrowers responsible for one another’s loans when the borrowers lack collateral
By noting that borrowers repaid just as reliably after being released from responsibility for other members’ debts
questions.rationale: Text 1 reports the assumption that without group liability “these borrowers could not be expected to repay.” In Giné and Karlan’s experiment, centers were converted so that “members were no longer responsible for one another’s debts,” yet “Repayment rates in the converted centers proved no lower than in centers that kept group liability.” The researchers would therefore note that repayment stayed high without shared responsibility.
reasons: Text 2 compares centers within one Philippine bank, not borrowers in different countries.
In the converted centers “The weekly meetings and repayment schedules were retained,” so the experiment cannot single out the meetings as the cause of high repayment.
The experiment shows repayment held up after borrowers were no longer responsible for one another’s debts, so the researchers would reject this.
questions.text:
Text 1

Microfinance institutions in Bangladesh, Bolivia, and elsewhere have reported remarkably high repayment rates on small loans to impoverished borrowers who have no collateral. Many observers credited this success to group liability. Borrowers were organized into groups whose members were jointly responsible for one another’s loans, giving each member an incentive to screen and monitor the others. <u>Without such shared responsibility, it was widely assumed, these borrowers could not be expected to repay.</u>

Text 2

Economists Xavier Giné and Dean Karlan collaborated with a Philippine bank that lent to groups of borrowers who met weekly. The bank randomly selected half of its existing lending centers and converted them to individual liability: members were no longer responsible for one another’s debts. The weekly meetings and repayment schedules were retained. Repayment rates in the converted centers proved no lower than in centers that kept group liability.

choices: Tailleferre wrote most of her important works while she belonged to Les Six and composed little once the group’s fame faded.
Although Tailleferre first became known as a member of Les Six, her work as a composer continued for decades beyond the group’s early fame.
Tailleferre became famous in Paris only after the music she wrote after 1946 was published following her death.
Tailleferre eventually left Les Six because the group’s other members did not take her music seriously.
questions.rationale: The text says Tailleferre “first gained renown in Paris as the only woman in Les Six” but that the group “accounts for only a small part of her career,” since she “continued composing until a few weeks before her death in 1983.” Choice B states this contrast.
reasons: The text says she kept composing for decades, producing concertos, operas, ballets, and film scores, so she did not stop composing after the group’s early fame.
She gained renown in Paris through Les Six; the posthumous publication of her later music came long after she was already known.
The text never says she left the group or that its members dismissed her music.
questions.text: Germaine Tailleferre first gained renown in Paris as the only woman in Les Six, a group of young composers who achieved sudden fame after the critic Henri Collet wrote about them. Membership in the group, however, accounts for only a small part of her career. Tailleferre continued composing until a few weeks before her death in 1983 at age ninety-one, producing concertos, operas, ballets, and more than thirty film scores, and most of the music she wrote after 1946 was not published until after she died.

questions.skill: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim
questions.stem: Which quotation from A Hero of Our Time most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “I feel within me that insatiate hunger which devours everything it meets upon the way; I look upon the sufferings and joys of others only from the point of view of their relation to myself, regarding them as the nutriment which sustains my spiritual forces.”

“Mine is an unfortunate disposition; whether it is the result of my upbringing or whether it is innate—I know not. I only know this, that if I am the cause of unhappiness in others I myself am no less unhappy.”

“In my early youth, from the moment I ceased to be under the guardianship of my relations, I began madly to enjoy all the pleasures which money could buy—and, of course, such pleasures became irksome to me.”
“The air is pure and fresh, like the kiss of a child; the sun is bright, the sky is blue—what more could one possibly wish for? What need, in such a place as this, of passions, desires, regrets?”
questions.rationale: The claim has two parts: Pechorin admits that he makes others miserable, and he insists that he is no happier himself. In choice B he says that if he is the cause of unhappiness in others, he himself is no less unhappy, which covers both parts.
reasons: Pechorin describes feeding on the sufferings of others, but he says nothing about being unhappy himself.
Pechorin says pleasures grew tiresome to him, but he does not mention making anyone else unhappy.
Here Pechorin delights in the landscape and wants nothing more, which shows neither misery caused to others nor his own unhappiness.

In the novel, the restless young officer Grigory Pechorin acknowledges that he causes suffering to the people around him but insists that he experiences comparable unhappiness himself: ______

questions.skill: Data description: a trend that matters only through a passage relation (urban share rises only when urban population grows proportionally faster than total population)
questions.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the geographer’s conclusion?
choices: Tajikistan’s urban population and its total population were both larger in 2020 than they had been in any of the earlier years shown in the table.
Tajikistan’s urban population declined slightly from 1990 to 2000, but it then grew by more than half, rising from about 1.7 million in 2000 to about 2.6 million in 2020.
From 1990 to 2000, Tajikistan’s urban population fell slightly as its total population grew, and from 2000 to 2020, the two populations each grew by a little over half.
Tajikistan’s urban population increased during every decade from 1990 to 2020, although in each of those decades it grew more slowly than the country’s total population did.
questions.rationale: The text says the urban share “rises only when the urban population grows proportionally faster than the population as a whole” and stays the same “when the two grow at the same rate.” From 1990 to 2000, the urban population fell (1.72 to 1.67 million) while the total grew (5.40 to 6.28 million), so the urban share fell: urbanization reversed. From 2000 to 2020, both grew by a little more than half (about 53 and 55 percent), so the share stayed almost the same: urbanization stalled. Choice C describes both parts.
reasons: Both populations did peak in 2020, but reaching a high level says nothing about whether the urban population grew faster or slower than the total, which is what determines the urban share.

This is accurate, but it never compares the urban population with the total population; growth of more than half after 2000 would mean rising urbanization only if the total population had grown less, which the choice does not say.
The urban population did not grow from 1990 to 2000; it fell from 1.72 to 1.67 million.
questions.text: The share of a country’s population living in urban areas, a standard measure of urbanization, rises only when the urban population grows proportionally faster than the population as a whole; when the two grow at the same rate, the share remains constant. Tajikistan, a largely mountainous country in Central Asia where most people have long lived in rural villages, became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991, and in the following decades its total population increased substantially. Comparing urban and national population figures for those decades, a geographer concluded that Tajikistan’s urbanization reversed during the 1990s and then stalled over the next twenty years.
