questions.skill: T3 consequence: a poetic device of double meaning applied to poems about the powerful
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: criticize a powerful figure while offering a harmless surface reading that the poet could claim was the intended one.
make a hidden message obvious to every listener, since the wordplay involved was taught in the church’s schools.
mock several powerful people in a single line, since each of them could recognize himself in its wax.
praise a ruler through the wax of a poem while reserving its gold for the religious lessons taught in the church.
questions.rationale: In qene, “a qene line presents an obvious interpretation, the wax, while ambiguous wordplay conceals a deeper significance, the gold,” and secular qene “historically served to ridicule individuals in positions of authority.” A poet could therefore place the ridicule in the hidden gold and point to the innocent wax if challenged, criticizing the powerful while keeping a safe surface meaning.
reasons: The device works because wordplay “conceals” the deeper meaning; making the message obvious to everyone would defeat that purpose.
The wax is the obvious interpretation, so mockery placed there would be open; the concealed meaning is the gold.
The text ties the device to secular poems that ridicule authority, not to praise in the wax and religious teaching in the gold.
questions.text: Qene, a form of improvised poetry traditionally taught in schools of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, depends on a literary device called sem-ena-werq, or “wax and gold.” The name derives from a goldsmithing technique in which wax is drained from a clay mold so that molten gold can replace it: a qene line presents an obvious interpretation, the wax, while ambiguous wordplay conceals a deeper significance, the gold. Because secular qene historically served to ridicule individuals in positions of authority, the device would have enabled a poet to ______

questions.skill: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: loom, using
loom; using
loom. Using
loom, and using
questions.rationale: “Since the late 1950s, American textile artist Sheila Hicks has made hundreds of ... minimes, small woven studies created on a portable wooden loom” is a complete clause. “using them to experiment with colors, materials, and techniques ...” is a participial phrase that adds information about Hicks, so a comma correctly attaches it to the clause.
reasons: A semicolon can't join a clause to the phrase “using them to experiment with colors ...,” which has no subject or main verb.
“Using them to experiment with colors, materials, and techniques ...” can't stand alone as a sentence.
“and” would join the clause to a phrase that isn't parallel with it, so the sentence doesn't hold together.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: 1852, unsigned
1852. Unsigned
1852 unsigned
1852 and unsigned
questions.rationale: The second sentence opens with the introductory phrase “Unsigned at the time,” which describes its subject, “the novel.” A period after “1852” ends the first sentence so that this phrase can begin the second one.
reasons: “Unsigned at the time, the novel is attributed ...” is an independent clause, so the comma alone joins two independent clauses.
With no mark, “unsigned at the time” attaches to the first clause, and the comma after “time” then splices two independent clauses.
“And” makes “unsigned at the time” part of the first clause's description of the novel, leaving the comma after “time” to splice two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

report rather,
report,
report; rather,
questions.rationale: “Rather” signals that the second clause corrects the first: the book is not simply a war report; instead, its opening sections examine the region’s land and people. A semicolon joins the two main clauses (“Os Sertões ... is not simply a war report” and “its opening sections examine ...”), and the comma after “rather” sets the adverb off from the clause it introduces.
reasons: The commas around “rather” leave the two main clauses joined with only a comma, a comma splice.
With no mark before “rather,” the two main clauses run together without the punctuation needed between them.
A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses “Os Sertões ... is not simply a war report” and “its opening sections examine ....”

choices: there are two traits that help giant sequoias survive for thousands of years:
two traits help giant sequoias survive for thousands of years:
giant sequoias have two traits that let them survive for thousands of years:

questions.rationale: The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. Choice C places “giant sequoias” immediately after the modifying phrase “In addition to growing as tall as a 25-story building,” making clear that the sequoias, and not another noun in the sentence, are what grow that tall.
reasons: The function word “there” follows the modifying phrase, which leaves the phrase with no noun it can logically describe.
“Two traits” follows the modifying phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the traits grow as tall as a 25-story building.
The subject is “giant sequoias’ survival,” so the sentence illogically says that the trees’ survival grows as tall as a 25-story building.

In other words,
Finally,

reasons: The 2009 discovery of eggs is not an example of the 2008 capture of adult eels; it is the next and last step.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Specifically,
Similarly,
Of course,
Thus,
questions.rationale: The first sentence says the walls were meant to preserve the remains of demolished villages. The blank sentence grants a point that cuts against this aim: some walls are concrete, not salvaged material. The next sentence, beginning with “Still,” returns to the main claim: much of the facade is made of salvaged bricks and tiles. “Of course” is the transition that concedes a point before such a turn.
reasons: Concrete walls are not a more precise account of how the walls preserve village remains; the clause names an exception to that aim.
The concrete walls are not a second case like the museum’s aim of preserving village remains; they are an exception the writer concedes before turning back with “Still.”
The aim of preserving village remains does not cause some walls to be made of concrete.

choices: A torii is a traditional gate that marks the entrance to a Shinto shrine in Japan.
Passing through a torii, which is often painted a bright orange-red, symbolizes entering a sacred space.
A torii has two upright pillars joined near the top by two horizontal crossbeams, the upper of which often extends past the pillars.
Torii, the gates at Shinto shrines, are built in a traditional style with several connected parts.
questions.rationale: A torii’s structure is how its parts fit together. Choice C describes them: two upright pillars joined near the top by two crossbeams, with the upper beam often extending past the pillars.
reasons: It says what a torii is for, not how it is built.
It gives the gate’s color and symbolic meaning, not its structure.
It says a torii has several connected parts but never says what they are or how they fit together.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how bidriware artisans make the silver designs stand out. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Bidriware, a metal handicraft that originated in the city of Bidar, India, in the 1300s, is cast into vases, boxes, and other objects from an alloy of zinc and copper.
Artisans make the silver designs on bidriware stand out with a soil paste that blackens the surrounding alloy but leaves the silver untouched.

questions.rationale: The silver stands out because of a contrast the artisans create at the end: the soil paste turns the zinc and copper alloy deep black but does not change the silver. Choice B explains this.
reasons: It tells where bidriware comes from and what it is made of, not how the silver designs are made to stand out.
It explains how the silver gets into the surface but not what makes it contrast with the metal around it.
It mentions the soil paste but not what the paste does to the alloy and the silver, so it does not explain why the designs stand out.

Varieties 1 and 2 both have shorter stalks than the traditional variety does, which may make them less useful to farmers who feed stalks to livestock.
questions.rationale: The goal is the significance of a similarity. Varieties 1 and 2 “matured in about 80 and 85 days,” both less than the rainy season’s “approximately 90 days,” while the traditional variety needed “about 110 days.” Because millet “still ripening afterward yields little grain,” Choice B gives the shared trait and why it matters: both new varieties can ripen before the rains end.
reasons: Only Variety 1 produced 30% more grain than the traditional variety; Variety 2 “produced 25% more,” so the stated similarity is wrong.
It notes that the two varieties matured at about the same time but never says why that matters.
The notes say only that “Variety 1 also had shorter stalks”; nothing is said about Variety 2’s stalks.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In southern Niger, the rainy season lasts approximately 90 days; millet still ripening afterward yields little grain.
• Researchers there grew two new varieties of pearl millet alongside a traditional variety in a drought year.
• The traditional variety matured in about 110 days; Varieties 1 and 2 matured in about 80 and 85 days.
• Variety 1 produced 30% more grain than the traditional variety; Variety 2 produced 25% more.
• Variety 1 also had shorter stalks, which farmers often use to feed livestock.

questions.skill: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: doubted
regretted
imagined
concluded
questions.rationale: Concluded means decided after reasoning. Because the other crocodile relatives in the region were “either too small or had jaws suited to different kinds of feeding,” the researchers ruled them out and reasoned that a young Purussaurus made the marks.
reasons: Doubted means questioned. The researchers ruled out the other crocodile relatives, which gave them a reason to accept, not doubt, that a young Purussaurus made the marks.
Nothing in the text suggests the researchers were sorry about their finding; they reasoned their way to it.
Imagined suggests a guess with no evidence behind it, but the researchers based their view on evidence, ruling out the other crocodile relatives one by one.
questions.text: A 13-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a ground sloth discovered in Peru bears 46 tooth marks. Because the other crocodile relatives known from that region and period were either too small or had jaws suited to different kinds of feeding, François Pujos and Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi ______ that the marks were made by a young Purussaurus, a giant caiman.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: unwavering
selective
contagious
erratic
questions.rationale: The second sentence explains the blank: investors checked their balances when the market had risen and stayed away when it had fallen, as if avoiding unwelcome information. Attention that people give to some news and withhold from other news is “selective.”
reasons: “Unwavering” attention would stay the same whatever the market did. The study found that logins rose after gains and fell after losses.
“Contagious” attention would spread from one investor to another. The text describes how each individual’s checking followed the market’s direction, not how investors influenced one another.
“Erratic” means irregular and unpredictable. The investors’ attention did change, but in a consistent pattern, rising after gains and falling after losses, so it was not random.
questions.text: Investors’ attention to their own savings appears to be strikingly ______. Analyzing daily logins to investment accounts, Nachum Sicherman and colleagues found that individuals checked their balances more often after the stock market rose and considerably less often after it fell, as if avoiding information they expected to be unwelcome.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ascribable to
tangential to
impervious to
commensurate with
questions.rationale: Something ascribable to a cause can be attributed to, or explained by, it. The text says immigrants “tended to settle in places offering better prospects for their children,” which is offered as a reason their sons rose further; so part of the sons’ advantage can be attributed to where their families chose to live.
reasons: Tangential to means only slightly related to. The colon clause presents where immigrants settled as a reason for the advantage, so the two are closely connected, not barely related.
Impervious to means unaffected by. The colon clause explains the advantage by where immigrants settled, so the advantage is affected by that choice, not unaffected by it.
Commensurate with means matching in size or degree. The text compares nothing in size with “where immigrants chose to live”; it says only that this choice helps explain the advantage.
questions.text: Economists Ran Abramitzky, Leah Boustan, and colleagues found that sons of immigrants to the United States, both a century ago and today, have typically risen further up the income ladder than sons of US-born fathers with similar incomes. This advantage is partly ______ where immigrants chose to live: they tended to settle in places offering better prospects for their children.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: The speaker responds to critics who fault his writing, then insists that he will keep to his own chosen path.
The speaker admits that his lack of schooling has weakened his poems, then asks his critics to help him improve them.
The speaker praises his critics for their careful reading, then explains why he has decided to accept their advice.
The speaker recalls a disagreement about punctuation, then predicts that his critics will soon change their opinion of his work.
questions.rationale: In the first stanza the speaker answers critics who seized on “a faulty line” and a dash used in place of a semicolon while staying “blind to the rest,” and he turns their charge that he was “taught too little” back on them. In the last lines he asks whether he must “turn aside from my destined way” for a task they would set him, a question that insists he will not. The poem responds to criticism of his writing and then affirms his commitment to his own course, as choice A says.
reasons: “I was taught too little?” repeats the critics’ charge as a question, and he answers that he “learnt too much / To care for a pedant’s diction”; he concedes nothing and asks for no help.
Their eyes were “keen” only for small faults and “blind to the rest”; this is a complaint, and he refuses their advice rather than accepting it.
The dash and semicolon are one example of the critics’ fault-finding, and the speaker makes no prediction about their opinions; he says he will not turn aside from his own way.
questions.text:
The following text is adapted from Henry Lawson’s 1897 poem “The Uncultured Rhymer to His Cultured Critics.”

You were quick to pick on a faulty line
That I strove to put my soul in:
Your eyes were keen for a ‘dash’ of mine
In the place of a semi-colon—
And blind to the rest. And is it for such
As you I must brook restriction?
‘I was taught too little?’ I learnt too much
To care for a pedant’s diction!

Must I turn aside from my destined way
For a task your Joss [idol] would find me?

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Perry and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
choices: Reefs near muddy coastlines grow quickly only in years when floods carry nutrients down from rivers.
Sediment poses less danger to corals than the loss of light caused by turbid water does.
Persistently murky conditions do not necessarily prevent a reef from growing.
The algae in Middle Reef’s corals depend less on sunlight than the algae in most other corals do.
questions.rationale: Text 1 says reefs are thought “to require clear water and to be unable to grow where waves or rivers keep sediment suspended.” Perry and colleagues found that Middle Reef, where the water is frequently “clouded with suspended sediment,” built upward for over 700 years, “growing fastest during periods of especially heavy sediment deposition.” They would respond that murky water does not necessarily prevent reef growth.
reasons: Text 2 mentions river floods only as a source of sediment; it never ties the reef’s growth to nutrients or limits it to flood years.
Neither text compares the danger of sediment with the danger of reduced light.
Text 2 does not discuss the algae in Middle Reef’s corals or how much they rely on sunlight.
questions.text:
Text 1

Reef-building corals depend on symbiotic algae in their tissues, which use sunlight to produce nutrients for their hosts. Turbid water obstructs that light, and the particles responsible can settle on corals and smother them. <u>Coral reefs are therefore widely thought to require clear water and to be unable to grow where waves or rivers keep sediment suspended</u>, and reefs along muddy coastlines are often described as marginal or degraded.

Text 2

Middle Reef lies about four kilometers off Townsville in northeastern Australia, where waves and river floods frequently keep the water clouded with suspended sediment. Yet when Chris Perry and colleagues drilled cores through the reef framework and radiocarbon-dated them, they discovered that it had built upward by more than eight millimeters a year for over 700 years, growing fastest during periods of especially heavy sediment deposition.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Pretzsch’s team found that city trees outlive rural trees because they grow more quickly.
Trees in rural areas have grown faster than city trees since the 1960s because the countryside is cooler.
Urban warmth seems to have accelerated city trees’ growth, which may also hasten the need to replace them.
Cities in several countries have begun planting more trees in an effort to lower urban temperatures.
questions.rationale: The text reports that city trees have grown faster than rural trees since the 1960s, which the researchers attribute to the warmth of cities, and then adds that faster growth brings faster aging, so cities may have to replace their trees sooner. The main idea joins the finding and its consequence.
reasons: The text says faster growth is accompanied by faster aging, so city trees may need replacing sooner, not that they live longer.
The study found that city trees, not rural trees, have grown faster since the 1960s.
The text says nothing about cities planting trees to cool themselves.
questions.text: Analyzing growth rings from nearly 1,400 mostly mature trees in ten cities on several continents, from Berlin to Brisbane, forest scientist Hans Pretzsch and colleagues found that since the 1960s, trees in cities have grown faster than trees in nearby rural areas. The researchers attribute the difference to the urban heat island effect, by which cities retain more heat than outlying rural land. Faster growth, however, is accompanied by accelerated aging, and Pretzsch warns that cities may need to replace aging and dying trees sooner than they once did.

questions.skill: Data completion (reverse lookup: find the row by year, report its area)
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: 7.5 million acres.
3.7 million acres.
4.7 million acres.
3.2 million acres.
questions.rationale: The table lists Denali, established in 1917, with an area of 4,740,911 acres, or about 4.7 million acres.
reasons: About 7.5 million acres is the area of Gates of the Arctic.
About 3.7 million acres is the area of Katmai.
About 3.2 million acres is the area of Glacier Bay.
questions.text: Of the 63 national parks in the United States, eight are in Alaska, and together they account for more than half of the territory in all the country’s national parks. Most of Alaska’s parks, including Gates of the Arctic and Katmai, were established by a single law passed in 1980. A student researching these parks notes that the oldest of them, Denali, which was established in 1917, covers approximately ______

questions.skill: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part contrast claim (rejects abundance, drawn to a stark landscape)
questions.stem: Which quotation from “Wild Peaches” most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Peaches grow wild, and pigs can live in clover; / A barrel of salted herrings lasts a year; / The spring begins before the winter’s over.”
“The autumn frosts will lie upon the grass / Like bloom on grapes of purple-brown and gold. / The misted early mornings will be cold; / The little puddles will be roofed with glass.”
“Down to the Puritan marrow of my bones / There’s something in this richness that I hate. / I love the look, austere, immaculate, / Of landscapes drawn in pearly monotones.”
“There’s something in my very blood that owns / Bare hills, cold silver on a sky of slate, / A thread of water, churned to milky spate / Streaming through slanted pastures fenced with stones.”
questions.rationale: The claim has two parts: the speaker dislikes the Eastern Shore’s plenty, and she prefers a plainer landscape. In choice C she says there is something in “this richness” that she hates and that she loves the “austere, immaculate” look of landscapes in “pearly monotones,” which covers both parts.
reasons: These lines describe the plenty of the Eastern Shore but show no dislike of it and no attraction to a starker landscape.
The frost and cold mornings are part of the speaker’s description of the Eastern Shore’s autumn, painted in rich colors; they do not show her rejecting that place.
The speaker feels bound to bare hills and stony pastures, but these lines do not say she is repelled by the abundance she has imagined.
questions.text: “Wild Peaches” is a 1921 poem by Elinor Wylie. After imagining an idyllic existence amid the abundant fruit and game of Maryland’s Eastern Shore, the speaker unexpectedly reveals that such extravagant plenty repels her and that she is drawn instead to a starker, more restrained landscape: ______

questions.skill: Data completion (treated vs untreated against an expected baseline)
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: although purchases of taxed beverages were 4.4% lower than expected, purchases of untaxed beverages were 10.9% higher than expected.
purchases of taxed foods were 7.0% lower than expected, and purchases of taxed beverages were 4.4% lower than expected.
purchases of untaxed foods and untaxed beverages were both lower than expected, though by less than purchases of taxed products were.
purchases of untaxed foods were 1.7% lower than expected, a decline in a group of products that the taxes did not cover.
questions.rationale: To show that the drop in taxed purchases was not just part of a general decline in buying, the text needs a comparison in which taxed products fell while untaxed products did not. The table shows taxed beverages 4.4% below the expected amount and untaxed beverages 10.9% above it, so households bought more of the untaxed drinks even as they bought fewer taxed ones.
reasons: Both figures are accurate, but they describe only taxed products; without the untaxed groups for comparison, they cannot rule out a general decline in buying.
Purchases of untaxed beverages were 10.9% higher than expected, not lower.
The figure is accurate, but a drop in purchases of an untaxed group is what the objection would predict, so it does not cast doubt on that explanation.
questions.text: In January 2014, Mexico began taxing sugar-sweetened beverages at one peso per liter and nonessential energy-dense foods, such as chips and candy, at 8%. Using national household surveys conducted between 2008 and 2018, researchers at Mexico’s National Institute of Public Health estimated how much of each kind of product households would have bought after 2014 had the taxes never been introduced, then compared these expected amounts with what households actually bought. One possible objection is that falling purchases of taxed products might simply reflect households buying less of everything, but the data cast doubt on that explanation: ______
questions.table_title: Expected and Observed Weekly Purchases per Person after Mexico’s 2014 Taxes

questions.skill: T2 evaluation: a whole-school comparison reveals why within-school trials understated an effect
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: may have underestimated the medication’s benefits, since the classmates used for comparison were themselves partly protected.
may have overestimated the medication’s benefits, since the pupils selected for treatment were likely healthier to begin with.
probably measured the medication’s effect on attendance accurately but overlooked its effect on pupils’ test scores.
may have exaggerated how much untreated pupils gained from the treatment of the classmates around them.
questions.rationale: Earlier trials “compared randomly selected pupils within schools with their untreated classmates.” But Miguel and Kremer found that “untreated pupils in those schools also experienced fewer infections and attended more regularly” than pupils at untreated schools. If untreated classmates also benefit, comparing treated pupils with them makes the medication look less effective than it is, so the earlier trials may have understated its benefits.
reasons: The earlier trials treated “randomly selected pupils,” so there is no basis for thinking the treated pupils were healthier to begin with.
The text says nothing about test scores, and its findings suggest the earlier trials misjudged even the effect on attendance, since their comparison pupils also benefited.

Trials that compared treated pupils with their own classmates could not measure what those classmates gained; the new results show the untreated pupils gained, so that benefit was missed, not exaggerated.
questions.text: Intestinal worms spread among children through soil contaminated by infected people, so treating some children can reduce infections even among other children who remain untreated. Earlier trials of deworming medication had compared randomly selected pupils within schools with their untreated classmates, but in Kenya, economists Edward Miguel and Michael Kremer instead assigned entire schools to begin treatment at different times. Absences declined by roughly a quarter in the participating schools, and untreated pupils in those schools also experienced fewer infections and attended more regularly than pupils at schools that had not yet begun the program. These results suggest that the earlier trials ______

questions.skill: Indirect question: statement word order and a period
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: are there now two pots?
are there now two pots.
there are now two pots.
there are now two pots?
questions.rationale: “Why there are now two pots” is an indirect question: it is part of the statement “the neighbor asks why ....” An indirect question uses statement word order (“there are”) and ends with a period, not a question mark.
reasons: This option uses the inverted word order and question mark of a direct question, but the question is reported inside a statement.
The period is right, but an indirect question uses statement word order (“there are”), not inverted order.
The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement, so it should end with a period.
questions.text: In a traditional folktale about Nasreddin, a comic character familiar from Turkey to Central Asia, a neighbor lends Nasreddin a cooking pot. When it is returned with a smaller pot inside, the neighbor asks why ______ Nasreddin solemnly explains that the pot has given birth.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: plastic,
plastic
plastic:
plastic;
questions.rationale: The sentence lists three inventions, and because the items contain commas of their own, they are separated by semicolons (as after “folding”). The second item ends with “paper, twine, and plastic,” so a semicolon is needed there before “and Abuzz.”
reasons: A comma here makes “Abuzz” read as part of the list of materials and breaks the pattern of semicolons between the items.
With no mark, “plastic and Abuzz” run together, and the second and third items are not separated.
A colon cannot separate two items within a list.
questions.text: Stanford bioengineer Manu Prakash designs scientific tools that cost almost nothing to make. His lab’s inventions include the Foldscope, a paper microscope assembled by folding; the Paperfuge, a hand-powered centrifuge made from about 20 cents of paper, twine, and ______ and Abuzz, a method for identifying mosquito species from wingbeat sounds recorded on cell phones.

questions.skill: Comma before a trailing appositive whose noun carries a relative clause
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: thylacine, a
thylacine; a
thylacine. A
thylacine a
questions.rationale: The main clause ends with “known as the thylacine.” The noun phrase “a detail that, because the animal vanished ..., helps archaeologists date some of the engravings” is a nonessential element commenting on that whole clause, and a comma correctly separates it from the clause.
reasons: The verb “helps” belongs to the relative clause beginning with “that,” so “a detail that ... helps archaeologists date some of the engravings” is not an independent clause and cannot follow a semicolon.
A period after “thylacine” makes “A detail that ... helps archaeologists date some of the engravings” a sentence fragment.
With no comma, “thylacine a detail” runs the noun phrase into the clause it comments on.
questions.text: Murujuga, on the coast of Western Australia, may contain more rock engravings than any other location. Among its estimated one million petroglyphs are depictions of the doglike marsupial known as the ______ detail that, because the animal vanished from mainland Australia roughly 3,000 years ago, helps archaeologists date some of the engravings.

questions.skill: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing participial phrase (result after a complete clause)
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: placing
placed
had placed
places
questions.rationale: The words before the blank already form a complete sentence: the subject “a German-Russian research team” with the verb “radiocarbon-dated.” The participle “placing” begins a phrase that states the result of that dating without adding a second main verb.
reasons: “Placed” would be a second main verb attached to a complete clause with only a comma.
“Had placed” is a finite verb with no subject or conjunction joining it to the complete clause.
“Places” is a finite present-tense verb, so the sentence would join two main verbs with only a comma.
questions.text: In the 1890s, gold miners working a peat bog in Russia’s Ural Mountains unearthed fragments of the Shigir Idol, a towering larch sculpture carved with human faces. In 2018, a German-Russian research team radiocarbon-dated the wood to roughly 11,500 years ago, ______ the sculpture’s creation about two thousand years earlier than previous estimates.

questions.skill: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank before the main verb; the work, not its author, is the right subject
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Shen wrote the novella Border Town (1934), which, set in a river town near the Sichuan border,
the setting of Shen’s novella Border Town (1934), a river town near the Sichuan border,
Shen’s novella Border Town (1934), set in a river town near the Sichuan border,
set in a river town near the Sichuan border, Shen wrote the novella Border Town (1934), which
questions.rationale: A lyrical portrait of a region is a work of writing, so the noun right after the opening phrase must name the work. Choice C places “Shen’s novella Border Town (1934)” there, so the phrase correctly describes the novella, and the verb “follows” then tells what the novella does.
reasons: “Shen” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the writer himself is a lyrical portrait of the region.
“The setting” of the novella follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the setting is a portrait of the region and that the setting follows Cuicui.
After two modifiers, “Shen” is the subject, so the sentence says that Shen is both a portrait of the region and set in a river town.
questions.text: A lyrical portrait of western Hunan, the mountainous region of rivers and market towns where Chinese novelist Shen Congwen spent his childhood, ______ follows Cuicui, a ferryman’s granddaughter, as she comes of age.

questions.skill: Addition: a second contribution by the same person
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Instead,
For example,
Additionally,
Nevertheless,
questions.rationale: The first sentence describes one part of Sálim Ali’s work in those decades: his bird surveys. The blank sentence adds a separate contribution, a field guide for general readers. “Additionally” introduces this further item of the same kind.
reasons: Ali did not write the book in place of the surveys; the book is a further accomplishment alongside them.
Writing a field guide is not an example of conducting surveys of princely states; it is a different kind of work.
Nothing about the surveys would lead a reader to expect that Ali would not write a field guide, so a “despite this” word does not fit.
questions.text: Indian ornithologist Sálim Ali spent much of the 1930s conducting systematic bird surveys of princely states such as Hyderabad and Travancore. He documented where each species lived and bred. ______ he wrote The Book of Indian Birds (1941), an accessible field guide that introduced generations of readers to birdwatching.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Granted,
For example,
Hence,
Additionally,
questions.rationale: The text says the tablet is often called the earliest surviving Latin written by a woman. The last sentence limits that claim without overturning it: a scribe wrote most of the tablet, and only the final lines are in Severa’s own hand. “Granted” signals this kind of qualification.
reasons: A scribe writing most of the invitation is not an instance of the tablet being in Severa’s own hand; it qualifies that claim, since she wrote only the final lines.
Calling the tablet the earliest Latin by a woman does not cause a scribe to have written most of it.
The sentence is not one more point in favor of the claim; it qualifies the claim by showing that only part of the tablet is Severa’s writing.
questions.text: Around 100 CE, Claudia Severa, a Roman commander’s wife, sent her friend Sulpicia Lepidina a wooden tablet inviting her to a birthday celebration. Excavated at Vindolanda, near Hadrian’s Wall, the tablet is frequently identified as the earliest surviving Latin written in a woman’s own hand. ______ a professional scribe wrote out most of the invitation; Severa personally added only the final lines.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the ukulele and the charango. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The ukulele and the charango were both adapted from guitar-like instruments brought from Europe.
The ukulele has four strings, while the charango has ten.
The ukulele, which developed in Hawaii in the 1880s, was adapted from the machete, a small Portuguese guitar.
Traditionally, charangos were made with the shell of an armadillo.
questions.rationale: Both instruments were adapted from guitar-like instruments brought from Europe: the ukulele from the Portuguese machete and the charango from the Spanish vihuela. Choice A states that shared origin.
reasons: It contrasts the number of strings.
It describes only the ukulele.
It gives a fact about charangos only.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The ukulele is a small, four-stringed instrument that developed in Hawaii in the 1880s.
• It was adapted from the machete, a small guitar brought from Portugal by immigrants.
• The charango is a small, ten-stringed instrument that developed in the Andes.
• It was adapted from the vihuela, a guitar-like instrument brought from Spain by colonists.
• Charangos were traditionally made with the shell of an armadillo.

questions.skill: Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
questions.stem: The student wants to describe the Space in Between sculptures to an audience unfamiliar with Margarita Cabrera. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Mexican American artist Margarita Cabrera’s Space in Between features replicas of Southwestern desert plants sewn from Border Patrol uniforms and embroidered with immigrants’ accounts of migration.
Cabrera’s Space in Between sculptures, which replicate desert plants of the US Southwest, are sewn from the fabric of Border Patrol uniforms.
Mexican American artist Margarita Cabrera, whose work addresses immigration and labor, began Space in Between with a 2010 workshop in Houston.
Immigrants from Mexico and Central America who took part in Space in Between used Otomi techniques to embroider accounts of their migration.
questions.rationale: Readers who do not know Cabrera need to be told who she is, and the goal is still to describe the sculptures. Choice A identifies her as a Mexican American artist and describes the works: replicas of desert plants sewn from Border Patrol uniforms and embroidered with immigrants’ stories.
reasons: It describes the sculptures but uses Cabrera’s name as if readers already knew who she is.
It introduces Cabrera and says when and where the project began but never describes the sculptures.
It explains who embroidered the works and how, but it never says what the sculptures are or who Cabrera is.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Margarita Cabrera is a Mexican American artist whose work addresses immigration, labor, and border relations.
• Her project Space in Between began in 2010 with a workshop in Houston, Texas.
• Participants, immigrants from Mexico and Central America, created fabric replicas of desert plants indigenous to the US Southwest.
• The sculptures are sewn from the fabric of US Border Patrol uniforms.
• Using embroidery techniques of Mexico’s Otomi communities, participants stitched their personal accounts of migration onto the sculptures.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how the cuckoo catfish gets cichlids to shelter its young. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The cuckoo catfish deposits its eggs directly into a female cichlid’s mouth, where she then protects the young catfish for several weeks.
Hatching before the cichlid’s own eggs do, young cuckoo catfish feed on those eggs while sheltered inside the female cichlid’s mouth.
By slipping its eggs in with a spawning cichlid’s, the cuckoo catfish leads her to take them into her mouth as though they were her own.
The cuckoo catfish’s eggs hatch before the cichlid’s do, and the female cichlid then gathers the newly hatched catfish into her mouth along with her own eggs.
questions.rationale: The goal is to explain how the catfish gets cichlids to shelter its young. The notes link three facts: a mouthbrooding cichlid scoops her eggs into her mouth and keeps the young there, the catfish releases its eggs among hers while she spawns, and she gathers the catfish eggs along with her own. Choice C joins these facts: because the catfish mixes its eggs into the cichlid’s, she takes them into her mouth with her own.
reasons: The notes say the catfish releases its eggs among the cichlid’s eggs and the cichlid gathers them; the catfish does not place its eggs in her mouth.
It describes what the young catfish do once inside the cichlid’s mouth but not how they come to be there, so it does not explain how the catfish gets the cichlid to shelter them.
The notes say the cichlid gathers the catfish eggs along with her own right after spawning and that the catfish hatch inside her mouth; she does not gather young catfish that have already hatched.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In Lake Tanganyika, in East Africa, many cichlid species are mouthbrooders.
• Immediately after spawning, a mouthbrooding female collects her fertilized eggs in her mouth, where the developing young remain protected for several weeks.
• The cuckoo catfish (Synodontis multipunctatus) deposits its own eggs among a cichlid’s eggs during spawning.
• The cichlid then collects the catfish eggs in her mouth along with her own.
• The catfish embryos hatch first and consume the cichlid’s own eggs inside her mouth.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: adopt
abandon
patent
reinterpret
questions.rationale: After his first stories, Töpffer kept working in the form: he published several more books and wrote essays about it. So he did not abandon it.
reasons: “Did not adopt the form” would mean he never took it up, but he published several books in it.
Nothing in the text concerns legal rights to the form; it describes Töpffer publishing more books and writing essays.
The text gives no sign of whether he reinterpreted the form; the second sentence explains that he kept making and writing about it.
questions.text: Swiss schoolteacher Rodolphe Töpffer initially drew humorous picture stories simply to entertain his students, but he did not ______ the form after those early experiments. He subsequently published several illustrated books of this kind, now regarded as possibly the earliest European comics, and composed theoretical essays examining the form.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: foregrounded
fabricated
repatriated
elided
questions.rationale: To elide something is to leave it out or pass over it in silence. The installation used objects the society owned but seldom displayed, and the empty pedestals stand for people its exhibitions had left out. What Wilson exposed, then, is what the exhibitions had long omitted.
reasons: To foreground something is to give it prominence. The text says the society seldom displayed the objects Wilson used, so its exhibitions had not given them prominence.
Fabricated means invented or faked. Wilson used objects from the society’s own collection, and nothing suggests the displays had made anything up.
Repatriated means returned to a country of origin, a word from museum practice. Nothing in the text concerns returning objects; the installation is about what the displays left out.
questions.text: Fred Wilson’s 1992 installation Mining the Museum used objects that the Maryland Historical Society owned but seldom displayed to expose what its exhibitions had long ______. In a case of ornate silver vessels, Wilson placed iron slave shackles, and beside a row of busts he installed empty pedestals inscribed with the names of Harriet Tubman, Benjamin Banneker, and Frederick Douglass.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: inextricable from
emblematic of
decoupled from
antecedent to
questions.rationale: To be decoupled from something is to be separated from it, so that the two no longer change together. Juveniles kept on algae “stopped growing” at about 16 to 18 millimeters, “remaining that size for years,” so a seastar of that size could be young or several years old: its size can be largely separated from its age.
reasons: Inextricable from means impossible to separate from. The text shows the opposite: juveniles stopped growing and kept the same size “for years,” so their size came apart from their age.
Emblematic of means serving as a symbol of. Nothing in the text treats a seastar’s size as a symbol of its age; the point is that size and age can come apart.
Antecedent to means coming before. The text says nothing about size coming before age; it shows that size stopped changing while the seastars kept getting older.
questions.text: Crown-of-thorns seastars, notorious coral predators, are herbivorous as juveniles, feeding on algae. In experiments by Dione Deaker and colleagues, juveniles maintained on algae for six and a half years reached a diameter of about 16 to 18 millimeters and then stopped growing, remaining that size for years until they were finally offered coral; in this species, then, size can be largely ______ age.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that libraries in other dry, remote regions should replace their delivery vehicles with camels
To describe a library service and explain why it uses an unusual means of transport
To explain why many families in northeastern Kenya have stopped moving with their herds
To compare the numbers of readers served by the library branches in Garissa and Wajir
questions.rationale: The text describes the Kenya National Library Service’s camel library, which carries books from Garissa to nearby communities, and explains why camels are used: many people in the region are nomadic herders, camels are a familiar means of transport that can cross the harsh terrain, and most schools in the region lie beyond the reach of four-wheel-drive vehicles. Choice B states this purpose.
reasons: The text describes one service in one region; it makes no recommendation to other libraries.
The text says many people in the region “are nomadic herders who move with their livestock,” not that they have stopped moving.
The text mentions Wajir only as the place the service was extended to and gives no numbers of readers for either town.
questions.text: In October 1996, the Kenya National Library Service began carrying books from its branch in Garissa, in the country’s dry northeast, to surrounding communities on the backs of three camels. Many people in the region are nomadic herders who move with their livestock. Camels, a familiar and valued means of transport in these communities, can cross the region’s harsh terrain with heavy loads. Most schools in the region lay deep in the savanna, beyond the reach of four-wheel-drive vehicles, and the service was later extended to the town of Wajir.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Sax, Gaines, and Brown (Text 2) most likely respond to the expectation presented in the underlined sentence in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that introduced plants have generally made the island ecosystems they’ve entered healthier than before
By pointing out that many native island plants had already gone extinct before Europeans arrived
By suggesting that most island extinctions have been caused by predators rather than by competitors
By noting that, at least among plants, introductions have tended to raise rather than lower island species counts
questions.rationale: Text 1 says introduced species are widely expected to leave islands with fewer species. Sax, Gaines, and Brown found that for plants, extinctions were relatively few while many introduced species became established, so plant species counts on islands have roughly doubled. They would point out that, for plants at least, introductions have raised rather than lowered the number of species, which limits how far the expectation holds.
reasons: The researchers explicitly caution that more species does not mean the ecosystems are better off.
Text 2 compares records from before and after colonization but says nothing about extinctions that happened before Europeans arrived.
Neither text compares the roles of predators and competitors in causing island extinctions.
questions.text:
Text 1

Ecologists have documented many cases in which species introduced by people crowd out native species. Islands have been especially vulnerable: their native plants and animals often evolved without mainland competitors or predators, and introductions there have been linked to many extinctions. <u>Thus, the arrival of nonnative species is widely expected to leave island ecosystems with fewer species than they originally supported.</u>

Text 2

Dov Sax, Steven Gaines, and James Brown compared records of the plant species found on oceanic islands before and after European colonization. Native plants had gone extinct, but relatively few of them, while large numbers of introduced plants had established wild populations. In New Zealand, about 2,000 nonnative species have become naturalized. Overall, plant species counts on the islands have roughly doubled—though the researchers warn that this doesn’t mean the ecosystems are better off.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Kauri stumps store water during the day and pass it on to neighboring trees at night, when those trees need it most.
Kauri trees whose roots have fused with a stump grow more slowly because they must share their water with it.
Research on a kauri stump suggests that trees joined by their roots may work together rather than as fully separate individuals.
Because the kauri stump had no leaves, it took in most of its water directly from the soil rather than through its neighbors.
questions.rationale: Although trees are “typically regarded as separate individuals,” the stump’s water levels rose and fell in step with its neighbors’ water use, and the researchers propose that connected trees “may share a ‘communal physiology.’” Choice C states this finding at the passage’s level of certainty.
reasons: The timing is reversed: the stump’s water levels declined by day, when its neighbors drew up the most water, and recovered at night, so the stump depends on its neighbors rather than storing water and passing it on to them.
The text says nothing about how fast the neighboring trees grow.
The stump’s water levels tracked its neighbors’ water use, which points to a link through fused roots, not to independent uptake from the soil.
questions.text: Trees are typically regarded as separate individuals, but the roots of neighboring trees of the same species frequently fuse, forming natural grafts. Martin Bader and Sebastian Leuzinger examined a leafless kauri stump in a New Zealand forest that had remained alive despite being unable to photosynthesize, measuring water movement in the stump and in surrounding kauri trees. The stump’s water levels declined during the day, when its neighbors were drawing up the most water, and recovered at night, when they drew up little. The researchers propose that trees connected this way may share a “communal physiology.”

questions.skill: Literary quotation illustrates a single-trait claim
questions.stem: Which quotation from Botchan most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Because of an hereditary recklessness, I have been playing always a losing game since my childhood.”
“Father did not like me in the least, and mother always sided with my big brother.”
“My brother was to be seen studying English hard, saying that he was going to be a businessman.”
“Kantaro was, it happens, a mollycoddle. Nevertheless he had the temerity to come over the fence to our yard and steal my chestnuts.”
questions.rationale: The claim is that the narrator’s habit of acting without thinking has caused him trouble all his life. In choice A he blames a “hereditary recklessness” for making him play “a losing game” ever since childhood.
reasons: The narrator describes how his parents treated him, not his own recklessness.
This describes the brother’s ambitions, not the narrator’s behavior.
This describes a neighbor boy who stole chestnuts, not the narrator’s own rashness.
questions.text: Botchan is a 1906 novel by Natsume Sōseki, translated in 1919 by Yasotaro Morri. In the novel, the narrator admits that his impulsive nature has caused him trouble throughout his life: ______

questions.skill: Hypothetical finding supports a conclusion about origin (source of a material)
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Skowronek and colleagues’ conclusion?
choices: In parts of West Africa, manillas were worn as jewelry and used in marriage payments as well as to buy goods.
The chemical signature of the lead in the Benin Bronzes matches that of manillas made with Rhineland ores but not that of manillas made with other ores.
Manillas made in England in the 1700s and 1800s have chemical signatures similar to those of other brass objects produced in England during the same period.
The chemical signature of the lead in the Benin Bronzes closely matches that of lead ores mined in West Africa.
questions.rationale: The researchers concluded that the brass in the Benin Bronzes came mainly from the Rhineland. If the metal in the bronzes carries the same chemical signature as manillas made from Rhineland ores, and not that of manillas made from other ores, the bronzes were probably cast from Rhineland brass, so Choice B supports the conclusion.
reasons: How manillas were used in West Africa says nothing about where their metal came from.
This finding concerns manillas and brass made in England, not the metal of the Benin Bronzes, so it cannot link the bronzes to the Rhineland.
A match with West African ores would suggest that the metal came from Africa rather than from the Rhineland, weakening the conclusion.
questions.text: Many of the Benin Bronzes, the sculptures and commemorative plaques cast in the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria, were made from brass that European traders transported to West Africa from the late 1400s onward. The brass arrived in the form of manillas, horseshoe-shaped rings that functioned as currency. The geographic origin of their metal, however, has long been uncertain. After chemically analyzing manillas recovered from shipwrecks and other archaeological sites, Tobias Skowronek and colleagues concluded that the principal source of the brass in the Benin Bronzes was the Rhineland region of Germany, where brass was made with zinc and lead ores mined nearby.

questions.skill: Hypothetical finding discriminates between two explanations (fewer severe freezes versus higher average temperature)
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Cavanaugh and colleagues’ conclusion?
choices: Mangrove area increased most at sites where severe freezes had become less frequent, including sites where average annual temperature showed no upward trend.
Mangrove area expanded more rapidly during the 2000s than during the 1980s, a period over which Florida’s climate became noticeably warmer in several respects.
In experiments, mangrove seedlings exposed to temperatures below −4°C survived about as often as seedlings that were kept above freezing.
As mangroves spread into the salt marshes, they shaded out marsh grasses and altered the habitat available to wading birds and crabs.
questions.rationale: The researchers conclude that mangroves spread because severe cold snaps became rarer, not because average temperatures rose. Choice A ties the growth to fewer severe freezes even at sites where average temperature did not rise, so the expansion there cannot be credited to the rival explanation. That makes A the finding that most directly supports the conclusion.
reasons: A warming climate brings both higher averages and fewer cold snaps, so faster spread during a warmer period does not show which of the two changes drove it.
If seedlings survived severe cold as well as mild conditions, fewer cold snaps would matter little, which weakens rather than supports the conclusion.
This describes what the mangroves did to the marshes, not why they were able to spread.
questions.text: Mangroves, salt-tolerant trees that are typically killed by hard freezes, have been spreading north into salt marshes along Florida’s Atlantic coast. Analyzing satellite images taken each summer from 1984 to 2011, Kyle Cavanaugh and colleagues found that mangrove area roughly doubled near the northern limit of the trees’ range. Researchers have offered two explanations for the expansion: a gradual rise in the region’s average temperatures, or a decline in the frequency of severe cold snaps, when temperatures fall below about −4°C. Cavanaugh and colleagues concluded that the second explanation better accounts for the mangroves’ spread.

questions.skill: X but not Y: tariffed and untariffed goods rose alike, so a washer-only estimate of the cost falls short
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: be accurate, since the tariffs applied only to washers and not to dryers.
understate that cost, since manufacturers again moved production to countries that the tariffs did not cover.
understate that cost, since consumers also paid more for a product that the tariffs did not cover.
overstate that cost, since washer prices had barely changed after the earlier duties on particular countries.
questions.rationale: Dryers were not taxed, yet their prices rose about as much as washer prices did, and the two are often bought together, so the tariffs raised what consumers paid for dryers as well. An estimate calculated only from washer prices would leave that extra cost out and so would come in too low, as C says.
reasons: The tariffs did cover only washers, but dryer prices rose by about as much as washer prices; an estimate that ignored dryers would miss that increase, so it would not be accurate.

Moving production abroad is what happened after the earlier duties; the 2018 tariffs covered washers from virtually all exporting countries and washer prices rose, and a move abroad would not make a washer-only estimate too low in any case.
What happened after the earlier duties says nothing about the size of the 2018 cost, and the rise in dryer prices means a washer-only estimate would leave costs out, not count too much.
questions.text: In 2012, the United States imposed antidumping duties on washing machines from South Korea and Mexico, and in 2016 on those from China, yet washer prices barely changed, partly because manufacturers relocated production to other countries. In 2018, by contrast, tariffs covered washers from virtually all exporting countries. Economists Aaron Flaaen, Ali Hortaçsu, and Felix Tintelnot found that washer prices subsequently rose by nearly 12 percent and that the prices of clothes dryers, which were not taxed but are often bought along with washers, increased by about the same amount. These findings suggest that an estimate of the tariffs’ cost to US consumers calculated only from washer prices would ______

questions.skill: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: sailors,
sailors
sailors;
sailors.
questions.rationale: The dependent clause “Although many early carvings were made for sale to visiting sailors” introduces the main clause “the artists filled them with figures from traditional Haida narratives.” A comma correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause.
reasons: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs straight into the main clause; a comma is needed after “sailors.”
A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Although many early carvings were made for sale to visiting sailors” is a dependent clause.
The period leaves “Although many early carvings were made for sale to visiting sailors” as a fragment.
questions.text: Haida artists have carved argillite, a soft black stone quarried exclusively on the islands of Haida Gwaii, since the early 1800s. Although many early carvings were made for sale to visiting ______ the artists filled them with figures from traditional Haida narratives.

questions.skill: Closing a comma pair around a nonrestrictive clause
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Wellington
Wellington,
Wellington—
Wellington;
questions.rationale: The clause “which opened in 1982 just outside Wellington” adds information about the first kōhanga reo and is opened by a comma after “reo.” A comma after “Wellington” closes the pair, and the sentence continues with its main verb, “inspired.”
reasons: Without a comma after “Wellington,” the clause opened by the comma after “reo” is never closed, so it runs into the main verb “inspired.”
The supplementary clause opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma; a dash can’t pair with a comma.
A semicolon would separate the subject “The first kōhanga reo” from its verb “inspired,” and neither side is a main clause.
questions.text: In a kōhanga reo, or “language nest,” preschool children are immersed exclusively in te reo Māori, the Indigenous language of New Zealand. The first kōhanga reo, which opened in 1982 just outside ______ inspired the establishment of hundreds more nationwide within a decade, helping to revive the language.

questions.skill: Complex series: semicolon after an item with a supplement, comma inside the option
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: plazas, many with benches and playgrounds;
plazas many with benches and playgrounds;
plazas; many with benches and playgrounds,
plazas, many with benches and playgrounds,
questions.rationale: The planners did three things, and the items contain commas, so semicolons separate them, as the semicolon before “and closed” shows. Within the first item, a comma sets off the supplement “many with benches and playgrounds” from “plazas,” and a semicolon ends the item.
reasons: The phrase “many with benches and playgrounds” describes the plazas and must be set off from “plazas” with a comma.
The semicolon cuts the first item in half, and the comma after “playgrounds” fails to separate it from the second item.
A comma after “playgrounds” does not match the semicolon used later between the second and third items.
questions.text: Barcelona created its first superblock, a grid of nine city blocks, in 2016. Within it, municipal planners converted intersections into ______ reduced the speed limit to 10 kilometers per hour; and closed the interior streets to through traffic, admitting only residents, deliveries, and emergency vehicles.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: will trace
have traced
traced
are tracing
questions.rationale: The phrase “In a 2016 study” places the work at a specific, finished time in the past, and the blank is the second verb in a predicate whose first verb, “mapped,” is in the simple past. The simple past “traced” fits both cues.
reasons: “Will trace” places the findings of a 2016 study in the future and does not match the past-tense “mapped.”
The present perfect “have traced” is not used with a specific past time such as “in a 2016 study,” and it breaks the parallel with “mapped.”
“Are tracing” describes an action in progress now, not part of a study completed in 2016.
questions.text: Because most folktales circulated orally for centuries before being transcribed, their ages are difficult to estimate. In a 2016 study, Sara Graça da Silva and anthropologist Jamshid Tehrani mapped 275 magic tales onto a phylogeny of Indo-European languages and ______ one tale, “The Smith and the Devil,” back to the Bronze Age, long before the emergence of the literary record.

questions.skill: Tense: past perfect (had already + participle) shared by a compound predicate, anchored by a later past event (when, in 1287, ...) 17 words after the blank
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: had already traveled
already traveled
has already traveled
was already traveling
questions.rationale: The journey and the years in Persia came before a later past event, the ruler’s appointment in 1287 (“when, in 1287, its ruler appointed him”). To show that one past action was finished before another, the past perfect is needed: “had already traveled,” whose “had” also carries “resided,” places both actions before that moment.
reasons: “Already traveled” is past, but the simple past doesn’t show that the journey and the years in Persia were over before another past event, the appointment in 1287; that order calls for the past perfect.
“Has already traveled” ties the journey to the present, not to a time before the ruler appointed him in 1287.
“Was already traveling” presents the journey as still under way when he was appointed, but by 1287 it was over and he had been living in Persia for years.
questions.text: Rabban Bar Sauma, a Christian monk born near present-day Beijing, ______ thousands of kilometers westward on a pilgrimage toward Jerusalem and resided for several years in Mongol-controlled Persia when, in 1287, its ruler appointed him ambassador to European monarchs.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: In many cases,
However,
Similarly,
Previously,
questions.rationale: The first sentence gives an overall verdict: results have been broadly encouraging. The blank sentence makes a stronger claim about how often the crossings work very well, citing drops of more than 80 percent where they were paired with fencing. “In many cases” signals this shift from the overall picture to what happens at many sites.
reasons: The large drop in collisions supports the encouraging results rather than contrasting with them.
The sentence does not describe a second, similar case; it gives evidence about the same crossings.
The drop in collisions came after the crossings were built, not before the studies described in the first sentence.
questions.text: Since the 1990s, transportation agencies have constructed overpasses and tunnels that allow wildlife to cross busy highways. Evaluations of these structures have produced broadly encouraging results. ______ collisions between vehicles and large mammals such as deer and elk have declined by more than 80 percent where crossings were combined with fencing.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: for example,
therefore,
similarly,
by contrast,
questions.rationale: The sentence sets two tuning systems side by side. Just intonation gives pure chords in one key; equal temperament gives up that purity in exchange for freedom to change keys. “By contrast” signals that the second system differs from the first on the same point.
reasons: Equal temperament is not an instance of just intonation or of its pure chords; it is a different system with the opposite result.
Tuning intervals to whole-number ratios does not cause equal temperament to divide the octave into equal steps; the second system is an alternative to the first, not its result.
The two systems are built the same way in the sentence, but they do opposite things: one keeps intervals pure, the other makes them slightly impure.
questions.text: Musicians have long debated how to tune a scale. In just intonation, each interval is tuned to a simple whole-number ratio of frequencies, so chords in a single key sound perfectly consonant; ______ equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical steps, leaving every interval except the octave slightly impure but permitting music to modulate freely between keys.

questions.stem: The student wants to specify the animal family to which the kinkajou belongs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The kinkajou is a small mammal inhabiting the rainforests of Central and South America.
The kinkajou belongs to the raccoon family, which also includes raccoons and coatis.
Because of its grasping tail, the kinkajou, a rainforest mammal, is frequently mistaken for a monkey.
The kinkajou spends most of its life in trees, gripping branches with its prehensile tail.
questions.rationale: The notes say that the kinkajou belongs to the raccoon family. Choice B specifies that family and names two of its other members.
reasons: It specifies where the kinkajou lives, not the family it belongs to.
It says what the kinkajou is often mistaken for, which is not the family it actually belongs to.
It describes how the kinkajou lives in trees, not its family.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The kinkajou is a small mammal inhabiting the rainforests of Central and South America.
• It spends most of its life in trees, gripping branches with its prehensile tail.
• Because of this grasping tail, it is frequently mistaken for a monkey.
• However, the kinkajou belongs to the raccoon family.
• Other members of this family include raccoons and coatis.

questions.skill: Difference on a named attribute (surface), wrong-dimension trap
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how the surface of buncheong ware differs from that of celadon. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Whereas celadon’s surface is a translucent blue-green glaze, buncheong ware is covered with white slip before it is glazed.
Celadon flourished under the Goryeo dynasty, which ended in 1392, while buncheong ware gained popularity after the Joseon dynasty began that year.
Buncheong pieces were covered with white slip, a liquid clay that potters often brushed with loose patterns.
Celadon and buncheong ware are both distinctive styles of stoneware developed by Korean potters.
questions.rationale: The goal asks about surfaces. Choice A contrasts them directly: celadon has a translucent blue-green glaze, while buncheong ware is first covered with white slip.
reasons: It contrasts when the two styles were popular, not their surfaces.
It describes the surface of buncheong ware but never mentions celadon.
It states what the two styles have in common, not how they differ.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Korean potters have developed several distinctive styles of stoneware.
• Celadon, which flourished during the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), is coated with a translucent blue-green glaze.
• Some celadon is inlaid with cranes and clouds.
• Buncheong ware gained popularity after the Joseon dynasty began in 1392.
• Before glazing, buncheong pieces are covered with white slip, a liquid clay, often brushed with loose patterns.

questions.stem: The student wants to summarize the history of waru waru. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: For more than two millennia, waru waru have protected crops from frost around Lake Titicaca, and in the 1980s their potato harvests surpassed those of neighboring fields.
Waru waru protect crops from frost because their canals absorb solar heat during the day and release it overnight.
First built by researchers and local farmers in the 1980s, waru waru now protect potato crops from frost on the high plains around Lake Titicaca.
Andean farmers built waru waru more than two millennia ago and later abandoned them, but fields rebuilt in the 1980s outproduced neighboring fields.
questions.rationale: The notes give three stages: farmers built waru waru more than two millennia ago, later abandoned them for centuries, and in the 1980s rebuilt some fields that outproduced neighboring ones. Choice D covers all three in order.
reasons: It presents waru waru as protecting crops for more than two millennia without a break, but the notes say the fields remained unused for centuries before the 1980s.
It explains how the canals protect crops from frost, not the history of waru waru.
Researchers and farmers rebuilt waru waru in the 1980s; Andean farmers first built them more than two millennia earlier.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Waru waru are raised planting beds separated by water-filled canals, built on the high plains around Lake Titicaca.
• Andean farmers began building waru waru more than two millennia ago.
• The canals absorb solar heat during the day and release it overnight, protecting crops from frost.
• Farmers later abandoned the fields, which then remained unused for centuries.
• In the 1980s, researchers and local farmers rebuilt several fields, whose potato harvests surpassed those of neighboring fields.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ineligible
hesitant
invited
obligated
questions.rationale: Lee could not use the newly extended voting rights “because the Chinese Exclusion Act still applied to her as a Chinese immigrant.” A law that keeps someone from voting makes that person ineligible to vote.
reasons: A woman who rode in a suffrage parade was not unsure about voting; the text gives a law, not her feelings, as the reason.
The Chinese Exclusion Act kept Lee from voting; it did not invite her to vote.
Nothing suggests Lee was required to vote; the text explains why she could not.
questions.text: In 1912, Mabel Ping-Hua Lee, a Chinese immigrant raised in New York City, rode on horseback in the city’s women’s suffrage parade. Yet after the Nineteenth Amendment extended voting rights to women in 1920, Lee herself remained ______ to vote, because the Chinese Exclusion Act still applied to her as a Chinese immigrant.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: profusion
verisimilitude
economy
spontaneity
questions.rationale: Here “economy” means a careful, sparing use of resources. The drawings use only black and white, faint lines, and a few forms on otherwise empty sheets, and Carrier observed that Mohamedi built varied compositions from extremely restricted means. That is a remarkable economy: doing a great deal with very little.
reasons: “Profusion” means a great abundance. The compositions are varied, but the text stresses that they are made from extremely restricted means, so abundance does not describe the drawings.
“Verisimilitude” is the appearance of being true to life. The drawings are abstract, so they make no attempt to look like real things.
“Spontaneity” is acting on impulse. The text describes how little the drawings are made of, not how impulsively they were made, and Carrier’s point concerns restricted means.
questions.text: Nearly all of Nasreen Mohamedi’s drawings are black-and-white abstractions, many consisting of little more than fields of faint parallel lines or geometric forms placed at the center of otherwise empty sheets. The drawings display a remarkable ______: as critic David Carrier observed, Mohamedi built surprisingly varied compositions from extremely restricted means.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: contingent on
incidental to
conducive to
inimical to
questions.rationale: Something conducive to an outcome helps bring it about. Because the meeting schedule was set by chance, the later differences can be traced to the meetings themselves: clients who met weekly went on to socialize more and to default less. So the frequent meetings helped build the informal ties that help borrowers withstand hardship.
reasons: Contingent on means depending on. The meeting schedule was assigned at random, so it did not depend on any ties among the clients; the text shows the ties following from the meetings, not the other way around.
Incidental to means only loosely connected to. The weekly groups ended up with more social contact and fewer defaults, so the meetings were closely connected to the ties, not peripheral to them.
Inimical to means harmful to. Clients who met more often socialized more, so frequent meetings strengthened the ties rather than damaging them.
questions.text: In a field experiment in India, economist Benjamin Feigenberg and colleagues randomly assigned first-time microfinance borrowers to repayment groups that met either weekly or monthly. Nearly two years later, members of weekly groups socialized more frequently and were substantially less likely to default on their second loan, suggesting that frequent meetings were ______ the informal ties that help borrowers withstand financial hardship.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: The speaker describes clouds breaking apart and then explains what causes them to form again.
The speaker praises the strength of the shapes in the clouds and then predicts that the shapes will last.
The speaker describes what the cloud shapes are striving for and then admits that they cannot succeed.
The speaker imagines animals living in the sky and then wishes that she could join them there.
questions.rationale: The first six lines describe what each cloud shape seems to want: the polar bears to reach where they belong, the mountains to stand firm in one place, the sheep to stop and graze. The last two lines say “never can these things be done, / Although they try and try!” The speaker describes the shapes’ efforts and then acknowledges a limit, as choice C says.
reasons: The lines say nothing about how clouds form or break apart; they describe what the shapes seem to want.
The mountains do try to stand “firm and strong,” but the speaker ends by saying the shapes can never do what they try to do, not that they will last.
The speaker imagines the shapes’ wishes, not her own, and never wishes to join them.
questions.text:
The following text is from Effie Lee Newsome’s poem “Sky Pictures,” published in the 1927 anthology Caroling Dusk. The speaker has been watching clouds shaped like polar bears, mountains, and sheep.

The polar bears would like to get
Where polar bears belong.
The mountains try so hard to stand
In one place firm and strong.
The little sheep all want to stop
And pasture in the sky,
But never can these things be done,
Although they try and try!

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the hypothesis about the narwhal tusk presented in Text 1?
choices: By questioning whether the tubules in the tusk are actually connected to nerves
