By suggesting that the tusk is used mainly to locate prey rather than to detect changes in salinity
By arguing that it leaves unexplained why the tusk is largely restricted to males and grows disproportionately long in larger ones
By agreeing that the tusk is a sensory organ but suggesting that female narwhals depend on it less than males do
questions.rationale: Text 1 presents Nweeia’s hypothesis that the tusk is a sensory organ. The author of Text 2 points out that a sensory organ should appear in both sexes, yet tusks are rare in females, and cites Graham’s finding that tusk length grows disproportionately with body size, as sexually selected traits do. The author would therefore say the sensory hypothesis leaves both of these patterns unexplained.
reasons: Text 2 does not dispute the anatomy described in Text 1; it questions what the tusk is for.
Text 2 does not propose any sensory use, such as finding prey; it argues for a role in competition among males.
Text 2 does not accept that the tusk is a sensory organ; it uses the tusk’s rarity in females against that idea.
questions.text:
Text 1

The narwhal’s spiraled tusk is an elongated canine tooth projecting from the left side of the upper jaw. In 2014, dental researcher Martin Nweeia reported that the tusk’s porous outer layer admits seawater into microscopic tubules connected to nerves in its core. When his team alternately exposed the tusks of live narwhals to salty and fresh water, the animals’ heart rates changed. The tusk, Nweeia proposed, functions as a sensory organ.

Text 2

An organ essential for sensing the environment would be expected in both sexes, yet tusks are nearly universal among male narwhals and rare among females. Analyzing measurements of 245 adult males collected over 35 years, biologist Zackary Graham found that tusk length increased disproportionately with body size and varied far more among similarly sized males than did the width of the tail flukes—patterns characteristic of sexually selected traits.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The crucian carp avoids oxygen-poor water in winter by moving from frozen ponds into larger lakes.
Biologists have found that ethanol stored in the crucian carp’s tissues helps protect it from freezing temperatures.
The crucian carp can survive long periods without oxygen because it turns a harmful by-product into a substance it can release.
Unlike most vertebrates, the crucian carp produces energy without forming lactate when the water around it runs out of oxygen.
questions.rationale: The text explains that lactate builds up to harmful levels in most vertebrates without oxygen, but that the crucian carp converts lactate into ethanol and releases it into the water, surviving without oxygen for 140 days in experiments. Choice C states this finding in general terms.
reasons: The text says the fish survives in ponds sealed by ice; it never says it moves elsewhere.
The fish releases ethanol into the water rather than storing it, and the text does not link ethanol to resisting cold.
The carp does form lactate; what sets it apart is that it converts the lactate into ethanol.
questions.text: Most vertebrates cannot survive for long without oxygen: when their cells are forced to generate energy without it, a by-product called lactate accumulates to damaging levels. The crucian carp, a fish inhabiting ponds and lakes in northern Europe, is a remarkable exception. In winter, ice can seal its ponds off from the atmosphere, and the water may become completely depleted of oxygen. Biologists have determined that the fish converts lactate into ethanol, which it excretes into the surrounding water rather than accumulating in its tissues, and in experiments crucian carp have survived without oxygen for 140 days.

questions.skill: Quotation from a participant illustrates a claim (two parts: belonging, linked to leaving work)
questions.stem: Which quotation from a shed member would best illustrate the student’s claim?
choices: “I’ve learned more about woodworking here in one year than I did in my whole life before, and now I can repair almost anything that breaks around the house.”
“When I retired, I didn’t know where I fit in anymore. Here, the other fellows expect me on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and if I don’t turn up, someone phones to check on me.”
“Last spring our shed built benches for the primary school down the road, and the children painted them in bright colors.”
“My doctor told me to stay active after I retired, so I joined the shed to keep my hands busy and get out of the house.”
questions.rationale: The student claims that sheds restore a sense of belonging that many men lost after retiring. In Choice B the member says he no longer knew where he fit in after retiring, and now the other members expect him and check on him if he is absent, which shows him belonging to the group again.
reasons: This member describes gaining practical skills, not a sense of belonging.
Building benches for a school shows what the shed does for the town, not how members feel about belonging.
This member mentions retiring and wanting to stay active, but says nothing about feeling part of a group.
questions.text: Men’s sheds are community workshops where members, mostly older men, gather to build, repair, and make things together. The first sheds opened in Australia in the 1990s, partly to improve the health of older men. Today there are hundreds in Australia alone, along with many in Ireland and the United Kingdom. After interviewing members of a local shed, a student claims that sheds give older men a sense of belonging that many lost after retirement.

questions.skill: Literary quotation: two-part claim (starving, yet too proud to ask for food)
questions.stem: Which quotation from Hunger most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “It was the very deuce that one must let oneself turn into a living deformity for sheer hunger’s sake.”

“Was it not I who, no later than yesterday, had decided to pass her proudly by if I met her, to treat her with the greatest indifference? Instead of that, I had only aroused her compassion, and coaxed an alms from her.”
“I was not in the least proud; I dared make the assertion roundly, that I was one of the least arrogant beings up to date.”
“But supposing I were to go in and beg for a bit of bread? Surely that was a fleeting thought, a flash; it could never really have occurred to me seriously.”
questions.rationale: The claim has two parts: the narrator is starving, and pride stops him from asking for food. In choice D he considers begging for “a bit of bread” but dismisses the idea as something that “could never really have occurred to me seriously,” so his hunger meets a refusal to ask.
reasons: The narrator complains that hunger is wasting his body, but nothing in the line shows pride keeping him from asking for food.
He recalls meaning to pass a woman proudly and then accepting her charity; the line involves pride but not food, and it shows him taking help rather than refusing to ask.
Here the narrator insists that he is not proud at all, as he prepares to return to a lodging house; the line neither shows pride nor concerns food.
questions.text: Hunger is an 1890 novel by Knut Hamsun, translated in 1899 by George Egerton. Its narrator, an impoverished young writer wandering the streets of Christiania (now Oslo), is frequently starving, yet his pride prevents him from asking anyone for food: ______

questions.skill: Hypothetical finding supports a no-harm conclusion from a case-control study; the key needs the change on the treated street measured against the change on the comparison street
questions.stem: Which finding from Arancibia and colleagues’ surveys, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion about the bike lane?
choices: From before the pilot to during it, average monthly customer spending rose by a larger percentage on Bloor Street than on the comparison street.
During the pilot, customers on Bloor Street spent more money per month, on average, than customers on the comparison street did.
From before the pilot to during it, merchants on the comparison street reported a larger increase in customers served than merchants on Bloor Street did.
During the pilot, shoppers on Bloor Street who arrived by bicycle spent less per visit, on average, but visited more often than shoppers who arrived by car.
questions.rationale: The researchers surveyed “a comparable retail street that received no bike lane, before and during the pilot.” Business on any street can rise or fall for reasons that have nothing to do with a bike lane, so the change on that street shows roughly how Bloor Street would have fared without one. To show that the bike lane did no harm, then, Bloor Street’s change from before the pilot to during it must be compared with the comparison street’s change over the same period. If spending rose by a larger percentage on Bloor Street than on the street with no bike lane, Bloor Street did at least as well as it would have without the bike lane, so choice A supports the conclusion.
reasons: Comparing the two streets only during the pilot ignores where each started; Bloor Street may have had higher spending before the bike lane and still lost ground during the pilot, so this does not show the bike lane did no harm.

If the comparison street gained more customers than Bloor Street over the same period, Bloor Street did worse than it would likely have done without the bike lane, which suggests the bike lane may have hurt business.

Knowing that cyclists spend less per visit but visit more often does not say whether total spending on Bloor Street fell, held steady, or rose relative to what would have happened without the bike lane.
questions.text: Merchants frequently oppose replacing on-street parking with bike lanes, anticipating that they will lose customers who arrive by car. In 2016, the city of Toronto removed 136 parking spaces from a stretch of Bloor Street, a busy downtown retail corridor, and installed a pilot bike lane. To determine the lane’s effects, Daniel Arancibia and colleagues surveyed merchants and shoppers both on Bloor Street and on a comparable retail street that received no bike lane, before and during the pilot. Based on these surveys, the researchers concluded that the bike lane had no negative economic impact on businesses along Bloor Street.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: twentieth-century feminist scholars misjudged Kempe’s importance, since the monks of Mount Grace valued her book only as a text to be read aloud to their community.
treating Kempe as a credible religious figure was not an innovation of twentieth-century scholarship, since the monks who owned her book had already done so.
Kempe’s visions and weeping were genuine mystical experiences rather than signs of hysteria, since monks familiar with such devotion recognized them as authentic.
the Mount Grace annotators regarded Kempe’s loud weeping as excessive, though they still judged the rest of her book to be suitable for reading aloud to the community.
questions.rationale: Sentence 1 frames a modern dispute: some scholars dismiss Kempe as hysterical, while others credit twentieth-century feminist scholarship with rehabilitating her. Sentence 2 turns to the medieval owners of the only manuscript, the Carthusian monastery of Mount Grace. Two pieces of evidence follow. Beside an episode of Kempe sobbing and roaring, an annotator noted that “father M.,” Richard Methley, a former prior of the monastery, habitually did likewise, setting her behavior beside that of a leading member of their own community. And annotators prepared the text for reading aloud to the community, treating it as worth hearing. Together these show that her medieval readers already treated Kempe as a credible religious figure, long before twentieth-century scholarship did, which is what choice B says.
reasons: The monks did prepare the book for reading aloud, but that was not the only way they engaged with it: an annotator also compared Kempe’s weeping with that of a former prior. And the evidence shows that the monks took her seriously before modern scholars did, not that the modern scholars misjudged her.

The annotations show how the monks of Mount Grace regarded Kempe; they cannot settle whether her experiences were genuinely mystical. The text uses them to date the effort to take her seriously, not to decide the dispute about her that sentence 1 describes.

D accounts for the preparation for reading aloud but misreads the annotation: noting that “father M.,” a former prior of the monastery, habitually did likewise places Kempe’s weeping alongside the practice of a figure from the monks’ own community rather than marking it as excessive. Nothing in the text expresses disapproval of her weeping.
questions.text: Since the sole surviving manuscript of The Book of Margery Kempe, an account of a fifteenth-century Englishwoman’s visions and paroxysms of weeping, resurfaced in 1934, scholars have disputed whether she was a genuine mystic; some still dismiss her as hysterical, while others credit twentieth-century feminist scholarship with rehabilitating her. The manuscript, however, belonged to the Carthusian monastery of Mount Grace in Yorkshire. Beside an episode in which Kempe sobs and roars, one annotator remarked that “father M.” habitually did likewise, comparing her to Richard Methley, a former prior of the monastery. Annotators also inserted punctuation and markers preparing the text for recitation to the community, suggesting that ______

questions.skill: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: with:
with—
with,
with
questions.rationale: In this sentence, “deep grooves that channel water down to the plant’s underground root” is the object of the preposition “with.” No punctuation should come between a preposition and its object.
reasons: A colon must follow an independent clause; here it would separate the preposition “with” from its object.
The dash has no partner and no role; it separates the preposition “with” from its object.
The comma separates the preposition “with” from its object, “deep grooves.”
questions.text: The desert rhubarb, a plant found in the mountains of Israel’s Negev Desert, collects a remarkable amount of rainfall for its size. Its broad leaves are covered ______ deep grooves that channel water down to the plant’s underground root, concentrating the moisture where it is needed.

questions.skill: Comma after an introductory participial phrase
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: arena; a
arena. A
arena, a
arena, and a
questions.rationale: “Recording the snakes ... inside a four-story arena” is an introductory participial phrase, not a complete sentence. A comma separates it from the main clause that follows, whose subject is “a team led by biologist Jake Socha” and whose verb is “determined.”
reasons: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the introductory phrase has no subject or main verb.
The period turns the introductory phrase into a sentence fragment.
“And” would join the introductory phrase to the main clause as if both were clauses, but the phrase has no subject or main verb.
questions.text: Paradise tree snakes of Southeast Asia glide between treetops by flattening their bodies. Recording the snakes with motion-capture cameras as they launched from a platform inside a four-story ______ team led by biologist Jake Socha determined that the snakes’ midair undulations prevent them from tumbling.

questions.skill: Complex series: semicolons between items, with a supplement inside the first item
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: shrines, many of them centuries old,
shrines; many of them centuries old,
shrines many of them centuries old;
shrines, many of them centuries old;
questions.rationale: The three traditions form a series whose items contain commas, so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after “decades” shows. Within the first item, a comma sets off the supplement “many of them centuries old” from “Persian shrines,” and a semicolon after it ends the first item.
reasons: The comma after “old” does not match the semicolon used later to separate the second and third items; in a series whose items contain commas, semicolons separate the items.
The semicolon falls inside the first item, cutting off “many of them centuries old” from the shrines it describes, and the comma after “old” does not match the semicolon used later between items.
A comma is needed to set off the supplement “many of them centuries old” from “Persian shrines”; without it the phrase runs into the noun it describes.
questions.text: Iranian artist Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian drew on three traditions in creating her mirror mosaics: the cut-glass interiors of Persian ______ the geometric patterns of Islamic architecture, which she studied for decades; and the abstract compositions she had encountered while living in New York in the 1950s.

questions.skill: Finite vs nonfinite: verb of a “that” clause split by a relative clause
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: dispersing
to disperse
having dispersed
disperse
questions.rationale: The clause beginning with “that” has the subject “tambaqui” and needs its own finite verb; the relative clause set off by commas only describes the fish. “Disperse” supplies that verb: the fish disperse some seeds as far as 5.5 kilometers.
reasons: With “dispersing,” the clause beginning “that tambaqui” has no main verb.
“To disperse” is an infinitive, so the “that” clause is left without a finite verb.
“Having dispersed” is a participle and cannot serve as the verb of the “that” clause.
questions.text: Tambaqui, large fruit-eating fish of the Amazon basin, forage in seasonally flooded forests. Combining radiotelemetry of wild fish in Peru’s Pacaya-Samiria National Reserve with feeding trials in captivity, ecologist Jill Anderson estimated in 2011 that tambaqui, which can retain ingested seeds for several days, ______ some seeds as far as 5.5 kilometers from the parent plant.

questions.skill: Finite vs nonfinite: absolute phrase (noun + -ing) after a complete clause; finite options make comma splices
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: has allowed
allows
allowing
allowed
questions.rationale: The convention being tested is the use of verb forms within a sentence. The nonfinite present participle “allowing” correctly forms a supplementary element with “their sharp angle” that modifies the main clause “the houses have steeply pitched thatched roofs,” describing what the roofs’ pitch does.
reasons: The finite verb “has allowed” creates a second main clause, and two main clauses can’t be joined with only a comma after “roofs.”
The finite verb “allows” creates a second main clause, and two main clauses can’t be joined with only a comma after “roofs.”
The finite verb “allowed” creates a second main clause, and two main clauses can’t be joined with only a comma after “roofs.”
questions.text: The villages of Shirakawa-gō, in a snowy, mountainous region of central Japan, are celebrated for their gasshō-zukuri farmhouses, a name meaning “constructed like hands in prayer.” Assembled without metal fasteners, the houses have steeply pitched thatched roofs, their sharp angle ______ accumulated snow to slide off before its weight can damage the timber framework beneath.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: However,
That is,
To that end,
Similarly,
questions.rationale: The first sentence states Kim Man-jung’s goal: to keep his mother from being lonely while he was in exile. The blank sentence describes what he did to serve that goal: he wrote a novel for her to read. “To that end” signals an action taken to achieve a stated aim.
reasons: Writing a novel for his mother does not contrast with his wish to spare her loneliness; it carries that wish out.
The blank sentence does not reword his hope; it describes a separate action he took because of it.
The blank sentence does not describe a similar, separate case; it tells what Kim Man-jung himself did to achieve his goal.
questions.text: When Korean scholar-official Kim Man-jung was banished to a remote province in 1687, he hoped to spare his widowed mother the loneliness of his absence. ______ according to a long-standing account, he composed The Cloud Dream of the Nine, a novel of romance and adventure, expressly for her to read while he was in exile.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: for this reason,
moreover,
in particular,
that said,
questions.rationale: The first sentence gives the advocates’ claim that vertical farms can feed growing cities, and the first half of the second sentence lists their advantages. The clause after the blank qualifies the claim: what these farms grow supplies few calories, so they cannot do much to feed a city. “That said” marks this limitation of a claim the passage has otherwise supported.
reasons: Saving land and water and harvesting year-round do not explain why the farms grow mostly greens and herbs; the clause limits the advocates’ claim rather than following from the advantages.
A crop mix that supplies few calories is not one more advantage of vertical farms; it works against the claim that they can feed cities.
The clause does not single out a particular case of the land, water, or year-round advantages; it names a limitation of the farms’ whole output.
questions.text: Advocates have promoted vertical farms, which cultivate crops in stacked trays under artificial lighting, as a means of feeding the world’s expanding cities. Such facilities require a fraction of the land and water that conventional agriculture consumes and can harvest continuously; ______ nearly all their output is leafy greens and herbs, which are low in calories.

questions.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the float glass process. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Developed in Britain in the 1950s, float glass is the flat glass manufactured for most windows.
In the float glass process, molten glass is poured continuously onto a shallow bath of molten tin.
In the float glass process, molten glass floats on a bath of molten tin, spreading into a smooth, flat sheet that is then gradually cooled and cut.
After float glass spreads into a smooth sheet, it is gradually cooled and cut to size.
questions.rationale: An overview should cover the whole process. Choice C does: molten glass is poured onto “a shallow bath of molten tin,” it “spreads into a smooth, flat sheet,” and the sheet is “gradually cooled and cut to size.”
reasons: It says where and when the process was developed and what the glass is used for, not how the process works.
It gives only the first step of the process.
It gives only the final steps, cooling and cutting.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Float glass is the flat glass manufactured for most windows.
• The float process was developed in Britain in the 1950s.
• In this process, molten glass is poured continuously onto a shallow bath of molten tin.
• The glass floats on the tin and spreads into a smooth, flat sheet of uniform thickness.
• The sheet is then gradually cooled and cut to size.

questions.stem: The student wants to contrast how rooms are arranged in the two styles of house. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Both shotgun houses and dogtrot houses were designed so that air could move through them and help cool the rooms.
Whereas a shotgun house’s rooms are lined up one behind another, a dogtrot house’s rooms sit on either side of an open central passageway.
A dogtrot house has two rooms or cabins on either side of a roofed passageway known as the dogtrot.
Shotgun houses and dogtrot houses, two styles of home that were once common across the southern United States, arrange their rooms in very different ways.
questions.rationale: The goal is to contrast the room arrangements. Choice B sets them side by side: in a shotgun house the rooms are “arranged one directly behind another,” while a dogtrot house has rooms “on either side of an open, roofed passageway.”
reasons: It states something the two styles share, letting air move through to cool the house, rather than contrasting how their rooms are arranged.
It describes only the dogtrot house; the shotgun house is not mentioned, so there is no contrast.
It says the two styles arrange their rooms differently but never says how either one does.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Shotgun houses and dogtrot houses are two traditional styles of home once common throughout the southern United States.
• A shotgun house is a single room wide, with its rooms arranged one directly behind another.
• Its front and back doors typically align, allowing air to pass straight through.
• A dogtrot house consists of two rooms or cabins on either side of an open, roofed passageway.
• This central passageway, called the dogtrot, channels breezes that help cool the house.

questions.stem: The student wants to identify who traditionally created the designs on Chilkat robes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Chilkat robes, worn on ceremonial occasions by the Tlingit and neighboring peoples, combine mountain goat wool with strands of cedar bark.
Traditionally, the curvilinear designs on Chilkat robes were created by male artists, who painted them on wooden pattern boards.
Chilkat robes were traditionally designed by the women who wove them, and their designs frequently represent clan animals.
A single Chilkat robe, with its curvilinear designs representing clan animals such as the raven, could require a year or more of weaving.
questions.rationale: The notes say male artists painted the designs on wooden pattern boards and that women then reproduced them as they wove. Choice B identifies those male artists as the ones who created the designs.
reasons: It tells what the robes are made of and when they are worn, not who created their designs.
The women wove the robes, but the notes say they reproduced designs that male artists had painted on pattern boards; they did not create the designs.
It tells how long a robe could take to weave, not who created the designs.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Chilkat weaving is a textile tradition of the Tlingit and neighboring peoples of the Northwest Coast.
• Chilkat robes, worn on ceremonial occasions, combine mountain goat wool with strands of cedar bark.
• Their curvilinear designs frequently represent clan animals, such as the raven or the bear.
• Traditionally, male artists painted these designs on wooden templates called pattern boards.
• Women then wove the robes, reproducing the designs from the boards.
• A single robe could require a year or more of continuous weaving.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “struck” most nearly mean?
choices: Hit
Erased
Discovered
Reached
questions.rationale: A bargain that is struck is one that the two sides reach, or agree to. The widow congratulates herself every year on “its conclusion,” so each spring she and the tanner came to the same agreement.
reasons: “Struck” can mean hit, as with a fist or a hammer, but a bargain is an agreement, not something that can be hit.
Something can be struck from a list, or erased, but the text says the widow congratulated herself on the bargain each year, so it was made, not removed.
Miners strike gold when they find it, but the bargain was not found; the widow and the tanner made it with each other every spring.
questions.text:
The following text is from Charles Egbert Craddock’s 1885 novel Down the Ravine. Each spring a poor widow in the Tennessee mountains hires a mule from a neighboring tanner who needs the animal himself, and she pays with her son Birt’s labor.

Nevertheless, this bargain was annually <u>struck</u>. The poverty-stricken widow always congratulated herself upon its conclusion, and it never occurred to her that the amount of work that Birt did in the tanyard was a disproportionately large return for the few days that the tanner’s mule ploughed their little fields.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: amplify
dictate
rationalize
supersede
questions.rationale: Local support for the Green Party, a sign of people’s own environmental views, “predicted green purchases only when no default was set.” Once green power was the default, those views no longer predicted what people bought; the default had taken their place. So a default can supersede people’s motivations.
reasons: If a default amplified people’s environmental motivations, those motivations would matter more under the default, but local Green Party support predicted purchases only when no default was set.
The default came close to dictating what people bought, but nothing suggests it decided what they cared about; their motivations simply stopped predicting their choices.
The text says nothing about a default supplying reasons or excuses for people’s motivations.
questions.text: When Felix Ebeling and Sebastian Lotz made a pricier “green” electricity contract the default option in a randomized trial in Germany, purchases of that contract rose nearly tenfold. And since local support for the Green Party predicted green purchases only when no default was set, the researchers suggest that a default can ______ people’s own environmental motivations.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: conflated
transcribed
sublimated
parsed
questions.rationale: To parse something is to break it into its component parts, as a sentence is broken into words. The text says the earliest signers broke complex events down “into basic elements” and then “recombined those elements in sequences,” so they parsed those events.
reasons: Conflated means merged into one. The signers did the opposite: they divided complex events “into basic elements.”
Transcribed means written down or copied into another form of writing. Nothing in the text involves writing; the signers broke events into elements of a sign language.
Sublimated means turned or redirected into a more refined form. The text describes events being divided into basic parts, not being transformed into something higher.
questions.text: Since the late 1970s, deaf children in Nicaragua have collectively created a new sign language. Ann Senghas and colleagues found that its earliest signers ______ complex events into basic elements and then recombined those elements in sequences, a pattern absent from the gestures that hearing Nicaraguans produce while speaking Spanish.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: The speaker describes a peaceful refuge and then acknowledges that it has not released the speaker from a busier life.
The speaker recalls a familiar town and then explains how the town has changed since the speaker last saw it.
The speaker describes the noise and hurry of a city and then expresses relief at having finally escaped to a calmer place.
The speaker praises the beauty of a university and then urges others to visit it during the summer.
questions.rationale: The first stanza pictures a quiet scene of “drowsy” chimes and fragrance where the speaker can “lie and dream alone.” The last stanza admits, “in vain I turned away, / I fled the town in vain,” since “the strenuous life of yesterday / Calleth me back again.” Choice A describes this movement from a peaceful retreat to the admission that the retreat has not freed the speaker.
reasons: The speaker says “The change / Is mine,” meaning that the speaker has changed; the place is “known of old and dear” and “not strange,” so the poem does not describe the town changing.
The poem begins with the calm scene, not the city, and ends by saying the escape was “in vain,” not with relief.
The speaker never addresses or urges other people; the poem is about the speaker’s own failed retreat.
questions.text:
The following text is adapted from Amy Levy’s 1889 poem “Cambridge in the Long.” The speaker, who has left a busy city, is spending the summer vacation in Cambridge, an English university town.

Where drowsy sound of college-chimes
Across the air is blown,
And drowsy fragrance of the limes [linden trees],
I lie and dream alone.

This is the place; it is not strange,
But known of old and dear.—
What went I forth to seek? The change
Is mine; why am I here?

Alas, in vain I turned away,
I fled the town in vain;
The strenuous life of yesterday
Calleth me back again.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Ding, Hwang, and Divringi (Text 2) most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that gentrification displaces many vulnerable residents but noting that most of those residents eventually find housing in more prosperous neighborhoods
By arguing that gentrification primarily drives out residents with high credit scores, who can more easily afford to relocate
By suggesting that the effects of gentrification cannot be assessed until a neighborhood has finished changing
By cautioning that gentrification may not push financially vulnerable residents out as often as the claim assumes
questions.rationale: The underlined claim says gentrification forces large numbers of the poorest longtime residents out. Ding, Hwang, and Divringi found that vulnerable residents were “generally no more likely to leave gentrifying neighborhoods” than similar residents elsewhere, though those who moved tended to go to lower-income areas. They would therefore suggest that such displacement happens less often than the claim assumes.
reasons: Text 2 does not agree that many vulnerable residents are displaced, and it says those who move tend to go to lower-income neighborhoods, not more prosperous ones.
Text 2 reports only on vulnerable residents; it says nothing about residents with high credit scores being driven out.
Text 2 reports findings from a period of rapid change; it never suggests that effects can be judged only after a neighborhood stops changing.
questions.text:
Text 1

When higher-income households begin moving into a lower-income urban neighborhood, rents and property values in the area typically rise. Many critics of this process, known as gentrification, contend that <u>it forces substantial numbers of longtime residents, particularly those with the fewest financial resources, out of their neighborhoods</u>. In this view, affluent newcomers do not simply join the existing community but gradually replace it.

Text 2

Using individual credit records, Lei Ding, Jackelyn Hwang, and Eileen Divringi followed Philadelphia residents through the housing boom and bust of the 2000s. Vulnerable residents—those with low credit scores and no mortgage—were generally no more likely to leave gentrifying neighborhoods than comparable residents of nongentrifying neighborhoods were. When vulnerable residents did move, however, they were more likely to relocate to lower-income neighborhoods.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Cassiopea jellyfish sleep for longer periods each night than animals with centralized nervous systems do.
Although sleep has been linked to the brain, a jellyfish that has no brain appears to enter a sleep-like state.
Researchers found that Cassiopea develops a centralized nervous system as it matures, which is what enables the jellyfish to sleep.
Cassiopea jellyfish pulse less often at night because cooler water slows their movements.
questions.rationale: The text begins with the view that sleep depends on the brain and then turns, with “however,” to Cassiopea, a jellyfish with no brain that shows signs of a sleep-like state. Choice B states both the earlier view and the finding that revises it.
reasons: The text never compares how long Cassiopea and animals with centralized nervous systems sleep.
The text says Cassiopea lacks a brain, having only a diffuse network of nerves.
The text presents the slower nighttime pulsing as a sign of sleep, not an effect of water temperature.
questions.text: Sleep has generally been regarded as a function of the brain, since every animal known to sleep possessed a centralized nervous system. The upside-down jellyfish Cassiopea, however, lacks a brain, having only a diffuse network of nerves. Monitoring the jellyfish continuously, Caltech researchers Ravi Nath, Claire Bedbrook, and Michael Abrams found that the animals pulsed less frequently at night, responded more slowly to disturbances then, and were sluggish the following day if deprived of rest, all indications of a sleep-like state.

Centuries later, several of these monuments were transported to cities outside Egypt. One of them, originally erected by the pharaoh Thutmose III at the temple of Karnak, now stands in Istanbul, Turkey. According to the table, this obelisk’s height, not including its base, is ______
questions.table_title: Four Ancient Egyptian Obelisks Now Standing outside Egypt

questions.skill: Literary quotation illustrates a contrast between two characters
questions.stem: Which quotation from The Patriot most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Franco was conservative only in matters of religion and art; he was an ardent radical as far as the domestic walls were concerned, always planning transformations of ceilings, walls, floors, and drapery.”

“And she would make suggestions without appearing to do so, letting him believe the ideas were his own, for Franco was jealous of the paternity of ideas, while Luisa was quite indifferent to this sort of maternity.”

“Luisa had worked far harder than her husband, and still continued to do so, but whereas he was proud of his labours and glad to speak of them, Luisa, on the contrary, never mentioned hers, nor was she in the least proud of them.”
“Thus Franco’s sentiments always flamed out in his eyes, his face, his words, while Luisa’s seldom burst into flames, and only tinged the depths of her penetrating glance, and her soft voice.”
questions.rationale: The claim contrasts how the two show their feelings: Franco openly, Luisa with restraint. Choice D says Franco’s feelings flamed out in his eyes, face, and words, while Luisa’s seldom did and showed only faintly in her glance and voice.
reasons: It describes Franco’s tastes in religion, art, and decorating; it neither shows him expressing feelings nor mentions Luisa.
It contrasts the two, but over who gets credit for ideas, not over how openly each shows feelings.
It contrasts how the two talk about their labors, not how they reveal their feelings.
questions.text: The Patriot is an 1895 novel by Antonio Fogazzaro, translated from the Italian in 1906 by M. Prichard-Agnetti. Set in the 1850s on the shores of Lake Lugano, the novel follows a young married couple, Franco and Luisa. Fogazzaro contrasts the ways the two disclose their emotions, portraying Franco as demonstrative and Luisa as considerably more restrained: ______

questions.skill: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (key supplies a missing premise: where reindeer lived)
questions.stem: Which finding about Ribe, if true, would most directly support the claim made by Ashby and colleagues?
choices: Craftworkers in Ribe in the 780s also produced glass beads, using raw glass that had been transported to the town from regions far to the south of present-day Denmark.
Some comb-making waste from layers dated to the 780s came from reindeer, which at that time lived only far to the north, in the mountains of the Scandinavian Peninsula.
Reindeer antler made up a steadily growing share of the combs and comb-making waste at Ribe in the decades after 850 CE.
Most of the antler worked in Ribe during the 780s came from red deer, which then lived both in the forests around the town and on the Scandinavian Peninsula.
questions.rationale: The researchers claim that Ribe was getting materials from the Scandinavian Peninsula by the 780s. Choice B supplies the fact the passage leaves out: waste from the 780s came from reindeer, an animal found then only far to the north on the Scandinavian Peninsula, so that antler must have reached Ribe from there by that date.
reasons: Imported glass shows that Ribe traded with someone, but the glass came from the south, so it says nothing about materials from the Scandinavian Peninsula.
Reindeer antler after 850 shows contact with the north only after the Viking Age had begun; the claim is about the 780s, before it.

Red deer lived in the forests around Ribe as well as on the Scandinavian Peninsula, so their antler could have come from nearby; this finding cannot show that any material reached Ribe from the peninsula.
questions.text: Combs assembled from thin plates of deer antler fastened with rivets were among the earliest products of specialized craftworkers in Ribe, a trading settlement established on the west coast of present-day Denmark in the early 700s CE. Because antler from different deer species is nearly indistinguishable once it has been sawn and polished, archaeologist Steven Ashby and colleagues determined the species behind hundreds of combs and fragments of manufacturing waste from Ribe by analyzing proteins preserved in the antler. The researchers claim that Ribe’s craftworkers were already obtaining raw materials from the Scandinavian Peninsula by the 780s CE, before the raids and voyages that historians conventionally treat as the beginning of the Viking Age.

questions.skill: T3 consequence: a finding about what predicts word length applied to two equally frequent words
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: be about as long as the other word, since the two words are used equally often.
be longer than the other word, which would help listeners tell the two apart.
be the shorter of the two, since it typically carries less information where it occurs.
gradually be replaced by a less predictable word that conveys more information.
questions.rationale: A word that is easy to guess from its context has low information content, and Piantadosi’s team found that low information content goes with short words. Since frequency is the same for both words, the easily predicted one should be the shorter, as C says.
reasons: Equal frequency would predict equal length only on the older frequency explanation; the team found information content a better predictor, and the two words differ in that.
Low information content goes with shorter words, not longer ones, and the text says nothing about length helping listeners tell words apart.
The text is about which words are short, not about words being replaced over time.
questions.text: In the 1930s, linguist George Kingsley Zipf observed that frequently used words tend to be short, and for decades word length was attributed principally to frequency of use. Analyzing texts in numerous languages, cognitive scientists Steven Piantadosi, Harry Tily, and Edward Gibson found that a word’s length is better predicted by its average information content, which is low when the surrounding context typically makes the word easy to anticipate, than by its frequency. If two words in a language occurred equally often but one usually appeared in contexts where it was highly predictable, that word would most likely ______

questions.skill: Commas between items in a simple series
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: classroom
classroom;
classroom,
classroom:
questions.rationale: The sentence lists three activities: building a classroom, clearing drainage ditches, and repairing a road. Commas separate the items in a simple series like this one.
reasons: Without a comma, “a classroom” and “clear drainage ditches” run together.
Semicolons separate series items only when the items contain commas, and the other items here are separated by commas.
A colon cannot separate one item in a series from the next.
questions.text: On the last Saturday of each month, many adults in Rwanda participate in umuganda, a morning of mandatory community service. Depending on their neighborhood’s needs, participants might help build a ______ clear drainage ditches, or repair a road before gathering to discuss local concerns.

questions.skill: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: nearby; indicating
nearby. Indicating
nearby indicating
nearby, indicating
questions.rationale: The main clause ends with “spoken nearby,” and “indicating that systematic grammatical structure had developed within a single generation” is a participial phrase that comments on the whole finding. A comma correctly separates this nonrestrictive phrase from the main clause.
reasons: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “indicating that ...” is a participial phrase.
The period turns “Indicating that ... generation” into a sentence fragment.
Without a comma, “indicating ...” seems to describe the Arabic and Hebrew spoken nearby rather than the researchers’ finding.
questions.text: A sign language emerged in the twentieth century among deaf members of the Al-Sayyid Bedouin community in Israel’s Negev region. In 2005, linguist Wendy Sandler and her colleagues reported that its signers consistently used a subject-object-verb word order unlike that of the Arabic and Hebrew spoken ______ that systematic grammatical structure had developed within a single generation.

questions.skill: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, colon before an explanation
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: look, however,
look, however
look, however:
look; however,
questions.rationale: The adverb “however” belongs to the first clause: the exhibition asking visitors to do more than look contrasts with the previous sentence, in which visitors expect only to contemplate what is displayed. The comma sets “however” off from that clause, and the colon introduces the second clause, which explains what more the exhibition asked of them.
reasons: A comma after “however” cannot join the two independent clauses “Thai artist ... however” and “he converted ... with strangers.”
Nothing marks the boundary after “however,” so the two independent clauses run together.

Placing “however” at the start of the second clause signals that converting the office into a kitchen and inviting visitors to eat and talk contrasts with asking them to do more than look, but it is exactly the “more” that the first clause describes.
questions.text: Visitors to an art gallery typically expect simply to contemplate whatever is on display. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s 1992 exhibition Untitled (Free) asked its visitors to do more than ______ he converted the New York gallery’s back office into a makeshift kitchen and invited them to linger, eat the curry he prepared, and converse with strangers.

questions.skill: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid (possessor + possessed noun), number cue “each”
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: characters thoughts
character’s thoughts
characters’ thoughts
character’s thought’s
questions.rationale: “Each” calls for a singular noun, and the thoughts belong to that character, so the singular possessive “character’s” is needed; “thoughts” is a plain plural, so it takes no apostrophe.
reasons: “Characters” is a plain plural, but the context requires the singular possessive “character’s.”
“Characters’” is a plural possessive, but “each” requires the singular “character’s.”
“Thought’s” is possessive, but nothing belongs to the thoughts; the plain plural “thoughts” is needed.
questions.text: Brazilian novelist Graciliano Ramos’s Vidas Secas (Barren Lives), published in 1938, follows a family fleeing drought in the backlands of northeastern Brazil. Though the family members rarely speak, the novel conveys each ______ through a narrator who moves freely between their minds, even entering that of their dog.

questions.skill: Tense: past perfect (earlier past, “at the time of”)
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: had published
has published
publishes
is publishing
questions.rationale: “When he won it” refers to the 2021 award, a moment in the past, and the three novels were published before that moment (one of them in 2018). The past perfect “had published” shows an action completed before another past moment.
reasons: “Has published” is present perfect, which does not fit a moment in the past (“when he won it”).
“Publishes” is present tense and clashes with the 2021 award and the 2018 novel.
“Is publishing” presents an action going on now, not novels already published before the 2021 award.
questions.text: Senegalese novelist Mohamed Mbougar Sarr received the 2021 Prix Goncourt for The Most Secret Memory of Men, a novel chronicling a young writer’s search for a vanished author. When he won it, Sarr ______ three other novels, among them De purs hommes (2018), an examination of the prejudice and violence surrounding homosexuality in Senegal.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: for instance,
therefore,
in contrast,
likewise,
questions.rationale: The first sentence says most bony fishes swim with a tail fin. The ocean sunfish has no true tail fin and swims with other fins instead. “In contrast” marks this difference between the sunfish and most bony fishes.
reasons: The sunfish is not an example of fishes that swim with a tail fin; it lacks one.
How most bony fishes swim does not cause the sunfish to lack a tail fin.
The sunfish does not swim the way most bony fishes do; it is the exception.
questions.text: Most bony fishes propel themselves by sweeping a caudal fin, or tail fin, from side to side. The ocean sunfish, ______ possesses no true caudal fin: its body terminates abruptly in a clavus, a stiff, rudderlike structure, and the animal generates thrust by flapping its elongated dorsal and anal fins.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Fittingly,
However,
Regardless,
That is,
questions.rationale: The first sentence says the series is about the explosion at a nuclear power plant. The blank sentence says that its music was made from sounds recorded inside a nuclear power plant. Music drawn from such a place suits a story about a nuclear disaster, so “Fittingly” is the logical choice.
reasons: The way the score was made does not contrast with the subject of the series; it matches it.
The first sentence is not something the score was made in spite of or without regard to; the score’s source matches the series’ subject.
The sentence about the score does not reword the description of what the series dramatizes.
questions.text: The 2019 miniseries Chernobyl dramatizes the 1986 explosion at a Soviet nuclear power plant, following the scientists and officials who struggled to contain the radiation. ______ Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir built the show’s eerie, pulsing score largely from hums, clanks, and drones that she recorded inside a nuclear plant in Lithuania that had been shut down.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how small Brookesia nana is. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: With a body only 13.5 millimeters long, the male Brookesia nana may be the smallest reptile in the world.
Brookesia nana belongs to a group of leaf chameleons found in Madagascar.
Glaw’s team described Brookesia nana in 2021 on the basis of just two specimens.
The two specimens of Brookesia nana that Glaw’s team described were both collected in northern Madagascar.
questions.rationale: To emphasize the species’ size, the sentence must foreground how small it is. Choice A gives the male’s body length of only 13.5 millimeters and adds that the species may be the world’s smallest reptile.
reasons: It classifies the species as one of Madagascar’s leaf chameleons but says nothing about how small it is.
It stresses how few specimens the team had, not how small the animal is.
It tells where the specimens were collected, which says nothing about how small the animal is.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Madagascar is home to a group of miniaturized leaf chameleons in the genus Brookesia.
• In 2021, Frank Glaw’s team described a new species in this group, Brookesia nana.
• They had just two specimens, both collected in northern Madagascar.
• The male’s body is only 13.5 millimeters long, not counting the tail.
• The team suggests that B. nana may be the world’s smallest reptile.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the baobab and the durian. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The baobab and the durian, though native to different continents, both rely primarily on bats for pollination.
The baobab is recognizable by its massive, swollen trunk, whereas the durian is known for its spiky, pungent fruit.
The baobab’s large white flowers, which open at night, are pollinated primarily by fruit bats.
Like numerous other flowering plants, the durian depends on animals to transfer pollen between its flowers.
questions.rationale: Choice A names both trees and the trait they share: each is pollinated primarily by bats.
reasons: It contrasts the trees’ best-known features instead of pointing to something they share.
It describes how the baobab is pollinated but never mentions the durian.
It compares the durian with flowering plants in general, not with the baobab.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Numerous flowering plants depend on animals to transfer pollen between flowers.
• The baobab, a tree of the African savanna, is recognizable by its massive, swollen trunk.
• Its large white flowers, which open at night, are pollinated primarily by fruit bats.
• The durian is a Southeast Asian tree known for its spiky, pungent fruit.
• Its flowers are pollinated primarily by nectar-feeding bats.

questions.skill: Identify a person’s contribution (misattributed role among the options)
questions.stem: The student wants to identify Gautier’s contribution to the 1959 research. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Drawing on techniques she had learned in the United States, Gautier prepared the cell cultures in which the team counted chromosomes.
Gautier was the lead author of the 1959 report showing that people with Down syndrome have 47 chromosomes rather than 46.
Gautier contributed to the 1959 research by teaching the team the cell culture procedure she had learned in the United States.
The 1959 report, which listed Lejeune first and Gautier second, showed that people with Down syndrome have an extra chromosome.
questions.rationale: Gautier’s contribution to the research was preparing the cell cultures in which the team counted the chromosomes. Choice A identifies that contribution and adds where her skill came from.
reasons: The notes say Lejeune was listed as first author and Gautier second, so she was not the lead author.
The notes say Gautier prepared the cell cultures herself; they do not say she taught the procedure to the rest of the team.
It gives the report’s finding and the order of its authors but never says what Gautier contributed.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1959, French researchers reported that people with Down syndrome have 47 chromosomes rather than the usual 46.
• Counting the chromosomes required growing cells in a laboratory, a procedure called cell culture.
• Physician Marthe Gautier had learned how to culture cells during her training in the United States.
• Back in Paris, she prepared the cell cultures in which the team subsequently counted the chromosomes.
• The team’s report listed geneticist Jérôme Lejeune as first author and Gautier as second author.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: fragmentary
comprehensive
fictional
exaggerated
questions.rationale: The second sentence says Fuentes works from “brief mentions” of these women in colonial records. Lives that survive only as brief mentions survive in pieces, so the archive preserves them only in fragmentary form.
reasons: Comprehensive means complete, but the women appear only in brief mentions, the opposite of a full record.
The women appear in colonial records, which are documents, not fiction; nothing suggests the archive invents their lives.
Nothing says the records overstate the women’s lives; the problem described is how little the records say.
questions.text: Historian Marisa J. Fuentes’s Dispossessed Lives (2016) examines eighteenth-century Bridgetown, Barbados, through the experiences of enslaved women whose lives survive in the archive only in ______ form. Reading the brief mentions of these women in colonial records alongside Black feminist theory, Fuentes shows how the power of slave owners and officials shaped what those documents preserve.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: unconstrained by
attuned to
hampered by
indebted to
questions.rationale: Because a player piano plays the rolls by itself, no pianist has to perform Nancarrow’s studies, so the music need not fit what human hands can do. The colon gives examples of what that freedom allows: extraordinary speeds and several melodies at different tempos at once. So the compositions could be “unconstrained by,” or free from, the physical limitations of human performers.
reasons: Music “attuned to” performers’ limitations would be adjusted to fit them, staying within what people can play. But the instrument played the rolls mechanically, so the music did not have to fit a performer, and the examples (extraordinary speeds, melodies at different tempos at once) show it did not.

If the compositions were “hampered by” performers’ limitations, those limitations would hold them back. But the instrument played the rolls mechanically, so no performer’s limits applied, and the examples show the music going where it pleased.

Being “indebted to” something means owing it a debt or depending on it. Nothing suggests the compositions owe anything to the limitations of human performers; they were written for a machine precisely so those limitations would not apply.
questions.text: Conlon Nancarrow wrote his Studies for Player Piano by punching each note into paper rolls that the instrument then played mechanically, so the compositions could be ______ the physical limitations of human performers: some race along at extraordinary speeds, and others superimpose independent melodies, each proceeding at its own tempo.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: obtrusive
versatile
sporadic
rudimentary
questions.rationale: The second sentence shows the vine imitating whatever host it happens to climb: its leaves change size, shape, and color to match the tree it grows on, so one vine can copy several species. A mimic that can adapt to many different models is “versatile.”
reasons: An “obtrusive” mimic would stand out and draw attention. The vine’s leaves change to resemble those of the tree it grows on, which helps it blend in rather than be noticed.
A “sporadic” mimic would imitate other plants only now and then. The text describes the vine matching each tree it climbs, and nothing suggests the mimicry is occasional.
“Rudimentary” mimicry would be crude or basic. The leaves change in size, shape, and color to match several species, which is detailed imitation, not crude imitation.
questions.text: The vine Boquila trifoliolata is a remarkably ______ mimic. In the temperate rainforests of Chile, Ernesto Gianoli and Fernando Carrasco-Urra found that as the vine climbs different trees, its leaves change in size, shape, and color to resemble those of whichever tree it is growing on, imitating several different species.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a hypothesis about seed predators that Bogdziewicz and colleagues set out to test.
It defines a reproductive pattern whose disruption the text goes on to describe.
It describes a recent change in beech trees’ behavior that the researchers attribute to rising temperatures.
It explains why moth larvae have destroyed a growing share of beech seeds in England.
questions.rationale: The first sentence explains what masting is. The text then notes why masting helps trees and reports that, as the climate warmed, beech seed production became less variable and less synchronized, the very features that define masting, while predators gained. So the first sentence defines the pattern whose breakdown the study describes.
reasons: The sentence describes how many trees reproduce; it is not a hypothesis, and nothing in the text is framed as a test of it.
The change linked to warming (less variable, less synchronized seed production) is reported in the third sentence; the first sentence describes masting itself.
Rising losses to moth larvae are mentioned only in the third sentence, and the first sentence gives no reason for them.
questions.text: <u>Many trees reproduce by mast seeding, or masting: individuals across a population synchronously produce enormous seed crops in some years and very few in others.</u> Bumper years satiate seed predators, allowing many seeds to escape consumption. Analyzing nearly four decades of seed production by European beech trees in England, ecologist Michał Bogdziewicz and colleagues found that as the climate warmed, the trees produced more seed overall but varied less from year to year and less in unison, while losses to seed-eating moth larvae climbed. The main beneficiaries of the trees’ increased seed production, the researchers conclude, are not the trees but their predators.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, the author of Text 1 and Estes and colleagues (Text 2) would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Steller’s sea cows were hunted mainly for their hides rather than their meat.
Steller’s sea cows would probably have survived if hunting had stopped soon after 1741.
Steller’s sea cows competed with sea otters for the sea urchins that lived among the kelp around the islands.
The arrival of the fur trade in the region contributed to the disappearance of Steller’s sea cow.
questions.rationale: The texts disagree about how the sea cow died out, but both tie its end to the fur trade. Text 1 says that “Fur traders and seal hunters” killed the animals until they were “hunted to extinction,” and Text 2 says the fur trade “drastically reduced sea otter populations,” setting off the loss of the kelp the sea cows ate. Both would therefore agree that the fur trade contributed to the species’ disappearance.
reasons: Text 1 says the animals were killed “for their meat and fat”; neither text says they were hunted mainly for their hides.
The author of Text 1 might accept this, but Estes and colleagues argue that the loss of otters and kelp “would probably have doomed the species” even without direct killing.
Text 2 says otters prey on urchins and sea cows ate kelp; neither text says sea cows ate urchins or competed with otters.
questions.text:
Text 1

When naturalist Georg Wilhelm Steller was shipwrecked on Bering Island in 1741, he described an enormous, slow-moving marine mammal that grazed on kelp around the Commander Islands, its only remaining habitat. Fur traders and seal hunters following the route of Steller’s expedition soon began stopping at the islands to slaughter the animals for their meat and fat. By 1768, Steller’s sea cow had been hunted to extinction.

Text 2

Ecologist James Estes and colleagues argue that hunting explains only part of the extinction. During those same decades, the fur trade drastically reduced sea otter populations around the islands. Because otters prey on sea urchins, their disappearance typically allows urchin populations to multiply and devour kelp forests—the sea cow’s food supply. Even if no sea cow had been killed directly, the researchers conclude, the loss of otters and kelp would probably have doomed the species.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Mary resents Lady Anne for having taken her away from her family and her home on Wistaria Terrace.
Mary decides to return to Wistaria Terrace because Lady Drummond has made her feel unwelcome.
Mary is confident that Lady Anne will always defend her, so she no longer worries about what Lady Anne’s fine friends might think of her.
Although Mary is grateful for Lady Anne’s kindness, she feels that she will never belong in Lady Anne’s world.
questions.rationale: Mary longs for Wistaria Terrace and tells herself there is no place for her in this world. She feels contrite when she remembers how good Lady Anne is to her, yet she thinks “it was not her world; it never would be.” Choice D captures both her gratitude and her sense of not belonging.
reasons: Mary’s “tender reproach” is aimed at her father, and she feels contrite about Lady Anne, so she does not resent Lady Anne.
Mary longs for home and hopes to be left at home on future visits, but she never decides to go back to Wistaria Terrace.
Mary does believe Lady Anne will stand up for her, but she still feels out of place and is near tears, so she is far from untroubled.
questions.text:
The following text is from Katharine Tynan’s 1909 novel Mary Gray. Mary, a girl from an impoverished household on Wistaria Terrace, now lives with Lady Anne, a wealthy elderly woman, as her companion.

Once again she longed for Wistaria Terrace. There was no place for her in this world, she said to herself; and sent a tender reproach in her own mind to the father who had given her up for her good. Then she felt contrite about Lady Anne. How good the old lady was to her, and how she stood up for her, would stand up for her, even to the terrible Lady Drummond! Still, it was not her world; it never would be. She thought, with sudden childish tears filling her eyes, that the next time Lady Anne went to see any of her fine friends she would pray to be left at home.

questions.skill: Data completion: the row that is the minimum on two columns
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the Tōdai-ji Temple Bell.
the Chion-in Temple Bell.
the Mingun Bell.
the Bell of Good Luck.
questions.rationale: The Tōdai-ji Temple Bell was cast in 732, earlier than any other bell in the table, and at about 44 metric tons it is also the lightest.
reasons: The Chion-in Temple Bell, cast in 1633 and weighing about 67 metric tons, is neither the earliest nor the lightest.
The Mingun Bell was cast in 1808 and weighs about 91 metric tons.
The Bell of Good Luck was cast in 2000, the latest of the five, and weighs about 116 metric tons.
questions.text: The heaviest bells known were cast for temples, monasteries, and public monuments in countries including Russia, Myanmar, China, and Japan, and a few weigh more than 100 metric tons. The Tsar Bell in Moscow, though broken, is the heaviest bell still in existence. Among the five bells in the table, the earliest to be cast is also the lightest: ______
questions.table_title: Five of the World’s Heaviest Bells

questions.skill: Data completion: treated vs control at the same site

questions.text: Like other legumes, chickpeas can obtain nitrogen with the help of rhizobia, soil bacteria that live in nodules on the plants’ roots. Because the soils at their study sites contained few rhizobia compatible with chickpeas, researchers led by Endalkachew Wolde-meskel tested whether coating seeds with the bacteria, a practice called inoculation, could raise yields on smallholder farms in Ethiopia. Inoculated plots generally outproduced uninoculated control plots on the same farms: for example, ______

questions.skill: Data description (two-part claim read through a passage relation: spread of values, not levels)
questions.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Pennock and colleagues’ conclusion?
choices: Each of the four species had a higher nitrogen-15 value in the reservoir than in the river and a lower carbon-13 value in the reservoir than in the river.

The four species’ nitrogen-15 values varied less in the reservoir, from 11.6 to 14.0, than in the river, where they ranged from 7.9 to 11.8, and every species had a lower carbon-13 value in the reservoir than in the river.
The four species’ nitrogen-15 values spanned a narrower range in the reservoir than in the river, while their carbon-13 values spanned a wider range in the reservoir than in the river.
In both habitats, channel catfish had a higher nitrogen-15 value than razorback sucker did, and flannelmouth sucker had a carbon-13 value more than 2 units higher than that of common carp.
questions.rationale: By the passage’s reasoning, a shorter food web shows up as a smaller spread of nitrogen-15 values among species, and a wider one as a larger spread of carbon-13 values. In the river, nitrogen-15 runs from 7.9 to 11.8 (a spread of 3.9) and carbon-13 from −23.9 to −21.3 (2.6); in the reservoir, nitrogen-15 runs from 11.6 to 14.0 (2.4) and carbon-13 from −30.5 to −25.0 (5.5). Choice C states both halves of that comparison.
reasons: Every species did shift this way, but moving all species up or down says nothing about how far apart they are, which is what the length and width of the web depend on.

The narrower nitrogen-15 range is accurate and fits a shorter web, but a lower carbon-13 value for every species shows that the fishes’ energy sources shifted, not that they became more varied; only a wider spread of carbon-13 values would show a wider web.
Both comparisons hold in each habitat, but they compare particular species with each other; they do not show how the overall spread of values differs between the river and the reservoir.
questions.text: Ecologists characterize a food web by its length, the number of feeding levels separating top predators from primary producers, and by its width, the diversity of energy sources supporting it. Chemical analysis of animal tissues can estimate both: a consumer’s nitrogen-15 value increases by a roughly constant amount at every successive trophic level, whereas its carbon-13 value indicates the energy source at the web’s base. Comparing these isotope values in fishes from the San Juan River in Utah and from Lake Powell, the reservoir into which the river empties, ecologist Casey A. Pennock and colleagues concluded that the reservoir’s food web is shorter and wider than the river’s.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: may have helped the birds shed heat on their warming breeding grounds, adding to the cooling advantage that their smaller bodies already provided.
may have compensated for the 2.4% decrease in tarsus length, so that the birds’ overall body size changed little over the period studied.
may have helped the birds keep up their long migrations, which their smaller bodies had made more difficult by causing them to retain more heat in flight.
may have offset a cost that the birds’ response to warmer summers would otherwise have imposed on their long migrations.
questions.rationale: Sentence 1 explains the shrinking: a smaller body sheds heat more efficiently, and the birds’ bodies shrank as summers on their breeding grounds warmed. The dash aside in sentence 2 names the price of that response: a smaller body raises the metabolic cost of flight, a liability on long migrations, while proportionally longer wings reduce that cost. Wings lengthened over the same period, so the researchers most plausibly see the longer wings as offsetting the flight cost that the warming-driven shrinking would otherwise have added. In choice D, “the birds’ response to warmer summers” is the shrinking and “a cost ... imposed on their long migrations” is the higher cost of flight.
reasons: The text links heat loss only to body size; the one effect it gives longer wings is a lower cost of flight, so nothing suggests the researchers see the wings as a way to shed heat.

Tarsus length is “a standard proxy for body size,” so its decrease means the birds’ bodies shrank; the text gives longer wings one effect, a lower cost of flight, and nothing suggests they kept body size constant.

The first half fits the text, but the reason does not: sentence 1 says a smaller body dissipates heat more efficiently, so shrinking would not make the birds retain more heat; the difficulty the text names is the higher metabolic cost of flight.
questions.text: Bergmann’s rule holds that individuals of a species tend to be smaller in warmer climates, since a smaller body dissipates heat more efficiently. For migratory birds, however, diminished body size also elevates the metabolic cost of flight—a considerable liability on journeys spanning thousands of kilometers—whereas proportionally longer wings reduce that cost. Analyzing 70,716 specimens of 52 migratory species that died after colliding with buildings in Chicago between 1978 and 2016, Brian Weeks and colleagues determined that tarsus length, a standard proxy for body size, decreased by 2.4% as summer temperatures on the species’ breeding grounds increased. Over the same period, wing length increased by 1.3%, a change that the researchers propose ______

questions.skill: Restrictive relative clause with that: no punctuation before it
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: firm,
firm, that
firm that
firm
questions.rationale: “That built and repaired Buddhist temples from 578 CE until 2006 ...” is essential to the meaning of “a firm”: it tells what kind of firm Kongō Gumi was. A restrictive clause like this isn’t set off by punctuation, and “that” is needed as the subject of “built and repaired.”
reasons: Without “that,” nothing serves as the subject of “built and repaired,” so the sentence is ungrammatical.
A comma can’t separate “firm” from the restrictive clause that describes it.
Without “that,” “a firm built and repaired Buddhist temples” has no subject for “built and repaired.”
questions.text: Japan is home to an unusually large number of companies that have operated for centuries. The oldest may have been Kongō Gumi, a ______ built and repaired Buddhist temples from 578 CE until 2006, when financial difficulties led to its absorption by a larger construction company.

questions.skill: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Celsius,
Celsius:
Celsius
Celsius—
questions.rationale: The subject of the main clause is the long noun phrase “embryos inside eggs whose narrower ends had been warmed to 30 degrees Celsius,” and its verb is “moved.” No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.
reasons: The comma separates the subject from its verb “moved.”
A colon must follow a complete clause, but “embryos inside eggs ... Celsius” is only the subject.
A single dash with no partner wrongly separates the subject from its verb.
questions.text: In three-keeled pond turtles, the temperature at which an egg incubates influences the hatchling’s sex. In a 2013 experiment led by ecologist Wei-Guo Du, embryos inside eggs whose narrower ends had been warmed to 30 degrees ______ moved toward the warmth, whereas embryos exposed to 33 degrees retreated from it.

questions.skill: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: builders
builders,
builders but
builders, but
questions.rationale: “In 1946, Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy began constructing New Gourna ... employing the mud bricks and vaulted roofs of traditional Nubian builders” and “because many of those families resisted relocation, the settlement was never completed” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “but” joins them and marks the contrast.
reasons: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation and no conjunction.
A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.
When “but” joins two independent clauses this long, a comma is needed before it.
questions.text: In 1946, Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy began constructing New Gourna, a village near Luxor intended to rehouse families residing among pharaonic tombs, employing the mud bricks and vaulted roofs of traditional Nubian ______ because many of those families resisted relocation, the settlement was never completed.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

depicts
is depicting
has depicted
questions.rationale: The subject is the plural noun “artisans,” so it needs the plural verb “depict.” The phrase “drawing freehand with this pen on a single cotton panel” only describes the artisans.
reasons: “Depicts” is singular and agrees with “panel” or “pen,” not with the plural subject “artisans.”
“Is depicting” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “artisans.”
“Has depicted” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “artisans.”

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

were
are
have been
questions.rationale: The subject of the second sentence is the gerund phrase “Documenting the ceremonial and social dances of Jamaica, Martinique, Trinidad, and Haiti during ethnographic fieldwork in the mid-1930s,” and a gerund phrase is singular. The singular past tense verb “was” agrees with it and fits a past event.
reasons: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular gerund subject; it agrees only with the nearby plural nouns such as “dances.”
The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular gerund subject “Documenting the ... dances ... mid-1930s.”
The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular gerund subject “Documenting the ... dances ... mid-1930s.”
