Documenting the ceremonial and social dances of Jamaica, Martinique, Trinidad, and Haiti during ethnographic fieldwork in the mid-1930s ______ fundamental to her development of the Dunham Technique, a movement vocabulary that dance schools still teach.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Similarly,
Thus,
For example,
In contrast,
questions.rationale: The first sentence explains that staff notation shows pitch by the position of a symbol on five lines. The second sentence describes jianpu, which shows pitch a different way, with digits and dots. “In contrast” signals the difference between the two systems.
reasons: Jianpu does not show pitch the same way staff notation does; it uses numbers rather than positions on lines.
How staff notation works does not cause jianpu to use digits; the two systems are simply described side by side.
Jianpu is not an example of Western staff notation; it is a different system.
questions.text: Western staff notation indicates a note’s pitch through the vertical position of its symbol on five horizontal lines. ______ jianpu, the numbered notation prevalent in China, assigns the digits 1 through 7 to the degrees of the scale, with dots above or below a digit indicating a higher or lower octave.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: nevertheless,
for example,
for this reason,
likewise,
questions.rationale: The first sentence describes Mrema’s habit: she “typically writes in Swahili.” The blank sentence presents an exception to that habit: the novel “is written in English,” the language its characters “must speak with callers throughout their shifts.” “Nevertheless” fits, since it signals that this novel departs from what the previous sentence would lead a reader to expect.
reasons: The novel’s Tanzanian setting may look like more of Mrema’s usual work, but a novel “written in English” is not an example of her writing in Swahili; it is an exception to that habit.
Writing in Swahili, the language of her readers, is not a reason for writing a novel in English; the call-center setting is the reason.
“Likewise” would mean the 2016 novel follows the same practice as her other work, but it is in English, not Swahili.
questions.text: Tanzanian novelist Zawadi Mrema typically writes in Swahili, the language spoken in the coastal communities where her narratives unfold and where most of her readership resides. Her 2016 novel, ______ follows the staff of a Dar es Salaam call center that handles complaints from British customers, and it is written in English, the language the characters must speak with callers throughout their shifts.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Bhutan’s pursuit of Gross National Happiness and New Zealand’s Wellbeing Budget. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Bhutan’s constitution called for promoting Gross National Happiness in 2008, whereas New Zealand introduced its first Wellbeing Budget in 2019.
Bhutan’s index of citizens’ well-being covers areas such as health, education, and community life.
Both Bhutan’s pursuit of Gross National Happiness and New Zealand’s Wellbeing Budget rely on measures of citizens’ well-being, not just economic output.
New Zealand’s first Wellbeing Budget, introduced in 2019, gave priority to mental health and child poverty.
questions.rationale: The notes describe both countries as looking at citizens’ well-being and not only at economic output. Choice C names both countries and states that shared trait.
reasons: It contrasts when each country acted instead of stating what their approaches share.
It describes Bhutan’s index and does not mention New Zealand.
It describes New Zealand’s budget and does not mention Bhutan.
questions.text:

questions.skill: Introduce a concept to a new audience
questions.stem: The student wants to introduce community land trusts to a new audience. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The first community land trust in the United States was established in Georgia in 1969.
A community land trust is a nonprofit that owns land for a community and sells the houses on it at lower prices, with resale limits that keep them affordable.
Purchasers of these homes, which cost less than comparable homes nearby, accept a price limit when they resell so that each home remains affordable.
Community land trusts sell the houses on their land but retain ownership of the land itself.
questions.rationale: Introducing community land trusts to a new audience means saying what they are and what they do. Choice B explains that a community land trust is a nonprofit that owns land for a community and sells the homes on it at lower prices, with limits that keep them affordable.
reasons: It gives a historical fact without explaining what a community land trust is.
It refers to “these homes” and a price limit without saying what a community land trust is, so a new audience would not follow it.
It gives one feature of community land trusts but not what they are or that they keep homes affordable.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A community land trust (CLT) is a nonprofit organization that owns land on behalf of a community.
• A CLT sells the houses on its land but retains ownership of the land itself.
• Because purchasers pay only for the house, these homes typically cost considerably less than comparable homes nearby.
• When owners resell, they accept a price limit so that the home remains affordable for subsequent buyers.
• The first CLT in the United States was established in Georgia in 1969.

questions.stem: The student wants to contrast the two explanations of how fairy circles form. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Whereas Jürgens blames the bare patches on sand termites that eat grass roots, Getzin’s team blames competition for water from the grasses surrounding the circles.
Jürgens holds that sand termites create the circles by eating grass roots, whereas Getzin’s team holds that the grasses inside the circles use up the soil’s moisture and die of water stress.
Jürgens found sand termites at most of the circles he examined, whereas Getzin’s team concluded that the surrounding grasses drain the circles’ soil moisture.

Jürgens blames the bare patches on the sand termites he found at every circle he examined, which consume grass roots, whereas Getzin’s team blames the surrounding grasses, which drain the circles’ soil moisture.
questions.rationale: The two explanations differ in what kills the grass inside a fairy circle: Jürgens blames sand termites that eat grass roots, while Getzin’s team blames the surrounding grasses, which draw water out of the circle and so outcompete the grasses inside. Choice A states this contrast accurately, calling the second mechanism competition for water. Choice B gives the water use to the grasses inside the circles; Getzin’s team found that the surrounding grasses depleted the circles’ soil moisture. Choice C sets what Jürgens observed against what Getzin’s team concluded, so Jürgens’s explanation (termites eating grass roots) is missing. Choice D states the right contrast but says Jürgens found the termites at every circle he examined; the notes say most.
reasons: Getzin’s team concluded that the surrounding grasses depleted the circles’ soil moisture; the grasses inside are the ones that die, not the ones that use up the water.
Both halves are accurate, but the first gives what Jürgens observed (termites at most circles), not his explanation of how the circles form, so the two explanations are not contrasted.
The termites-versus-grasses contrast is right, but Jürgens found the termites at most of the circles he examined, not at every one.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Fairy circles are bare, approximately circular patches encircled by grasses in the Namib Desert.

• In 2013, ecologist Norbert Jürgens found the sand termite Psammotermes allocerus present at most circles he examined.

• Jürgens argued that termites create the circles by consuming grass roots, leaving bare soil that stores rainwater.

• In 2022, ecologist Stephan Getzin’s team documented that grasses inside the circles died shortly after rainfall.

• The team concluded that surrounding grasses depleted the circles’ soil moisture, killing the grasses inside through water stress.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: audience
material
assistant
title
questions.rationale: A material is the substance something is made from. The text names gunpowder and says Cai “has incorporated it into drawings” and burned it on garments “to imprint images into the fabric,” so gunpowder is a material for his art.
reasons: An audience is a group of people watching. Gunpowder is not a group of viewers; the text describes Cai making images with it.
An assistant is a person who helps. Gunpowder is a substance Cai works with, not a helper.
A title is the name of a work. The text does not say any work is named “gunpowder”; it describes how he uses the powder.
questions.text: Since the 1990s, Chinese artist Cai Guo-Qiang has created artworks using an unconventional ______: gunpowder. He has incorporated it into drawings and has even arranged it on garments and ignited it, allowing the burning powder to imprint images into the fabric.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “studied” most nearly mean?
choices: Scrutinized
Scholarly
Deliberate
Distrustful
questions.rationale: As used here, “studied” describes Alice’s amiability as something she produces on purpose. She is surprised by Theron’s sudden journey yet shows no suspicion, and she defers “with such unexpected tact” to his wish not to be questioned: her friendliness is a careful, intentional effort, so “studied” most nearly means deliberate.
reasons: To study something can mean to scrutinize it, or examine it closely, but Alice is not examining anything; “studied” describes the kind of amiability she shows.
A studied person can be learned, or scholarly, but nothing in the text concerns learning; the word describes the care Alice takes in being friendly.
The text says Alice’s face showed “no trace of suspicion,” so her amiability is not distrustful; she defers to Theron with “unexpected tact,” and his mood warms toward her.
questions.text:
The following text is from Harold Frederic’s 1896 novel The Damnation of Theron Ware. Theron has abruptly informed his wife, Alice, that he must depart tonight.

Alice’s face showed surprise, but no trace of suspicion. She spoke with <u>studied</u> amiability during the meal, and deferred with such unexpected tact to his implied desire not to be questioned as to the mysterious motives of the journey, that his mood instinctively softened and warmed toward her, as they finished supper.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: corroborated
eulogized
usurped
impugned
questions.rationale: The journalists guessed that “Rebecca Clarke” was a cover name for Bloch, so they called into question whether Clarke had written the sonata at all. To impugn something is to challenge it as false or doubtful, so the journalists impugned her authorship.
reasons: To corroborate something is to confirm it. The journalists did the opposite: they suggested the sonata was really Bloch’s, which is why the text opens by saying that the sonata was in fact Clarke’s own work.
To eulogize is to praise highly. The sonata shared first place, but the text describes the journalists’ doubts about who wrote it, not praise for it.
To usurp something is to seize it for oneself without right. The journalists did dispute Clarke’s claim, but they credited the sonata to Bloch; they did not take the authorship for themselves.
questions.text: Rebecca Clarke’s Viola Sonata tied for first place among 72 entries in a 1919 composition competition sponsored by music patron Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge. Though the sonata was Clarke’s own work, journalists ______ her authorship, speculating that “Rebecca Clarke” was merely a pseudonym for Ernest Bloch, the composer with whom she had tied.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains how seahorses are able to approach prey that can easily detect predators.
It describes the method the researchers used to measure how water moved around the seahorses.
It explains why copepods are able to escape from most of the fish that hunt them.
It presents a finding that the researchers say contradicts an earlier explanation of the seahorse’s hunting success.
questions.rationale: The text first says that copepods can sense an approaching predator’s water movements and escape, yet seahorses usually catch them. The underlined portion gives the reason: the snout’s shape leaves the water in front of the mouth nearly still, so the seahorse can get close without being noticed. It explains how seahorses approach such alert prey, as choice A says.
reasons: The method (tracking water flow with lasers) is in the part of the sentence before the underline; the underlined portion reports what the researchers found.
The underlined portion explains the seahorse’s success, not the copepods’ escapes; copepods’ ability to sense predators is in the first sentence.
No earlier explanation of the seahorse’s success appears in the text, so the finding cannot be contradicting one.
questions.text: Copepods, tiny crustaceans eaten by many fish, can detect the faint water disturbances generated by an approaching predator and escape within a few thousandths of a second. Dwarf seahorses (Hippocampus zosterae) nonetheless capture them more than 90 percent of the time. Using lasers to visualize the flow of water around the fish, marine scientist Brad Gemmell and colleagues discovered why: <u>the shape of a seahorse’s snout produces a zone of almost undisturbed water immediately in front of its mouth, allowing the fish to come within striking distance without alerting its prey</u>. The strike itself takes less than a millisecond.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Delgado and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in the underlined portion of Text 1?
choices: By pointing out that the evidence favors paper for some kinds of texts but not for every kind
By arguing that the advantage of paper disappears whenever readers are allowed as much time as they need
By noting that students skim printed texts about as often as they skim texts on screens
By questioning whether the studies comparing paper and screens included enough participants to be trusted
questions.rationale: The underlined portion claims that students will understand “any text” less well on a screen. Delgado and colleagues found a modest paper advantage overall, but it “appeared for informational texts, such as explanations of scientific topics, yet not in studies that used only narrative texts.” They would point out that the advantage holds for some kinds of texts but not for all, which limits the claim.
reasons: Text 2 says the paper advantage “grew when readers faced time constraints”; it does not say the advantage disappears without them.
Skimming is mentioned only in Text 1, as the critics’ concern; Text 2 reports nothing about how often students skim.
Text 2 relies on the pooled studies, with “more than 170,000 participants,” and gives no reason to doubt their size.
questions.text:
Text 1

As schools replace printed textbooks with tablets and laptops, some educators and parents have expressed concern that students will absorb less of what they read. Reading on screens, these critics argue, encourages skimming and makes it harder to recall where in a text particular information appeared. On this view, <u>students will understand any text less well on a screen than they would understand the same text printed on paper</u>.

Text 2

Pablo Delgado and colleagues combined the results of 54 studies, involving more than 170,000 participants in all, that compared readers’ understanding of printed and digital texts. Overall, paper held a modest advantage, which grew when readers faced time constraints. But the advantage depended on the kind of text: it appeared for informational texts, such as explanations of scientific topics, yet not in studies that used only narrative texts.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Pan joined European and Chinese artistic traditions to develop her own approach to painting.
Pan gave up oil painting in favor of ink painting after she completed her studies in Europe.
Pan was the most widely praised Chinese painter working in Europe during her lifetime.
Pan learned the techniques of Chinese ink painting while studying at academies in Lyon and Rome.
questions.rationale: The text says that Pan “did not simply adopt European methods”: her training gave her “command of oil paint and anatomical accuracy,” while “Chinese ink painting shaped her emphasis on line, contour, and brushwork.” Critics also praised her for “incorporating Chinese ink techniques into Western styles.” Choice A sums up this blend.
reasons: The text says she made ink paintings “alongside her oils,” not that she gave up oil painting.
Critics praised her, but the text never ranks her above other Chinese painters in Europe.
The text links her European academies to oil painting and figure drawing; it does not say she learned Chinese ink painting there.
questions.text: Pan Yuliang, one of the first Chinese women to paint in the Western style, studied oil painting and figure drawing at academies in Shanghai, Lyon, Paris, and Rome. Yet she did not simply adopt European methods. Her academic training gave her command of oil paint and anatomical accuracy, while Chinese ink painting shaped her emphasis on line, contour, and brushwork. She produced hundreds of ink paintings alongside her oils, and critics praised her for incorporating Chinese ink techniques into Western styles.

questions.stem: Which quotation from a work by an art historian would be the most effective evidence for the curator to include in support of this claim?
choices: “In addition to painting, Nguyễn Gia Trí drew cartoons for Hanoi magazines during the 1930s, many of which mocked or criticized French colonial rule in Vietnam.”
“Nguyễn Gia Trí built up his pictures in many thin coats of lacquer, a Vietnamese craft method, and used the layers to create depth as European painters did.”

Choice B says he built his paintings from many coats of lacquer, a long-standing Vietnamese craft method, and used those layers to create depth as in European painting, so it names a technique from each tradition.
reasons: His political cartoons say nothing about the techniques in his lacquer paintings.
What the paintings show does not reveal which artistic techniques he used.
The museum that holds his works says nothing about how they were made.
questions.text: Lacquer, a glossy coating derived from tree sap, had traditionally been used in Vietnam as a decorative finish for objects. In the 1930s, painter Nguyễn Gia Trí, who studied at the École des Beaux-Arts de l’Indochine in Hanoi, became one of the first artists to master lacquer as a medium for paintings. In a statement accompanying a new exhibition, a museum curator claims that Nguyễn Gia Trí’s lacquer paintings combine techniques from Vietnamese and European artistic traditions.

rhinos with oxpeckers detected the researchers at an average distance of 27 meters, more than twice the distance at which rhinos without oxpeckers detected them.
rhinos with oxpeckers detected the researchers in every approach, at an average of 61 meters, compared with 23% of approaches, at 27 meters, for rhinos without them.
rhinos with and without oxpeckers detected the researchers at similar distances, although rhinos with oxpeckers detected the researchers in more of the approaches.

questions.text: Black rhinoceroses have poor eyesight and are typically solitary, lacking a herd to watch for predators. Red-billed oxpeckers, birds that ride on rhinos and feed on the ticks embedded in their skin, produce a loud alarm call whenever humans approach; in Swahili, the bird is called askari wa kifaru, “the rhino’s guard.” To determine whether the birds genuinely protect rhinos, Roan Plotz and Wayne Linklater repeatedly approached rhinos on foot in South Africa’s Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park. The birds’ presence made a considerable difference: ______
questions.table_title: Black Rhinos’ Detection of Researchers Approaching on Foot

questions.skill: Data completion: two thresholds stated in the passage applied to the table (above one boundary, below the other)
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Robert White’s 1962 flight, which reached 314,750 feet, higher than the boundary the Air Force used but lower than the boundary used for aviation records.
Joseph Walker’s August 1963 flight, which reached 354,200 feet, higher than the boundary the Air Force used but lower than the boundary used for aviation records.
Joe Engle’s 1965 flight, which reached 266,500 feet, lower than the boundary the Air Force used but higher than the boundary used for aviation records.
William Dana’s 1966 flight, which reached 306,900 feet, higher than both the boundary the Air Force used and the boundary used for aviation records.
questions.rationale: A flight reached space by only one standard if it climbed above 264,000 feet but stayed below about 328,000 feet. Robert White’s 1962 flight reached 314,750 feet, which falls between the two boundaries, and Choice A describes it correctly.

questions.text: Between 1962 and 1968, pilots of the X-15, an experimental rocket-powered aircraft operated jointly by NASA and the US Air Force, exceeded an altitude of 50 miles, or 264,000 feet, on thirteen occasions. The Air Force designated 50 miles as the boundary of space and awarded astronaut wings to its pilots who surpassed it. The Fédération Aéronautique Internationale, which certifies aviation records, instead places the boundary at 100 kilometers, or approximately 328,000 feet, so a flight could qualify as reaching space according to one standard but not the other, as was the case with ______
questions.table_title: Peak Altitudes of Five X-15 Flights

questions.skill: T6 function of a behavior, from a perception experiment
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: make an approaching animal stop farther from the snake than it otherwise would.
convince an approaching animal that the snake is larger than it actually is.
signal that the snake is about to strike, regardless of how far away the intruder is.
make the rattle audible to animals that are still too far away to hear the slower rattling.
questions.rationale: When the rate jumped, listeners believed the snake was closer than it really was. An animal that thinks it is already near the snake would halt sooner, leaving more distance between them, so the switch likely serves to keep intruders farther away, as A says.
reasons: Participants misjudged how far away the snake was, not how big it was.
The switch comes as the intruder gets close and changes how near the snake seems; the text gives no sign that it announces a strike, let alone at any distance.
The high rate begins only after the intruder has come close; animals still far away hear the slower rattling, so the switch is not aimed at them.
questions.text: As a large animal approaches, a rattlesnake shakes its rattle progressively faster until, at a certain point, it abruptly switches to a considerably higher rate of roughly 60 to 100 shakes per second. To investigate how human listeners perceive this escalating display, neurobiologist Boris Chagnaud and his colleagues moved participants through a virtual grassland toward a concealed snake whose rattling followed the same pattern; when the rate suddenly jumped, participants judged the snake to be nearer than it actually was. This observation suggests that the abrupt switch most likely serves to ______

questions.rationale: “The hinged lip of the hammer orchid ... looks and smells like a female thynnid wasp” and “males attempting to carry it away are swung against the flower’s reproductive structures” are both independent clauses. A comma plus “and” correctly joins them.
reasons: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.
A comma is needed before “and” when it joins two independent clauses like these.
A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.
questions.text: The hinged lip of the hammer orchid, native to Western Australia, looks and smells like a female thynnid ______ males attempting to carry it away are swung against the flower’s reproductive structures.

questions.skill: Closing dash of a pair around an appositive between subject and verb
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

patterns
patterns;
patterns—
questions.rationale: The dash after “jarana” opens a supplementary element that describes the instrument. A second dash after “patterns” closes it, so the subject “the jarana” connects to its verb, “is joined.”
reasons: The element was opened with a dash, so it must be closed with a dash; a comma does not pair with a dash.
Without a closing dash, the description of the jarana runs straight into the verb “is joined.”
A semicolon would cut the subject “the jarana” off from its verb “is joined,” leaving neither side a complete clause.
questions.text: Son jarocho, a musical tradition from the Mexican state of Veracruz, is performed at community celebrations called fandangos. There, the jarana—a small, eight-string guitar strummed in rapid, syncopated ______ is joined by a harp and by dancers whose footwork on a wooden platform adds a percussive layer.

questions.skill: Joining two independent clauses: period before a Because-clause opener
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: sun, because
sun because
sun that, because
sun. Because
questions.rationale: “Unlike conventional white paint ... under a midday sun” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the dependent clause “Because the paint reflects ... infrared light,” and its main clause is “a coated surface can remain cooler than the surrounding air.” A period is needed between the two sentences.
reasons: The “because” clause seems to explain the first clause, but “a coated surface can remain cooler” is a second independent clause, so the sentence joins two independent clauses with only a comma.
Without punctuation the “because” clause attaches to the first clause, and the comma after “light” then joins “a coated surface can remain cooler ...” to it, a comma splice.
“That” starts a relative clause that never gets a verb of its own, so the sentence breaks down; it also leaves the two main clauses joined with only a comma.
questions.text: Unlike conventional white paint, which reflects only 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight, the paint that engineer Xiulin Ruan and his colleagues unveiled in 2021 stays cool even under a midday ______ the paint reflects roughly 98 percent of sunlight while radiating heat as infrared light, a coated surface can remain cooler than the surrounding air.

novels most vivid scene’s
novels’ most vivid scenes
novel’s most vivid scene’s
questions.rationale: The scenes belong to one novel, Bygone Days, so the singular possessive “novel’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the scenes, and the passage refers to many of them, so “scenes” is a plain plural.
reasons: “Novels” is a plain plural rather than a possessive, and “scene’s” is a singular possessive where a plain plural is needed.
“Novels’” is a plural possessive, but the scenes belong to a single novel.
“Scene’s” is a singular possessive, but nothing belongs to the scenes and there are many of them.
questions.text: Abdulla Qodiriy’s Bygone Days, serialized in the early 1920s, is widely considered the first modern Uzbek novel. Set in the 1840s, it chronicles a young Tashkent merchant’s doomed marriage to a woman from Margilan, and many of the ______ unfold in the streets and bazaars of Tashkent, the author’s birthplace.

questions.skill: Specification: the more common case (more often)
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

that said,
more often,
in addition,
questions.rationale: Ogburn and Thomas argued that once the needed knowledge existed, an invention was unlikely to occur to just one person. The clause after the blank gives what usually happened instead: several people reached the same idea at about the same time. “More often” introduces this more common case.
reasons: An idea being unlikely to occur to only one person does not cause several people to reach it; the second clause states the usual case, not a result of the first.
The clause after the blank does not qualify or limit Ogburn and Thomas’s claim; it spells out the common pattern that supports it.
The clause is not a separate, further point; it describes the usual case that is the other side of “unlikely to occur to only one person.”
questions.text: Popular histories often credit each major invention to a lone genius. In a 1922 paper, however, sociologists William Ogburn and Dorothy Thomas argued that once the necessary knowledge existed, a new idea was unlikely to occur to only one person; ______ several people reached it independently at about the same time, and the pair listed 148 such cases, including calculus and the telephone.

After World War II, Australian physicist Ruby Payne-Scott turned to studying radio waves emitted by the Sun.

reasons: It describes her radar work during the war, which the notes do not present as unique.
It gives a contribution she made but does not show what was unique about her place in astronomy.
It says what she studied after the war, not what made her position in the field unique.

Researchers found that native tree seedlings grew approximately one-third less in soil from beneath tree of heaven stands than in other soil, possibly because of a compound from the tree’s decomposing leaves.
To study allelopathy, in which plants release chemicals that inhibit the growth of neighboring plants, researchers grew native tree seedlings in soil from beneath the tree of heaven.

questions.text: While a female Eurasian hoopoe is incubating her eggs, a gland near the base of her tail produces a secretion that smells like rotting meat, which she rubs into her plumage. Because this odor is thought to discourage predators and parasites, the substance may help ______ the nest and the vulnerable nestlings inside it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: amplify
offset
outpace
dictate
questions.rationale: The second sentence shows the trade-off: languages with information-light syllables are spoken faster, and all seventeen end up conveying information at about the same rate. Faster speech makes up for less information per syllable, so speech rate tends to offset differences in information density.
reasons: If speech rate amplified the differences, information-dense languages would also be the fast ones and their rates would pull further apart, but the text says the light languages are faster and the rates come out about equal.
“Outpace” suits a text about speed, but the point is not that speech rate moves faster than differences in density; it is that the two balance each other.
The text reports that speech rate and information density trade off, not that speech rate determines how much information a language packs into its syllables.
questions.text: Vietnamese packs considerably more information into an average syllable than Basque does, yet when linguist Christophe Coupé and colleagues compared recordings of speakers of seventeen languages, they found that speech rate tends to ______ such differences in information density. questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: a substitute for
a constraint on
a spur to
a symptom of
questions.rationale: A spur to something is an incentive that drives it on. Copyright arrived in Lombardy and Venetia under French rule, and afterward the two states’ production of new operas rose far faster than elsewhere in Italy, so the protection encouraged composers’ work. Because later extensions brought no further gains, the text credits basic protection, not longer terms, with that effect.
reasons: Nothing in the text suggests that copyright took the place of creative work; the law and a rise in new operas went together.
A constraint on creativity would hold it back, but opera output rose faster after the law was adopted, not more slowly.
A symptom of creativity would be a result of it. The law came with French rule, and the rise in new operas followed it, so the protection preceded the creativity rather than reflecting it.
questions.text: Economists Michela Giorcelli and Petra Moser found that after Lombardy and Venetia adopted copyright law in 1801 under French rule, the two states’ output of new operas rose far faster than that of other Italian states. Since later extensions of copyright terms brought no comparable gains, basic protection, not its prolongation, appears to have been ______ creativity.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why a group of artists chose to model its posters on the ones once used to recruit military pilots
To trace how an artists’ collective formed, how it got its name, and what it went on to create
To argue that a collective’s sense of humor weakened the political message of its art
To compare the posters made by one collective with murals made by other artists in California
questions.rationale: The text says when, where, and why the collective formed, explains how a confusion over its initials led the artists to rename it the Royal Chicano Air Force, and then describes its later work: murals, posters, and a community arts center. Choice B covers all three parts: the group’s origins, its name, and its work.

The text presents the group’s humor neutrally and makes no judgment about its political message.

questions.text: In 1969 a group of Chicano artists in Sacramento, California, among them José Montoya and Esteban Villa, formed a collective to support the farmworkers’ labor movement and to bring art to Mexican American neighborhoods. They called themselves the Rebel Chicano Art Front, but because people repeatedly mistook the initials RCAF for those of the Royal Canadian Air Force, the artists good-humoredly renamed the group the Royal Chicano Air Force. Its members subsequently produced murals and silkscreen posters, many decorated with old-fashioned biplanes, and in 1972 they established a community arts center in Sacramento.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
choices: Jacquet de La Guerre probably modeled Céphale et Procris on the opera that Caccini wrote for the Medici court.
Another woman had composed an opera roughly seventy years before Céphale et Procris was staged.
Women composers found greater acceptance at the Medici court than they did at the court of Louis XIV.
Céphale et Procris was the first opera by a woman to be performed outside its composer’s home country.
questions.rationale: Text 1 claims that Jacquet de La Guerre became the first woman to compose an opera when Céphale et Procris was staged in 1694. Text 2 describes an opera by Francesca Caccini that was performed for the Medici court in 1625, about seventy years earlier. The author of Text 2 would therefore point out that a woman had composed an opera long before Jacquet de La Guerre did.
reasons: Neither text suggests that Jacquet de La Guerre knew Caccini’s opera or modeled her work on it.
Neither text compares how the two courts treated women composers; both women were employed or celebrated at court.
It was Caccini’s opera that was performed again abroad, in Warsaw; Céphale et Procris was staged in Paris, in its composer’s own country.
questions.text:
Text 1

Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre was celebrated as a harpsichordist at the court of Louis XIV, where she had performed since childhood. In 1694 the Paris Opéra presented her Céphale et Procris, a five-act tragedy set to music. Although the production was unsuccessful, it secured her a permanent place in music history: <u>with Céphale et Procris, Jacquet de La Guerre became the first woman to compose an opera</u>.

Text 2

In February 1625, the Medici court in Florence entertained the visiting Polish prince Władysław with an opera, La liberazione di Ruggiero dall’isola d’Alcina, in which a knight is liberated from a sorceress’s enchanted island. Its composer, Francesca Caccini, was a singer and instrumentalist employed by the Medici family. The prince was evidently impressed: he arranged for the opera to be performed again in Warsaw in 1628.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The narrator is hurt to discover that his cat would rather spend time with the housekeeper than with him.
The narrator’s cat becomes frightened as the narrator’s voice grows louder and harsher.
The narrator imagines that his cat, though pleased at first, comes to find his speech pointless compared with the housekeeper’s practical words.
The narrator realizes that the housekeeper’s strict manner has made his cat impatient with any kind of talk.
questions.rationale: At first the speech “pleased Hamilcar,” but as the narrator grows louder the cat signals “that it was bad taste on my part so to declaim.” The narrator then imagines the cat thinking that he “talks to no purpose at all,” while the housekeeper’s words are “full of good sense” because they announce a meal or a whipping. Choice C states this main idea.
reasons: The cat’s imagined comparison concerns the way the two people speak, not whose company it prefers, and nothing suggests the narrator is hurt.
The cat lowers its ears to show the narrator that his loud speech is in “bad taste,” not out of fear, and the voice is described as louder, not harsher.
The cat values the housekeeper’s words because they are “full of significance”; the text never says her manner made it dislike talk.
questions.text:
The following text is from Anatole France’s 1881 novel The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard (translated by Lafcadio Hearn in 1890). The narrator, an elderly scholar, has been delivering an elaborate speech to his cat, Hamilcar.

The beginning of this discourse pleased Hamilcar, who accompanied it with a throat-sound like the song of a kettle on the fire. But as my voice waxed louder, Hamilcar notified me by lowering his ears and by wrinkling the striped skin of his brow that it was bad taste on my part so to declaim.

“This old-book man,” evidently thought Hamilcar, “talks to no purpose at all, while our housekeeper never utters a word which is not full of good sense, full of significance—containing either the announcement of a meal or the promise of a whipping. One knows what she says. But this old man puts together a lot of sounds signifying nothing.”

questions.skill: Data completion (two comparisons between two rows, full factorial options)
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the comparison?
choices: earlier and is larger.
earlier but is smaller.
later but is larger.
later and is smaller.
questions.rationale: Pallas was discovered in 1802, five years before Vesta (1807), and its average diameter of 511 kilometers is smaller than Vesta’s 525 kilometers. Choice B states both comparisons correctly.
reasons: Pallas was discovered earlier, but it is smaller than Vesta, not larger.
Pallas was discovered earlier than Vesta and is smaller.
Pallas is smaller, but it was discovered in 1802, earlier than Vesta.
questions.text: The first asteroids were discovered in the early 1800s, when astronomers searching the region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter spotted several faint objects moving against the background stars. The largest, Ceres, now classified as a dwarf planet, was found in 1801, and others soon followed. Comparing two of the largest asteroids in the table, a student notes that compared with Vesta, Pallas was discovered ______
questions.table_title: Four of the Largest Bodies in the Asteroid Belt

questions.skill: Quotation from an art historian supports a two-part claim (abstract appearance, observed source)
questions.stem: Which quotation from an art historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
choices: “Even the glacier canvases that read as pure arrangements of shape and color began with what Barns-Graham saw at Grindelwald: the fractured ice, its crystalline edges, and the light passing through it.”
“In 1950 the British Council bought Barns-Graham’s painting Upper Glacier, her largest sale up to that time, and the work soon appeared in a book surveying contemporary British art.”
“Barns-Graham’s mature paintings are built from simple geometric shapes and bands of color, arranged across the canvas with an almost mathematical sense of balance.”
“When she first settled in St Ives in 1940, Barns-Graham took the town’s harbor and the surrounding Cornish landscape as the main subjects of her paintings.”
questions.rationale: The student claims that the glacier paintings “appear almost entirely abstract” yet “originated in her firsthand observation of the ice.” Choice A covers both parts: it describes the canvases as reading like “pure arrangements of shape and color” and traces them to what Barns-Graham “saw at Grindelwald.”
reasons: The sale and publication of Upper Glacier show how the work was received, not where its forms came from.
This describes the abstract look of her paintings but says nothing about their origin in what she saw at the glacier.
This shows that Barns-Graham painted places she knew, but it concerns her earlier harbor and landscape paintings, not her abstract glacier works.
questions.text: Scottish painter Wilhelmina Barns-Graham (1912–2004) belonged to the community of modernist artists working in St Ives, Cornwall, during the mid-twentieth century. In 1949 she visited the Grindelwald Glacier in Switzerland, and glaciers became a subject she returned to for decades. In an essay, a student claims that although Barns-Graham’s glacier paintings appear almost entirely abstract, they originated in her firsthand observation of the ice.

questions.skill: Data completion: each treatment against the control in every period
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: both of the coated houses were cooler than the bare-metal house during the evening, the hours when residents typically decide whether to sleep under a bed net that night.
the white-roofed house was cooler than the red-roofed house in each of the three periods shown in the table.
the red-roofed house was cooler than the bare-metal house during the day but warmer than the bare-metal house at night.
the white-roofed house was cooler than the bare-metal house in all three periods, but the red-roofed house was not cooler than the bare-metal house during the day.
questions.rationale: The conclusion compares each coating with the bare-metal roof and says only one kept the house cooler at all times. The white-roofed house was cooler than the bare-metal house in the evening (29.8 °C against 31.5 °C), at night (27.8 °C against 29.4 °C), and during the day (a maximum of 33.1 °C against 34.0 °C), while the red-roofed house was not cooler during the day (34.4 °C against 34.0 °C). Choice D states both halves.
reasons: It is true that both painted houses were cooler in the evening, but this covers only one period and does not show that just one paint kept the house cooler at all times.
The conclusion compares each coating with the bare-metal roof; comparing the two coatings with each other does not show whether either was cooler than bare metal at every time of day.
The table shows the opposite: the red-roofed house was cooler than the bare-metal house at night (28.4 °C against 29.4 °C) but not during the day.
questions.text: In rural Gambia, thatched roofs are increasingly being replaced by metal roofs, which can make houses so uncomfortably hot at night that residents are less likely to sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets. To evaluate an inexpensive remedy, Majo Carrasco-Tenezaca, Steve Lindsay, and colleagues constructed two identical experimental houses with metal roofs and monitored indoor temperatures during the malaria season while the roofs were left bare, coated with a red primer, or painted white. Comparing each coated roof with the bare-metal roof, the researchers concluded that only one of the two coatings kept the house cooler throughout the day and night: ______
questions.table_title: Indoor Temperature (°C) of Experimental Houses in Gambia, by Roof Type

questions.skill: T2 belief: a company’s choice of performers reveals what it knew about its recordings
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: wanted audiences to notice the moments when the singer fell silent and the recording continued alone.
recognized that its recordings did not fully reproduce the natural sound of a singer’s voice.
dimmed the lights mainly to conceal how much louder the phonograph was than the singer.
expected singers who could imitate their recordings to sell more records than other singers would.
questions.rationale: The recitals were meant to leave audiences unsure “whether they had been listening to a person or to a machine,” and Edison chose singers for “their ability to imitate the sound of their own recordings.” If the recordings had matched a natural voice, no imitation would have been needed; choosing singers who could sound like the record suggests the company knew its recordings differed from a singer’s unaltered voice.
reasons: The tests were built so the audience could not tell singer from machine; the singer even left “unobserved,” so noticing the switch was what the company hoped to avoid.
The lights were dimmed “so the singer could depart unobserved”; the text says nothing about the phonograph being louder than the singer.
The text never discusses record sales by different singers; the singers were chosen to make the comparison with the recordings succeed.
questions.text: Between 1915 and 1925, the Thomas A. Edison company staged public recitals called tone tests, in which a singer performed alongside a phonograph playing the company’s Diamond Disc recording of that same singer. Periodically the singer would fall silent while the recording continued, and at the conclusion the lights were dimmed so the singer could depart unobserved, leaving audiences to determine whether they had been listening to a person or to a machine. Edison selected singers partly for their ability to imitate the sound of their own recordings, suggesting that the company ______

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: societies that
societies, that
societies
societies,
questions.rationale: The clause “that pooled members’ dues to help pay for medical care, funerals, and other needs” is a restrictive clause that tells what kind of societies the mutualistas were. It needs the relative pronoun “that,” and no comma separates a noun from a restrictive clause.
reasons: A comma can’t separate “societies” from the restrictive clause beginning with “that.”
Without “that,” “mutual aid societies pooled members’ dues ...” becomes a second main clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

Without “that,” the commas set off “mutual aid societies” as an appositive, so the predicates “formed mutualistas” and “pooled members’ dues ...” are stacked with no conjunction joining them, and the sentence is not grammatical.
questions.text: Before government programs such as Social Security existed, many working families relied on community groups in times of hardship. In the late 1800s, Mexican American communities in the Southwest formed mutualistas, mutual aid ______ pooled members’ dues to help pay for medical care, funerals, and other needs.

questions.skill: Semicolon before a conjunctive adverb that opens clause 2
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: time; however,
time, however;
time however,
time, however,
questions.rationale: The semicolon joins two independent clauses, and “however” begins the second one. It signals the contrast between librarians’ assumption that fines encouraged returns and what happened in Chicago when fines were dropped.
reasons: Placing “however” at the end of the first clause signals that the librarians’ assumption contrasts with the previous sentence, but it simply explains why libraries charged fines.
Nothing marks the boundary between the two independent clauses before “however.”
Commas around “however” cannot join two independent clauses.
questions.text: For decades, most public libraries in the United States charged fines for overdue books. Librarians generally assumed that the fines encouraged borrowers to return items on ______ after Chicago’s public library system eliminated late fines in 2019, the number of long-overdue items that borrowers brought back rose sharply within a few weeks.

questions.skill: Colon between independent clauses; the second, opening with “whereas,” explains the first
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: tunings:
tunings,
tunings
tunings and
questions.rationale: “A complete gamelan contains two sets of instruments built to different tunings” is an independent clause, and so is “pelog divides it into seven unequal ones” (the whereas-clause depends on it). The second explains the first by describing the two tunings, so a colon correctly joins them.
reasons: The whereas-clause makes the second part look dependent, but its main clause is “pelog divides it into seven unequal ones,” so a comma alone would join two independent clauses.
The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation.
“And” without a comma does not properly join two long independent clauses, and it presents the description of the tunings as an added fact rather than as the explanation of “different tunings.”
questions.text: Traditional gamelan ensembles of Java consist mainly of bronze gongs and metallophones played with mallets. A complete gamelan contains two sets of instruments built to different ______ whereas slendro divides the octave into five roughly equal intervals, pelog divides it into seven unequal ones.

questions.skill: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun with a singular antecedent a sentence back, plural rivals between
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: it
they
those
one
questions.rationale: The pronoun must refer to the thing that shields the sleeping fish: the singular noun “cocoon” in the first sentence. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with “cocoon.”
reasons: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “cocoon”; the plural nouns nearby, such as “isopods” and “researchers,” can’t be what shields the fish.
The plural demonstrative “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “cocoon.”
“One” would refer to an unspecified person or thing, not back to the cocoon the passage describes.
questions.text: At dusk, many parrotfish species spend up to an hour enclosing themselves in a cocoon of mucus secreted by glands in their gills. Blood-feeding parasites called gnathiid isopods attack reef fishes at night, and researchers in Australia found that ______ can shield sleeping parrotfish from these pests.

questions.skill: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener, passage-final clause
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: a black metaltail’s torpor produced a body temperature of 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
a black metaltail registered a body temperature of 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
it was a black metaltail that registered a body temperature of 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
a black metaltail’s body temperature reached 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
questions.rationale: The opening phrase says something fell below “that of an active hummingbird,” so the noun it describes must be the same kind of thing a hummingbird has, here a body temperature. Choice D places “a black metaltail’s body temperature” right after the phrase, so the sentence says the bird’s body temperature fell more than 30 degrees below the body temperature of an active hummingbird. In every other choice, “that” has nothing to stand for.
reasons: The head of “a black metaltail’s torpor” is “torpor,” a state, so the sentence illogically says the torpor fell below that (the torpor) of an active hummingbird.

“A black metaltail” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the bird itself fell below “that of an active hummingbird”; a bird cannot be compared with a hummingbird’s body temperature, so “that” has nothing to stand for.
The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.
questions.text: Hummingbirds inhabiting the high Andes endure frigid nights by entering torpor, a hibernation-like state of drastically reduced metabolic activity. After falling more than 30 degrees below that of an active hummingbird during one such episode in 2020, ______

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Likewise,
As a result,
For instance,
Previously,
questions.rationale: The first two sentences describe Herrera’s success beginning in 2004. The last describes the long period before that, when she worked in obscurity. “Previously” signals that the last sentence describes an earlier time.
reasons: Decades of obscurity are not similar to the acclaim described in the second sentence.
Her late success did not cause the obscurity, which came first.
Working in obscurity is not an example of selling paintings and drawing acclaim.
questions.text: In 2004, Cuban American painter Carmen Herrera, then 89, sold a canvas for the first time. Within a few years, her crisp, hard-edged geometric abstractions were attracting international acclaim. ______ she had labored for roughly six decades in near obscurity, exhibiting infrequently and receiving scant attention from dealers or critics.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Ultimately,
Similarly,
Thus,
Moreover,
questions.rationale: The first two sentences describe a long period in which Takemitsu kept Japanese instruments out of his music and modeled his work on French composers. The blank sentence gives where that path finally led: a 1967 work that brings the two musical worlds together, setting two Japanese instruments against a Western orchestra. “Ultimately” signals the eventual outcome of a long development.
reasons: Writing for the biwa and shakuhachi is not like looking to French composers or keeping Japanese instruments out of his music; it is a change in direction.

Keeping Japanese instruments out of his music did not cause Takemitsu to bring them into November Steps; the 1967 work reverses that long avoidance. It is where his development finally led, not a result that follows from the earlier sentences.
“Moreover” would add a further point of the same kind about his avoidance of Japanese music, but writing for Japanese instruments is the opposite of keeping them out of his work.
questions.text: For years after World War II, Japanese composer Tōru Takemitsu kept traditional Japanese instruments out of his music, linking their sounds to the militarism of the war years. He looked instead to French composers such as Claude Debussy. ______ in November Steps (1967), Takemitsu brought the two musical worlds together, setting the Japanese biwa and shakuhachi against a full Western orchestra.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the mudpuppy and the greater siren. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The mudpuppy has four legs, while the greater siren has only two small front legs.
The greater siren keeps its feathery external gills throughout its life.
Salamanders typically lose their gills during metamorphosis into adults.
Unlike most salamanders, the mudpuppy and the greater siren both keep their feathery external gills throughout their lives.
questions.rationale: The goal is a similarity. Each animal “keeps its feathery external gills throughout its life,” and Choice D states this shared trait with “both.”
reasons: It contrasts the two animals’ legs rather than stating something they share.
It describes only the greater siren, so no similarity is stated.
It describes salamanders in general without mentioning either animal.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Salamanders typically lose their gills during metamorphosis into adults.
• The mudpuppy, which has four legs, lives in lakes and rivers of eastern North America.
• It keeps its feathery external gills throughout its life.
• The greater siren, which has only two small front legs, lives in swamps of the southeastern United States.
• It, too, keeps its feathery external gills throughout its life.

questions.skill: Describe a work to an audience unfamiliar with its author
questions.stem: The student wants to describe the Compendium of the Languages of the Turks to an audience unfamiliar with Mahmud al-Kashgari. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Al-Kashgari’s Compendium of the Languages of the Turks, written in Arabic, explained Turkic vocabulary and includes a circular map of the world.
Written by Mahmud al-Kashgari, an eleventh-century scholar from Kashgar, the Compendium of the Languages of the Turks explained Turkic vocabulary to Arabic-speaking readers.
Mahmud al-Kashgari, a scholar from the city of Kashgar in present-day western China, lived and worked during the eleventh century.
The only surviving manuscript of the Compendium of the Languages of the Turks, copied in 1266, is preserved in a library in Istanbul.
questions.rationale: An audience that does not know al-Kashgari needs to be told who he was before the book is described. Choice B identifies him as an eleventh-century scholar from Kashgar and then says what the book did: it explained Turkic vocabulary to Arabic-speaking readers.
reasons: It describes the book but uses al-Kashgari’s name without saying who he was, which an unfamiliar audience would need.
It identifies al-Kashgari but says nothing about the Compendium itself.
It tells where the surviving copy is kept; it does not describe the book or identify its author.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mahmud al-Kashgari was an eleventh-century scholar from Kashgar, a city in present-day western China.
• He completed his Compendium of the Languages of the Turks in Baghdad around 1074.
• Written in Arabic, the book explained Turkic vocabulary and grammar to Arabic-speaking readers.
• It also contains a circular map depicting the world as its author understood it.
• The only surviving manuscript, copied in 1266, is preserved in a library in Istanbul.

questions.stem: The student wants to describe how a salt glaze forms on a pot. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Potters heat unglazed vessels to about 1,200°C and then add ordinary salt to the kiln, where the salt melts and spreads over the clay to form a thin glassy coating.
When salt is introduced into a kiln heated to about 1,200°C, silica from the salt vapor combines with sodium in the clay to form a thin glassy coating.
Salt introduced into a kiln at about 1,200°C turns to vapor, and its sodium bonds with silica on the vessels’ surfaces, producing a thin glassy coating.
Salt-glazed stoneware is fired at about 1,200°C and frequently has a thin glassy coating with a pitted texture that resembles orange peel.
questions.rationale: The goal is to describe how the glaze forms, so the sentence must follow the process in the notes: salt is added to the hot kiln, “The salt vaporizes, and sodium from the vapor combines with silica in the clay’s surface,” producing the glassy coating. Choice C traces those steps with each substance in its right role.
reasons: It gets the order of steps right, but the notes say “The salt vaporizes, and sodium from the vapor combines with silica in the clay’s surface”; the salt does not melt and spread over the clay.
It follows the right steps but swaps the substances: the sodium comes from the salt vapor and the silica from the clay.
It gives the firing temperature and what the finished coating looks like, but it never says what the salt does, so it does not describe how the glaze forms.
questions.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Salt glazing gives stoneware a glassy surface during firing rather than beforehand.
• Potters stack unglazed vessels inside a kiln and heat them to about 1,200°C.
• At that temperature, they introduce ordinary salt through small openings in the kiln’s walls.
• The salt vaporizes, and sodium from the vapor combines with silica in the clay’s surface.
• This reaction produces a thin glassy coating, frequently with a pitted texture resembling orange peel.
